title: How to read dog play, and when to interrupt it
summary: Good play is bouncy, lopsided on purpose, and full of pauses. Here is what to watch for, and the four-second test that answers whether both dogs are still enjoying it.
content:
Two dogs meet, and within thirty seconds you are watching something loud, fast and full of teeth. Is that play or is that a fight starting? Most owners guess from volume, which is the one signal that tells you almost nothing. A rowdy, growling, body-slamming wrestle between two dogs who like each other looks and sounds alarming. A quiet, still, staring standoff looks like nothing at all and is far more likely to end badly.

Here is what to actually look at.

Play is exaggerated and inefficient.

Real play movement is bouncy and over-the-top. Dogs bounce sideways, they take a long route to get somewhere, they fling themselves around. Nothing about it is economical. Predatory or aggressive behaviour is the opposite: direct, efficient, low, quiet. If you find yourself thinking that a dog looks businesslike, that is the moment to step in.

The play bow is punctuation, not just an opening line.

Front end down, back end up. Most owners know it as an invitation. It is also used mid-play, as a reset — a way of saying that everything that just happened was still a game. Research on dog and wolf puppies found play bows clustered around moments of self-handicapping, where the stronger partner had just given up an advantage.

Watch for self-handicapping.

The bigger, faster, stronger dog deliberately making itself vulnerable is one of the best signs you will see. The Labrador rolling onto its back so the terrier can get on top. The adult letting a puppy win. The fast dog running at half speed. That is a dog managing the game so the other one stays in it.

Watch for role reversals.

Chaser becomes chased. The dog on top ends up underneath. If one dog is always on top, always chasing, always the one initiating contact, the game has stopped being mutual even if nobody has snapped.

Watch for pauses.

Healthy play has natural lulls. Both dogs stop, shake off, reset, and go again. Continuous escalation with no breaks is where trouble builds. If they are not pausing on their own, make them pause.

The four-second test.

This is the one thing to take away. When you are not sure whether both dogs are enjoying it, calmly take hold of one dog's collar and hold them back for about four seconds. Then let go.

If the other dog immediately re-invites — bounces in, play bows, circles back — and the held dog goes straight back to the game, they were both having fun. Carry on.

If the released dog goes back in but the other one moves away, tries to leave, hides behind a person, or starts sniffing the ground very intently, then one dog was playing and one was coping. Stop the game.

If the released dog does not go back at all, it is over. That dog has told you.

The consent test costs four seconds and it is the only way to check something you cannot see from the outside, which is whether both animals want this.

Signs it is time to intervene.

Stop the interaction, calmly and without shouting, if you see any of these:

One dog is repeatedly pinned and cannot get up, or keeps trying to leave and is followed.

Play has gone silent and still. A freeze that lasts more than a beat is a decision being made.

A stiff, high, slowly wagging tail on a dog whose whole body has gone rigid. A wagging tail is not the same as a happy dog.

Hard staring, especially a fixed stare from one dog at another who is not looking back.

Piloerection — the raised strip of hair along the spine — combined with stiffness. On its own it just means arousal, which can be excitement.

One dog mounting another repeatedly and ignoring the other's attempts to disengage.

A third dog joining as a pair plays. Groups of three change the maths fast, and a chase with two chasers is a different event to the dog being chased.

How to interrupt without making it worse.

Do not reach into a tangle of dogs, and do not shout. Move in with a cheerful call and walk in the opposite direction; most dogs will follow. If you need to physically separate, take your own dog by the base of the tail or the hind legs and move backwards. Grabbing collars puts both your hands next to two sets of teeth in a high-arousal moment.

Then take a break. A three-minute pause with both dogs doing something calm — sniffing, a few treats scattered in the grass — resets the arousal level so play can start again from a lower baseline. Most conflicts that happen between dogs who like each other happen because arousal climbed with no ceiling.

Play styles differ, and that is where most mismatches come from.

Some dogs body-slam. Some chase. Some wrestle and mouth. Some like to be chased and some very much do not. A dog is not being rude because it plays differently, but two incompatible styles produce a lot of misunderstanding, and the dog on the receiving end is the one who pays for it. If your dog's play style routinely bothers other dogs, that is worth knowing before you arrange a playdate rather than after.

title: What "up to date on shots" actually means
summary: The puppy series runs to at least 16 weeks for a reason, and leptospirosis became a core canine vaccine in 2024. A short guide to what the guidelines say, so you can have the conversation before the playdate rather than after.
content:
Two owners arranging a first meeting will usually ask each other whether the dogs are up to date on their shots. Almost nobody knows what the answer should contain. Here is what the current professional guidelines say, so the question can mean something.

This describes published guidance. Your vet decides what your individual animal needs, and local rabies law overrides everything below.

Dogs: what counts as core.

The American Animal Hospital Association classes a vaccine as core when it is recommended for all dogs regardless of lifestyle, unless there is a specific medical reason not to give it. As of the 2024 update to AAHA's 2022 guidelines, the core canine vaccines are:

Canine distemper virus. Canine adenovirus type 2. Canine parvovirus type 2. Leptospirosis. Rabies.

Leptospirosis is the change worth knowing about. It moved from noncore to core in 2024, following consensus statements from the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine and the World Small Animal Veterinary Association, on the grounds of rising prevalence, improved vaccine safety, and how widely the bacteria are distributed in the environment. ACVIM's recommendation is annual administration to all dogs from twelve weeks of age, regardless of breed. If your dog's protocol was set before 2024, this is worth raising at the next visit.

Rabies is given as a single dose at twelve to sixteen weeks in accordance with local law, with a booster one year later regardless of the formulation or the age at the first dose.

Why sixteen weeks is the line.

Puppies get antibodies from their mother. Those maternal antibodies protect the puppy and also block vaccines from working. They fade at an unpredictable age, somewhere between about six and sixteen weeks, and there is no practical way to know when for a given puppy.

That is why the series is a series. Doses are given every two to four weeks so that whenever the maternal antibody finally drops, a vaccine follows soon after. The final dose is given at sixteen weeks or later because before that you cannot be confident any of them took.

A puppy who finished at twelve weeks has not finished. This is the single most common misunderstanding in this area, and it is the one that puts unprotected puppies in dog parks.

Cats: what counts as core.

Under the 2020 AAHA/AAFP feline guidelines the core vaccines for pet cats are feline herpesvirus-1, feline calicivirus and feline panleukopenia — given together as FVRCP — plus rabies. Feline leukaemia virus is core for cats under one year old.

Rabies is recommended for every cat regardless of lifestyle, indoor-only cats included.

The kitten schedule runs FVRCP from six to eight weeks with boosters every three to four weeks until at least sixteen weeks of age. Rabies is a single dose at twelve to sixteen weeks, a booster at one year, then per the product label. FeLV takes two doses three to four weeks apart from eight weeks, after a negative FeLV test.

Same principle, same sixteen-week line, same reason.

Noncore is not the same as unnecessary.

Noncore vaccines are recommended based on risk, and a dog going to playdates, parks, daycare, boarding or group classes has a different risk profile to a dog who sees no other dogs.

Worth discussing with your vet: Bordetella and canine parainfluenza, for kennel cough; canine influenza; and regionally, Lyme disease. These are exactly the diseases that spread where dogs gather, so "my dog socialises a lot" is the relevant thing to tell your vet.

What to ask before a playdate.

Are they through the full puppy series, or an adult on a current protocol? Are they on year-round parasite prevention? Have they been anywhere with a known outbreak recently? Are they coughing, sneezing, or off their food?

That last one matters more than people expect. A dog incubating kennel cough is contagious before it looks ill, and "he has a bit of a cough but he's fine in himself" is the sentence that spreads it around a neighbourhood.

Parasites belong in the same conversation.

The American Heartworm Society and the FDA recommend all dogs and cats in the US stay on heartworm preventives year-round, with annual testing even for animals on prevention, because prevention can fail and a missed dose matters. Heartworm has now been diagnosed in all fifty states. The 2024 AHS guidelines added routine heartworm screening for cats as well as dogs.

Most monthly heartworm preventives also cover several intestinal worms, which matters because roughly one in five fresh faecal samples collected at US dog parks in one multi-city survey carried worm eggs.

The reasonable position.

Not a demand for paperwork. A short, normal conversation between two people who are about to let their animals share a patch of grass, in which both can say their pets are on a current protocol and neither is unwell today. If someone will not have that conversation, that is information too.

And if there is anything unusual about your animal — a vaccine reaction history, immune-mediated disease, immunosuppressive medication, pregnancy, or an age extreme — the protocol should be individual, and that is a conversation with your own vet rather than a guideline you can look up.

title: The sniffari: why twenty minutes of sniffing beats forty of marching
summary: In a small controlled study, two weeks of daily nosework made dogs measurably more optimistic. Two weeks of heelwork did not. Letting your dog choose the route is a real intervention, not a soft option.
content:
Most dog walks are organised around distance. You leave the house, you go a set way, you come back, and you spend a good part of it asking the dog to stop sniffing and come on.

There is decent evidence that the sniffing is the part that does the dog the most good.

The study.

Duranton and Horowitz ran a small experiment with twenty pet dogs. Ten did daily nosework for two weeks — searching for hidden food, being allowed to use their noses freely. Ten did daily heelwork for two weeks — walking in position, not searching.

Both groups took a cognitive bias test before and after. This is a standard way of measuring something like optimism in animals: the dog learns that a bowl in one place always has food and a bowl in another place never does, and then you put a bowl in an ambiguous middle position and time how fast the dog goes to it. A dog who hurries to the ambiguous bowl is behaving as though it expects good things.

After two weeks, the nosework dogs approached the ambiguous bowl faster than before. The heelwork dogs did not change.

It is a small study — ten dogs per group — and it should be read as a good indication rather than settled fact. But it is the best available evidence for something that costs nothing, needs no equipment, and can be done in a back garden.

Why sniffing might do this.

A dog's olfactory apparatus is an enormous share of what its brain is for. Sniffing is not idle behaviour, it is information processing, and it is one of the few things a dog on a lead gets to decide for itself. There is a reasonable argument that the agency matters as much as the smelling: on a normal walk almost every decision is made by the human.

What a sniffari actually is.

A walk where the dog picks the route and sets the pace, and your job is to hold the other end of the lead and be patient.

Use a long line — fifteen to thirty feet, or five to ten metres — clipped to a well-fitted harness, not a collar. On a collar a dog that hits the end of a long line at speed takes the whole force through its neck.

Go somewhere with things to smell. Rough grass, hedgerows, woodland edges, the scruffy bit behind the car park. Manicured lawns are boring. A patch of long grass where a fox walked last night is a novel.

Do not set a destination. You may cover four hundred metres in half an hour. That is a successful sniffari.

Do not interrupt a sniff. If the dog is nose down and working on something, stand still. It ends when they lift their head.

Thirty minutes is plenty. Many dogs are noticeably tired afterwards in a way an hour of trotting does not achieve.

How to build the same thing indoors.

Scatter feeding. Instead of a bowl, throw the meal across a patch of grass or over a snuffle mat and let them hunt for it. Cheapest enrichment there is.

Find-it games. Have the dog wait, hide a few treats around a room, release them with a cue word. Start easy — visible, on the floor — and get harder as they work out the game.

The muffin tin. Treats in the cups of a muffin tin, tennis balls on top.

Boxes. A cardboard box with some scrunched paper and food in it. The box is disposable and the dog does not care that it was free.

Formal scent work. Many trainers run introductory classes teaching dogs to find a specific target odour. Dogs of any age, any size and almost any physical condition can do it, which is one of the things that makes it useful for old dogs and for dogs who cannot be around other dogs.

Where this helps most.

Dogs on restricted exercise after surgery, who still need to be tired.

Elderly and arthritic dogs who cannot run any more and are bored.

Reactive dogs, who often cannot do a normal walk without a difficult encounter but can do a scent game in the garden every day.

Puppies, who should be doing low-impact, self-directed, varied activity rather than long forced marches.

Dogs who are unmanageable in the evening. A sniffari before dinner beats a longer walk fairly reliably.

It is not a replacement for physical exercise in a fit young dog, and this is not a claim that a Border Collie can be satisfied with a snuffle mat. It is that the sniffing part of a walk is doing more work than most people give it credit for, and that ten of your forty minutes handed back to the dog is a good trade.

title: The five pillars of a cat's home, and the litter box numbers nobody knows
summary: AAFP and ISFM say meeting a cat's environmental needs is essential, not optional. That includes two litter boxes for a single cat, and a box one and a half times the length of the animal.
content:
The American Association of Feline Practitioners and International Cat Care publish guidelines describing five pillars of a healthy feline environment. The guidelines are explicit that addressing environmental needs is essential rather than optional for a cat's wellbeing, and that this applies everywhere a cat lives — home, clinic or shelter.

Most feline behaviour problems people bring to a vet are environmental problems wearing a disguise.

Pillar one: a safe place.

Somewhere the cat can retreat and feel genuinely secure. In practice that means enclosed on several sides, elevated, and inaccessible to dogs, children and other cats.

A cardboard box on a shelf satisfies this better than an expensive open cat bed on the floor. The requirement is not comfort, it is the ability to observe without being approached. In multi-cat homes there must be one per cat, in different places, so the safe place cannot be occupied by somebody else.

Pillar two: multiple, separated key resources.

Food, water, litter, scratching, resting places, play areas. The word doing the work is separated.

A cat that must walk past another cat to reach the litter tray does not, functionally, have a litter tray. Six bowls in a row in the kitchen is one resource station, not six. Resources in different rooms and on different levels mean no single cat can control access to everything, which is the mechanism behind a startling proportion of house-soiling, over-grooming and inter-cat tension.

Here is where the guidelines get specific, and where almost everybody is surprised.

Number of litter boxes: the rule of thumb in multi-cat households is at least one more box than there are cats. And: households with a single cat should have two litter boxes, in two separate locations.

Size: a rectangular box one and a half times the length of the cat from nose to base of tail. In one study, adult cats preferred a box measuring 34 by 15 inches (86 by 39 cm) over a smaller one. Most commercially sold litter trays are considerably smaller than that. A large plastic storage tub is often a better litter box than anything marketed as one.

Litter: fine, sand-like, unscented and clumping, at a depth of at least 1.25 inches (3cm). Avoid liners, slotted grilles and deodorising powders.

Cleaning: remove waste at least once a day; wash the box every one to four weeks.

Placement: do not put food and water next to the box. And cats perceive boxes placed side by side as one large box, so separate them, or set their openings at right angles or around a corner from each other.

One behavioural marker from the guidelines: cats without house-soiling problems dig in the box before eliminating more than house-soiling cats do. A cat who steps in, goes immediately, and leaps out is telling you something about the substrate or the box.

Pillar three: opportunity for play and predatory behaviour.

Not optional entertainment. Predatory behaviour is a behavioural need, and a cat that cannot express it finds other outlets — usually your ankles, or another cat.

Pillar four: positive, consistent, predictable human interaction, on the cat's terms.

Predictable is the key word. Cats do well with interactions they can anticipate and opt out of. The reliable formula is to offer rather than impose: hold out a hand, let the cat come, pet the head and cheeks rather than the belly and the base of the tail, and stop before the cat asks you to.

Pillar five: an environment that respects the cat's sense of smell.

Cats mark their territory with facial pheromones by rubbing. Scrubbing every surface with strongly scented cleaner removes the scent map they built, in a house that then smells like a stranger's.

Practically: unscented or mildly scented cleaning products, do not wash all the bedding at once, do not clean every cat-marked surface at the same time, and be careful with scent-mixing between cats. And be aware that some cleaning products are toxic to cats.

If you fix one thing.

Litter. The guidelines are unusually specific about it, most homes are set up wrong, and inappropriate elimination is the single most common reason cats are surrendered to shelters.

Two boxes for one cat, in different rooms. Big and uncovered. Unscented fine clumping litter, three centimetres deep. Scooped daily. Nowhere near the food.

One important caveat.

Any change in elimination behaviour is a veterinary question before it is a behaviour question. Cystitis, urinary obstruction, kidney disease, diabetes, hyperthyroidism and arthritis all present as litter box problems. A male cat straining to urinate and producing nothing is a life-threatening emergency that needs a vet immediately, not tonight.

Get the medical causes ruled out, then fix the environment.

title: Puppy exercise: the five-minute rule is folklore, the surface is not
summary: Nobody can point to a study behind "five minutes per month of age". What was actually measured: stairs before three months raised hip dysplasia risk, and free off-lead exercise on varied ground lowered it.
content:
Ask about exercising a puppy and you will be told the five-minute rule: five minutes of exercise per month of age, once or twice a day. Fifteen minutes for a three-month-old, thirty for a six-month-old.

It is repeated everywhere, including by people who should know. It cannot be traced to a study. Nobody who cites it can produce the research, because there does not appear to be any.

That does not mean joint development is a myth. It means the rule is the wrong shape.

What was actually measured.

Krontveit and colleagues followed more than five hundred large-breed puppies in Norway — Newfoundlands, Labrador Retrievers, Leonbergers and Irish Wolfhounds — and looked at housing and exercise factors against radiographic hip dysplasia.

Two findings stand out.

Climbing stairs in the first three months of life was associated with an increased risk of hip dysplasia.

Daily off-lead exercise in park-like, moderately rough terrain was associated with a reduced risk. So was being born on a farm, and exercise on soft ground.

Read those together and the conclusion is not "less exercise". It is a different kind of exercise. The puppies who did better were the ones doing more free, varied, self-paced movement on forgiving ground. The risk factor was a specific repetitive, high-load activity performed before the skeleton was ready for it.

Why growth plates matter.

A growing dog's long bones lengthen at the growth plates near each end — areas of cartilage that have not yet turned to bone. They are structurally weaker than mature bone, and they close at different ages in different bones, broadly between about eight months in small dogs and eighteen months or more in giant breeds.

Repeated high-impact loading during that window is the concern: forced repetitive movement, jumping down from height, hard stops and twists, running on hard surfaces at a pace set by a human rather than the dog.

The damage does not announce itself at the time. It shows up years later as joint disease.

What this means in practice.

Free movement is good, and lots of it. A puppy playing in a garden or a field, sniffing, trotting, stopping, lying down, and going again is regulating its own effort. That is the exercise the Norwegian data associated with better outcomes. Do not put a stopwatch on it.

Forced movement is what needs limiting. Jogging or cycling with a puppy at your pace. Long road walks on pavement. Repetitive ball throwing with hard stops and turns. Agility jumps at full height. Long flights of stairs, particularly for a large-breed puppy under three months.

Surface matters more than duration. Grass, forest floor, sand and varied uneven ground are far kinder than concrete and are better for building proprioception and stabilising muscle.

Lift a young large-breed puppy up and down stairs and in and out of the car. This is the concrete takeaway from the study, and it is easy.

Avoid jumping down from height. Out of a car boot, off furniture. Going up is much less loading than coming down.

Slippery floors are worth fixing. Rugs and runners cost little and stop the splaying and scrambling that repeatedly stresses hips and elbows.

Keep the puppy lean. Bodyweight is one of the strongest modifiable factors in hip dysplasia. Restricted-feeding studies in Labradors are among the clearest evidence in the field: leaner dogs developed less hip dysplasia and less osteoarthritis, and lived longer. An overweight puppy is loading immature joints with every step.

Tire the brain instead. A puppy who needs to be exhausted does not need more miles. Scatter feeding, a snuffle mat, short shaping sessions, a stuffed frozen food toy, and a long-line sniffing walk where the puppy sets the pace will all do more than distance and cost the joints nothing.

And the other thing puppies need.

While you are managing the joints, do not lose the window. AVSAB's position is that the first three months is the period when sociability outweighs fear — the primary opportunity for a puppy to adapt to new people, animals and experiences — and that puppies should begin socialisation before the vaccine series is complete, from around seven to eight weeks, after one set of vaccines, provided they are healthy and stay up to date.

AVSAB also states that more deaths in dogs under three are attributable to behavioural problems than to infectious disease.

So the balance is: lots of low-impact, varied, self-directed movement, plenty of controlled exposure to the world in clean and safe places, and very little forced repetitive exercise. Not a stopwatch.

And if you have a large or giant breed, ask your vet about breed-appropriate growth: growth rate, diet formulation and neutering timing all interact with joint development, and the right answer genuinely differs by breed and size.

title: Before the first playdate: how to introduce two dogs
summary: Nose-to-nose on tight leads is the worst possible first meeting. Walk them in parallel on ground neither dog owns, and let the greeting be the last step rather than the first.
content:
The single most common way a dog introduction goes wrong is the version almost everyone does by default: two dogs on short leads, walked straight at each other, meeting head-on while both owners hold the leashes tight and say "be nice".

Almost everything about that is wrong from a dog's point of view.

Dogs greeting each other politely do not approach head-on. They arc, they curve, they approach from the side, they sniff the ground on the way in. A leash prevents all of that. Worse, a taut leash changes a dog's posture — it pulls the head and chest up and forward, which is exactly the shape a confident, pushy dog makes. Two dogs each reading the other as forward and staring, neither able to move away, is a bad situation you have manufactured out of good intentions.

Here is the version that works.

Pick ground neither dog owns.

Not your garden, not their garden, not the pavement outside either house. Somewhere neither dog has marked, patrolled, or claimed. A quiet park, a school field out of hours, a trail. Territory is a real factor and there is no reason to introduce it into the first meeting.

Start further apart than feels necessary.

Thirty feet, about nine metres, is a good starting distance for the first few minutes. Far enough that both dogs can see each other and neither feels pressure. If either dog cannot take food, cannot look away, or is fixated, you are too close. Add distance. Distance is free and it is the only tool that works before the dog is over threshold.

Walk in parallel, same direction.

This is the core of it. Both dogs walk in the same direction, roughly ten to twenty feet apart, with the humans on the inside so the dogs are on the outside edges. You are not trying to get them to meet. You are letting them exist near each other while doing something normal.

Mark and reward calm. Every time a dog glances at the other and then looks away, that gets a quiet "yes" and a treat. You are paying for exactly the behaviour you want: notice, disengage, carry on.

Close the gap slowly.

Three to five feet at a time, and only while both dogs stay loose. Loose means a soft body, a low or neutral tail with a relaxed wag, a mouth that opens, ears that move around, and the ability to take a treat. If either dog stiffens, stops eating, or fixates, go back to the distance where they were fine and stay there longer.

Swap sides. Let each dog walk where the other has been and sniff the ground. Scent is doing a lot of the work here.

Let them sniff each other last, briefly, then move on.

When you finally allow contact, keep leads loose and give it three to five seconds. Then cheerfully call both dogs away and walk on. Ending a greeting early, on a good note, is what makes the next one better. Long first greetings are where things curdle.

Off-lead in a safely fenced space is the goal, once both dogs are relaxed. If you can get to a securely fenced private area — not a public dog park — that is the ideal place for the first real play session, because leads are the thing adding most of the friction.

How long does this take?

Sometimes fifteen minutes. Sometimes it is three separate parallel walks across a week before you let them interact off lead. The dogs decide, not the calendar. If both are relaxed and loose after ten minutes of parallel walking, you are ahead of schedule. If one is not, another walk next week costs you nothing and a bad first meeting can cost months.

Set the first play session up to succeed.

No toys, no food, no bones anywhere in the space. High-value items are the most common trigger for a fight between two dogs who otherwise get on. Pick them all up before either dog arrives.

Have water available but supervise it, since a water bowl is a resource too.

Keep it short. Twenty minutes of good play beats an hour that ends in a squabble. End it while both dogs still want more.

Give them a break every few minutes. Call your dog to you, do something calm for thirty seconds, then release. This teaches both dogs that being called out of play is not the end of play, and it stops arousal climbing to the point where somebody makes a bad decision.

When not to do this at all.

If either dog has a bite history with other dogs, if either has injured a dog before, or if either is showing severe fear rather than mild caution, an introduction is not a DIY project. That is a job for a qualified behaviour professional — a Certified Dog Behavior Consultant, a CBCC-KA, or a veterinary behaviourist. Getting it wrong there does not produce an awkward afternoon; it produces an injured dog and a much harder problem.

For everyone else, the whole method is one sentence: same direction, enough distance, and let the greeting be the last thing that happens rather than the first.

title: The parasite conversation nobody has at the dog park
summary: About one in five fresh faecal samples collected at US dog parks carried worm eggs, and park entrances are the most contaminated spot of all. Year-round prevention and picking up every time is most of the answer.
content:
Dog parks are, epidemiologically, a shared bathroom. That is not a reason to avoid them. It is a reason to understand what circulates there.

The numbers.

A survey across thirty US cities found roughly twenty per cent of fresh faecal samples collected at dog parks tested positive for gastrointestinal worm eggs. Hookworms were the most common finding, particularly in the South and Midwest; roundworm was more prevalent in Western cities.

Studies of park soil have found widespread contamination with hookworm and Toxocara eggs, and identified park entrances as the most heavily contaminated locations within a park — followed by playgrounds. That makes intuitive sense: the entrance is where every dog stops, sniffs and eliminates.

Prevalence in dogs themselves follows a regional gradient. In the US Northeast, roughly one in ten dogs carries roundworms, hookworms or whipworms. In the Midwest it approaches one in five. In parts of the South it runs between one in five and one in two.

What is actually circulating.

Roundworms (Toxocara). Eggs are shed in faeces and become infective in the environment after a period of days to weeks. Once infective they are extremely durable and can persist in soil for years. This is a zoonosis: Toxocara can infect people, and children are the group most at risk because of hand-to-mouth behaviour on contaminated ground.

Hookworms. Larvae in soil can penetrate skin directly, which is why bare feet on contaminated ground are a route of transmission. In dogs they cause blood loss, which can be serious in puppies. Drug-resistant hookworm has become a genuine and growing problem in the US, particularly in dogs from racing greyhound backgrounds and in parts of the South.

Whipworms. Long-lived eggs, hard to eliminate from a contaminated yard.

Giardia and coccidia. Protozoa, spread by the faecal-oral route, frequently picked up from contaminated water and shared bowls.

Fleas and ticks, which are picked up in long grass and at edges rather than on open ground.

Leptospirosis, which is a bacterium rather than a parasite but belongs in the same mental category: shed in the urine of wildlife and dogs, survives in standing water, and became a core canine vaccine in the 2024 update to AAHA's guidelines.

What actually works.

Year-round broad-spectrum prevention. The American Heartworm Society and the FDA recommend all dogs and cats in the US stay on heartworm preventives year-round. Most monthly heartworm products also cover several intestinal worms, so this is one action that covers a lot of ground. Ask your vet which parasites your product actually covers, because that varies a great deal between products.

Annual heartworm testing even for dogs on prevention. Prevention can fail — a spat-out tablet, a topical applied to a wet coat, a missed month — and the point of the test is to catch that.

Faecal testing. Frequency should be based on your dog's risk. A dog who visits parks and daycare is a higher-risk dog than one who does not, and that is the relevant thing to tell your vet.

Pick up every single time, immediately. This is not just etiquette. Roundworm eggs are not infective at the moment they are passed — they need days to weeks in the environment to develop. Prompt removal breaks the cycle before the eggs become dangerous. Faeces left for a day is a meaningfully different hazard to faeces left for a week.

Bring your own water. Communal water bowls are an efficient way to share giardia. A collapsible bowl and a bottle costs nothing.

Discourage eating other dogs' faeces, drinking from puddles, and rolling. Easier said than done, but worth working on the recall.

Wash your hands, and your children's hands, after a park visit, and take shoes off at the door. Soil contamination is what makes this a human health question.

The bit that involves other people.

Around a fifth of samples being positive means a meaningful number of dogs at any given park are shedding, and their owners do not know. Nobody is being negligent — a healthy adult dog with worms usually looks completely fine.

Which means the answer is not to work out who the culprit is. It is that everyone stays on prevention and everyone picks up, and the load in that park drops for all of them.

The dogs who should not be there at all.

Puppies before the vaccine series is complete, since parvovirus persists in the environment for months and is the specific reason public parks are off-limits.

Dogs with active diarrhoea, until it has been sorted out. This is the one where individual behaviour matters most, and it is the easiest rule to follow.

Immunocompromised dogs and dogs on immunosuppressive medication.

None of this makes a dog park a bad place. It makes it a place with known hazards and known countermeasures, most of which cost a monthly tablet and thirty seconds with a bag.

title: Six games that tire a herding dog out
summary: Herding breeds need a job more than they need a longer walk. These six give them one, and most of them fit in a back garden.
content:
If you have a Border Collie, an Australian Shepherd, a Kelpie or a Malinois, you have probably discovered the central problem: physical exercise makes them fitter, not tireder. Walk one for two hours and you get a dog who can walk for two hours and is now looking at you expectantly.

Herding breeds were built to solve problems under their own steam for a working day. The tiredness you are looking for comes from thinking, from decision-making, and from getting to do the thing their body is set up to do. Here are six games that provide it.

One. Hide and seek with a person.

Have someone hold the dog. Go and hide — behind a door, behind a tree, up the stairs. Call once. Let the dog find you, and make a genuine fuss when they do.

This is much harder than it looks for the dog, it uses scent and problem-solving, and it doubles as recall practice with an enormous built-in reward. Make it harder by hiding without calling at all.

Two. Scatter feeding and the sniffari.

Stop using a bowl. Throw the meal across rough grass, or over a snuffle mat, and let them hunt. A meal that took eleven seconds now takes fifteen minutes of concentrated work.

Then take the principle outside. Long line, harness, somewhere scruffy, and let the dog choose the route and the pace for half an hour. In a small controlled study, dogs given two weeks of daily nosework became measurably more optimistic on a cognitive bias test; dogs given two weeks of heelwork did not.

Three. A proper flirt pole, with rules.

A flirt pole is a long handle, a length of rope and a lure on the end. It is a cat wand for dogs and it is the single most efficient way to exhaust a chase-driven dog in a small space.

The rules matter. Keep the lure low and along the ground rather than up in the air, so the dog is not jumping and twisting. Let them catch it regularly — a chase they can never win gets frustrating rather than satisfying. Build in a "drop" every catch, so the game becomes a chain of chase, catch, release, chase. Five minutes is a real workout; ten is plenty. Not for puppies whose growth plates are still open, and not on a hard or slippery surface.

Four. Shaping games.

Put an object on the floor — a box, a book, a mat. Mark and reward any interaction with it. Look at it: yes. Step towards it: yes. Touch it with a foot: yes. Two feet on it: yes. Do not lure and do not tell the dog anything. Let them offer.

The dog is running experiments, and that is genuinely tiring. Herding breeds are usually extremely good at it, and after five minutes of shaping you will often see the dog go and lie down of its own accord.

The classic version is "101 things to do with a box": put a box down and reward every distinct new behaviour the dog offers with it.

Five. A real job with real rules.

Herding dogs are motion-obsessed, and the answer is not to suppress that but to give it structure. Formal outlets: treibball, where the dog drives large exercise balls into a goal and which was designed specifically for herding dogs without sheep; agility; obedience; scent work; canicross.

The garden version: teach directional cues. Send the dog around a tree to the left on one word and to the right on another. Teach them to move a toy from one end of the garden to the other. Teach a distance down — the dog drops at fifty feet on a single cue. That last one is a serious mental workout and is also the most useful safety behaviour a fast dog can have.

Six. Frozen puzzles for the wind-down.

The end of a session should be calm, not another spike. Licking and chewing are self-soothing behaviours.

Stuff a rubber food toy with the dog's soaked kibble and a little wet food, and freeze it. Freeze a mixture of food and water in a tub for a hot day. Use a lick mat with something spreadable smeared thin.

Twenty minutes of steady licking after a hard game is what actually turns the dog off.

What to avoid.

Endless ball throwing. It is the default answer and it is a poor one for these breeds. Repetitive high-speed chase with hard stops and twists is rough on joints, and more importantly a dog who has done it every day for two years is often a dog who now cannot settle without it. If you use a ball, use it as a reward inside a game with rules, not as the whole activity.

Laser pointers. A chase that can never be caught, with no resolution, in a breed already prone to obsessive motion fixation. Some dogs develop persistent light-chasing behaviour that is genuinely hard to undo.

Adding more distance. If your dog needs a two-hour walk to be manageable, you have built a dog who needs a two-hour walk. Trading half of it for fifteen minutes of thinking usually gets you a calmer dog on less of your time.

A note on the actual sheep.

If you have access to a herding instinct test or an introductory stock-work session, and you have a dog from working lines, it is worth doing once. Watching a dog do the thing its entire body was designed for is informative in a way nothing else is, and it will tell you a lot about what your dog is asking for at home.

title: Introducing cats: slower than you think, in five steps
summary: Scent first, then site swaps, then food either side of a door, then a barrier, and only then a meeting. Two to four weeks is typical and shy cats take months — the failure mode is rushing to step five.
content:
Cats are territorial in a way dogs are not. A resident cat has built a map of scent, routes and resources over months or years, and a new cat is not a visitor to that map — it is a competitor who has appeared inside it overnight.

Done well, an introduction takes two to four weeks. Shy cats take months. The failure mode is almost always the same: someone decides it is taking too long and puts them in a room together.

Before the new cat arrives.

Set up a base camp — one room the new cat will live in, containing everything they need: food, water, a litter box well away from the food, a hiding place at floor level, somewhere high to get up to, a scratching post and toys.

Add resources across the rest of the house for the resident cat, so nothing has to be shared later. In particular, litter boxes: the guidance is at least one more box than there are cats, in separate locations. Get that in place before the new cat, not after the first accident.

A door that closes properly is the essential piece of equipment.

Step one: separation and scent exchange. Several days at least.

The new cat lives in base camp. Neither cat sees the other.

Exchange scent deliberately. Swap bedding between the two. Or take a soft cloth, rub it gently on one cat's cheeks where the facial glands are, and leave it near the other cat's resting place — not on it, near it. Watch the reaction. Sniffing, then ignoring it, is good. Hissing at the cloth means keep going and do not move on.

Feed each cat near the other's scented item, so the smell predicts something good.

Step two: site swapping.

Let the new cat explore the house while the resident is shut somewhere else, then reverse. Nobody meets. Both scents spread through the whole territory, and the new cat learns the layout without an audience.

Repeat over several days.

Step three: food either side of a closed door.

Put both cats' bowls on opposite sides of the closed base camp door. Start far enough back that both eat normally. Over successive meals, move the bowls a little closer.

The rule: move closer only while both cats are eating comfortably. If either stops eating, stalls, or leaves, you have moved too fast. Go back to the distance that worked and stay there for several meals.

Step four: visual access through a barrier.

A cracked door with a doorstop, a stacked pair of baby gates, or a screen. They can see each other and neither can reach the other.

Keep it short — five to ten minutes — and make good things happen: treats, a wand toy, meals. End before either cat becomes uncomfortable, not after.

Do this many times over several days. Many short exposures beat one long one.

Step five: supervised meetings in the open.

Only when step four is boring for both cats.

Short sessions. Escape routes available in every direction. Vertical space so a worried cat can get up rather than be cornered. A wand toy in your hand to redirect attention. No food on the floor, since that concentrates both cats into one spot.

End on a good note, before anything happens. Increase the time gradually.

Signs it is going well: ears forward, relaxed body, soft eyes, tails up, both able to eat and play, and each cat able to ignore the other.

Signs to go back a step: hissing, flat ears, a stiff tail, a hard stare, one cat blocking a doorway or a corridor, or either cat freezing.

If there is a hiss or a swipe, do not punish anyone. Calmly separate, and next time return to the last step that was going well and spend longer there. Going back is not failure — it is the method.

Common mistakes.

Putting them in a room together to sort it out. They do not sort it out. They form a first impression that then has to be undone.

Holding a cat during an introduction. A restrained cat cannot leave, which is the one thing it needs to be able to do.

Judging by the calendar rather than the cats. Two to four weeks is typical, not promised.

Not enough resources. Cats compete over the things they need. Multiple boxes, multiple feeding stations, multiple beds, multiple high places, and all of them separated.

Missing the quiet version of conflict. Cats rarely fight outright. They block corridors, stare, sit on the stairs, occupy the doorway to the litter room. A cat who has stopped using a route, or has started eliminating outside the box, is in a conflict you have not noticed.

Neglecting the resident cat. Their whole world has changed and they did not ask for it. Keep their routine, their spaces and their attention intact.

When to get help.

Sustained fighting with injuries, a cat who stops eating for more than a day or two, a cat hiding continuously for more than a week, or house-soiling that persists. Vet first, because pain and illness affect tolerance enormously, then a cat behaviour consultant.

And an honest note: not every pair of cats becomes friends. Many settle into polite mutual avoidance in a house with enough resources, and that is a perfectly successful outcome. The aim is a house where nobody is stressed, not a photograph of two cats in one bed.

title: Bringing a rescue home: the 3-3-3 rule is made up, the patience is not
summary: Three days, three weeks, three months is rescue folklore rather than research. In a 2025 adopter study only 30% felt their dog had settled by three months, and 41% said four to six.
content:
Adopt a dog and somebody will tell you the 3-3-3 rule: three days to decompress, three weeks to learn your routine, three months to feel at home.

It is a kind and useful piece of framing. It is also not based on research. It comes from rescue practice, and it is repeated as though it were a finding.

What the evidence suggests instead.

In a 2025 study of adopters, only 30% felt their dog had settled within three months. 41% said adjustment took four to six months.

Commonly reported estimates for full decompression run from about six weeks to three months and well beyond, and some behaviour gets temporarily worse around the three-month mark — which makes sense if you think about what is happening. A dog who is shut down does not show you problems. A dog who has relaxed enough to have opinions does.

So the shape of the rule is right and the numbers are invented. Expect a slow, uneven, non-linear settling, and expect it to take longer than anyone told you. Do not judge the animal by week one, and do not conclude at month three that you have failed.

What the first fortnight should look like.

Do less than you want to. The instinct is to show them everything, introduce everyone, and start training. Almost everything you want to do can wait.

Keep the world small. One room or one part of the house to start. A crate or bed in a quiet corner that nobody disturbs. Space narrows the number of new things per hour, which is the actual variable.

Keep the routine boring and identical. Same feeding times, same walk route, same people, same order of events. Predictability is what tells an animal it is safe. Novelty is what you are rationing.

No visitors. Not the neighbours, not the extended family, not the friend who is really good with dogs. Two weeks.

No dog park, no daycare, no group class, and no meeting the neighbourhood dogs. You do not yet know this dog's history with other dogs, and the first week is when you have least information and the dog has least capacity.

Leads on, doors managed, garden checked. A newly adopted dog is a flight risk, and the first fortnight is when most escape and get lost. Use a well-fitted harness and a collar with a tag, double-clipped if there is any doubt, and get the microchip transferred into your name immediately rather than eventually.

Let them sleep. A great many newly adopted dogs are seriously sleep-deprived. Shelters are loud around the clock. Some new dogs will sleep for eighteen hours a day for the first week and that is not illness, it is debt being repaid.

Do not test them. Do not see if they are good with cats by putting them near a cat. Do not check if they guard food by reaching into the bowl. There is nothing to learn there that is worth what it costs.

Cats need the same thing, more so.

A newly adopted cat goes in one room with all its resources — food, water, litter, a hiding place, somewhere high, and a scratching post — and stays there for days to weeks depending on the cat. Sit in the room and read out loud without approaching. Let the cat come out from under the bed on its own schedule.

A cat who is hiding is not sulking or ungrateful. Hiding is the coping mechanism, and taking it away by dragging them out slows everything down. Full-house access comes after the cat is confidently using the room, not before.

The things people misread in the first months.

The honeymoon period. Many dogs are unusually quiet for the first week or two and then become considerably more themselves. That is not a bait and switch. That is the shut-down lifting.

Behaviour appearing at week three or month three. Resource guarding, separation distress, reactivity on lead. These are not usually new problems; they are old problems becoming visible now the dog is relaxed enough to express them.

Regression. Progress is not linear. A dog who was fine on walks for a fortnight and then has a bad week has not gone backwards permanently.

House-training lapses. Very common for weeks, in adult dogs who were reliable somewhere else. Treat it as a house-training problem from scratch, not as a statement.

When to get help early rather than waiting it out.

Do not wait three months if you are seeing: aggression towards people or other animals in the household, severe distress when left alone, refusal to eat for more than a day or two, or self-injury.

Those need a vet visit first — pain and illness look like behaviour problems — and then a qualified professional: a veterinary behaviourist, or a certified behaviour consultant. Early intervention is much cheaper, faster and more effective than intervention after six months of a problem being practised.

What actually helps most.

Time, predictability, sleep, and low expectations. A new dog does not owe you gratitude, an immediate bond, or good behaviour in the first month. Give it six months before you decide who this animal is.

title: Dog park or playdate? Choosing the right kind of meeting
summary: A public dog park is a room full of strangers with no bouncer. Around one in five faecal samples collected at US dog parks carried parasite eggs. For a lot of dogs, a one-to-one playdate is simply the better product.
content:
The public dog park is the default answer to "my dog needs to see other dogs", and for some dogs it is a great one. For a lot of dogs it is the wrong venue, and the reason is structural rather than anything to do with your dog.

What a dog park actually is.

It is an enclosed space containing an unpredictable number of unknown dogs, of unknown vaccination status, with unknown play styles, supervised by people you have never met, many of whom are on their phones. There is no screening at the gate and no one in charge. It is the only social environment we routinely put dogs into that has none of the structure we would insist on for a child.

That does not make it bad. It makes it a specific thing that suits specific dogs.

The health arithmetic.

A survey across thirty US cities found roughly twenty per cent of fresh faecal samples collected at dog parks were positive for intestinal worm eggs. Hookworm was most common in the South and Midwest; roundworm dominated in Western cities. Park entrances turn out to be the most contaminated spot in a park, which makes sense — it is where every dog stops.

Regional dog prevalence follows the same shape. Roughly one in ten dogs in the US Northeast carries roundworm, hookworm or whipworm. It approaches one in five in the Midwest. In parts of the South it runs between one in five and one in two.

Parks are also where airborne respiratory disease circulates — kennel cough, canine influenza — and where leptospirosis can be picked up from standing water and wildlife urine.

None of this is an argument against dog parks for a healthy, fully vaccinated adult dog on year-round parasite prevention. It is an argument for being that dog before you go, and for picking up faeces every time, including the ones nobody saw you not pick up.

Who should not be at a public dog park.

Puppies who have not finished their vaccination series. This is the big one and it is the one owners get wrong most often, because the socialisation advice is to get puppies out early and the parasite and parvo advice is to keep them off contaminated public ground. Both are correct. The resolution is controlled exposure — known, vaccinated dogs, in clean private spaces — not the public park.

Dogs who guard things. If your dog stiffens over a ball, a water bowl, a stick, or over you, a dog park is a series of trigger events waiting to happen.

Dogs who are recovering, immunocompromised, elderly, or in season.

Dogs who do not enjoy it. This is worth saying plainly, because a lot of dogs at dog parks are not having a nice time. A dog who hides under a bench, presses against your legs, or spends the visit in low-grade avoidance is not being socialised. They are being flooded, and repeated flooding makes dogs worse with other dogs, not better.

Dogs whose play style routinely upsets others. A dog who body-slams, or who herds and nips at other dogs' legs, or who cannot stop chasing, is going to end up in a conflict eventually, and it will not be their fault so much as a venue problem.

What a playdate gives you that a park does not.

Choice of partner. You can pick a dog with a compatible size, energy level and play style, which is most of what determines whether two dogs enjoy each other.

Choice of ground. Somewhere neither dog owns, or somewhere securely fenced and private.

A known health status. Two owners can just tell each other.

Numbers you control. Two dogs is a manageable interaction. Add a third and the dynamic changes completely — chases become pursuits, and the dog being chased has two chasers.

A known exit. You can end it at twenty minutes while everyone is still enjoying themselves, rather than waiting for a natural pause that never comes.

If you are going to use the park anyway.

Go at quiet times. Early morning on a weekday is a different park to Saturday at three.

Take the leash off in the airlock, before the inner gate. A leashed dog surrounded by loose dogs is trapped, and that is where a lot of gate fights start.

Move away from the entrance immediately. Do not stand and chat by the gate — that is the pinch point.

Bring one or two dogs at most, so you can genuinely watch them.

Leave the toys and the treats at home. Food and high-value items measurably raise the odds of conflict in a group.

Put your phone away. In reported dog-park incidents, most happened when owners were not watching.

Keep moving, and keep your dog moving with you. Dogs who orbit a stationary owner get into fewer disputes than dogs left to work out group politics alone for an hour.

Leave early. The best visit ends before the dog is tired and cranky, not after.

The honest summary: a dog park is a good tool for a confident, healthy, well-socialised adult dog who genuinely likes other dogs, used briefly and at quiet times. For everyone else there is a better option, and this app exists to help you find it.

title: The poison list: what actually sends pets to the emergency room
summary: The ASPCA's poison line took over 451,000 calls in 2024. Chocolate was 13.6% of exposures. For cats, one houseplant is in a category of its own — and for birds, the danger is a frying pan.
content:
Save this number now, before you need it: the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center, (888) 426-4435, twenty-four hours a day. There is a consultation fee. It is worth it, and having it in your phone in advance saves the ten minutes you will not have.

The centre handled more than 451,000 calls about toxic exposures in 2024, a rise of roughly four per cent on the previous year.

Here is what actually turns up.

Chocolate: 13.6% of exposures in 2024.

The toxic agent is theobromine, and dogs clear it far more slowly than we do — roughly 17.5 hours against two to three in humans — so it accumulates.

Reported thresholds in dogs: mild signs such as vomiting, diarrhoea and excessive thirst around 20 mg/kg; effects on the heart at 40 to 50 mg/kg; seizures at 60 mg/kg and above.

What makes this hard to eyeball is that theobromine content varies enormously by product. Cocoa powder runs around 737 mg per ounce and baking chocolate around 376 mg per ounce. Dark chocolate is around 130 to 138 mg per ounce. Milk chocolate is far lower, and white chocolate is essentially irrelevant toxicologically.

The practical version: a bar of milk chocolate and a small piece of baking chocolate are not remotely the same event. Do not try to work out whether a dose is safe. Call the line with the dog's weight, the product, and the amount, and let them do the arithmetic.

Xylitol.

An artificial sweetener found in sugar-free gum, some peanut butters, baked goods, mouthwash and some medicines. Sugar-free gums make up a large share of the food and drink category, which was the second-ranked toxin group in 2024. Xylitol causes a rapid drop in blood sugar in dogs and can cause liver failure. Check peanut butter labels before you use it in a food toy.

Grapes and raisins.

Exposure can cause gastrointestinal upset, lethargy, excessive thirst, tremors, abdominal pain and, in severe cases, irreversible kidney damage. There is no established safe dose and susceptibility varies between individuals, which means the only sensible policy is none.

Also on the list from the same food and drink group: onions, garlic, and protein drinks.

Lilies and cats: the one absolute rule.

All species of Lilium — true lilies — and Hemerocallis — daylilies — are lethally toxic to cats.

Every part is dangerous: flower, leaf, stem and pollen. Documented cases include acute kidney injury from pollen exposure alone, from a cat licking pollen off its own coat, and from drinking water out of a vase that held cut lilies.

Gastrointestinal signs start two to twelve hours after ingestion; kidney effects show up between twelve and ninety-six hours. Treatment is early aggressive intravenous fluids, and affected cats typically need forty-eight to seventy-two hours in hospital.

There is very little pet advice that is genuinely absolute, and this is one piece of it: do not have lilies in a house with a cat. Not on a high shelf. Not in a closed room. Not for one evening. Tell people who send you flowers.

Birds: it is the kitchen.

Overheated non-stick coatings kill birds, frequently before an owner notices anything is wrong. Heating PTFE releases carbonyl fluoride, hydrogen fluoride and perfluoroisobutylene — all colourless and odourless.

Pyrolysis is usually cited above 260C (536F), but the lowest temperature at which a non-stick coating has been reported in peer-reviewed literature to kill birds is 202C (396F). That is an ordinary pan on an ordinary hob.

The sources go well beyond the frying pan: self-cleaning ovens, PTFE-coated drip pans under burners (which exceed 315C/600F within minutes of normal use), heat lamp covers, irons and ironing board covers, some space heaters, and some hair appliances.

Birds have an extremely efficient respiratory system, which is exactly why inhaled toxins hit them so hard. Acute death from respiratory failure is the most common outcome. If you keep birds, the kitchen should not have non-stick cookware in it, and the bird should not live in or near the kitchen.

What to do if you think something has been eaten.

Do not wait to see if signs develop. Many of these are much more treatable before signs appear.

Do not make an animal vomit unless a veterinary professional has told you to for that specific substance. For caustic substances and petroleum products it makes things considerably worse.

Do not use hydrogen peroxide, salt or mustard on the say-so of a search result.

Do gather the packaging, work out the maximum amount that could have been consumed, and know your animal's weight. Then call your vet, an emergency hospital, or the ASPCA line on (888) 426-4435. The Pet Poison Helpline, (855) 764-7661, is an alternative.

Bring the packaging with you if you travel to a clinic.

Prevention that is worth the ten minutes.

Handbags and rucksacks off the floor — that is where gum, medication and chocolate live. Medication in a closed cupboard, not on a counter. Bins with lids that latch. Check the plants you already own against the ASPCA's toxic plants list, and if you have a cat, start with lilies.

title: Playdates in the heat: the seven-second test and what to do if you get it wrong
summary: At 87F air temperature asphalt can hit 143F. Flat-faced dogs had over four times the odds of heat-related illness in a 2024 emergency-practice study. And the advice to only use tepid water is wrong.
content:
This is the article to read before an August playdate in Phoenix, and it has three parts: the ground, the dog, and what to do when it goes wrong.

The ground is much hotter than the air.

Air temperature is a bad guide to what your dog is walking on. Reported figures: at 86F (30C) air, asphalt reaches around 135F (57C). At 87F (31C), around 143F (62C). Pavement at about 125F (52C) — which happens at roughly 77F (25C) air — can burn a paw pad in about sixty seconds.

Seventy-seven degrees is a pleasant day. Your dog can be burned on a pleasant day.

The seven-second test settles it. Press the back of your hand flat on the surface and hold it there. If you cannot manage seven seconds, your dog should not be walking on it. Do it every time, on the actual surface you are about to use — asphalt, concrete, artificial turf, sand and metal all behave differently, and dark asphalt is the worst of them.

Surfaces stay hot long after the sun has moved. A path in shade at six in the evening may have been in full sun until four.

If you cannot pass the test, the options are grass, dirt trails, early morning, after dark, water, or staying home and doing scent games indoors.

Some dogs are at much higher risk than others.

A 2024 study of dogs under UK emergency veterinary care found brachycephalic — flat-faced — dogs had 4.21 times the odds of heat-related illness compared with medium-muzzled dogs. Earlier work by Hall and colleagues, across more than 900,000 dogs, found flat-faced dogs had greater odds of all three categories of heat-related illness.

If you have a French Bulldog, a Pug, an English or American Bulldog, a Boxer, a Boston Terrier, a Shih Tzu or a Pekingese, the summer rules for your dog are genuinely different. Panting is how a dog sheds heat, and a shortened airway makes panting less effective at exactly the moment it is needed most.

Also higher risk: overweight dogs, very young and very old dogs, thick double-coated northern breeds, dogs with laryngeal paralysis or heart or airway disease, and any dog not yet acclimatised to the season.

And the biggest risk factor is not weather. It is exertion. UK data found exercise-related heat illness far outnumbered hot-car cases. The dangerous scenario is not a parked car. It is a fit dog having a wonderful time chasing another dog in the sun, because a dog in a good game will not stop itself.

Warning signs during a playdate.

Frantic, noisy panting that does not settle during breaks. A very wide, curled tongue that looks longer than usual. Thick, ropey drool. Bright red gums or, worse, pale or grey ones. Wobbling, stumbling, confusion, or a dog who stops responding to their name. Vomiting or diarrhoea. Collapse.

Enforced breaks are the intervention that works. Every five to ten minutes, call both dogs out of play, into shade, and hold them there until breathing settles. Dogs in a group will not do this themselves.

If you think it is heatstroke: cool first, transport second.

This is the part most owners have backwards, and one piece of common advice is actively dangerous.

The advice to use only tepid or lukewarm water is not supported by evidence. Cold-water immersion and water spray combined with air movement are the recommended cooling methods for dogs with heat-related illness. Cold-water immersion suits young, healthy dogs; spraying plus a fan or air conditioning is preferred for older dogs and dogs with underlying disease. The practical instruction is to use whatever water you have, provided it is cooler than the dog.

The 2016 prehospital guidance is summarised as cool first, transport second. Cooling on the way to the vet, or before you set off, matters more than the minutes saved by leaving immediately without cooling.

So: get the dog out of the heat. Pour or spray cool water over the whole body, not just the feet. Get air moving over the wet coat. Offer small amounts of water to drink if the dog is conscious and can swallow, and do not force it. Keep cooling while somebody calls the vet and while you travel.

What not to do: do not pack the dog in ice or immerse in ice slush, which constricts skin blood flow and slows heat loss. Do not cover the dog with wet towels and leave them on — a warm wet towel becomes insulation. Do not delay cooling to get in the car.

Heatstroke is an emergency even if the dog seems to recover. Organ damage can appear hours later. Go to a vet regardless.

Planning a summer playdate.

Choose morning or evening. In Arizona in July that means before seven or after nine at night.

Prefer water and shaded trails to open parks.

Take more water than you think, and something to pour it out of and into.

Keep the session short, and make breaks compulsory rather than optional.

Skip it entirely on the worst days. A sniffari through the house and a frozen food toy is a perfectly good afternoon, and it is a much better one than an emergency admission.

title: Play is how an indoor cat hunts
summary: In a study of 355 cats, five minutes of daily wand-toy play cut prey brought home by about a quarter. A collar bell did nothing. And giving a cat its whole ration through a puzzle feeder made hunting worse.
content:
Cats hunt because they are cats, not because they are hungry. Predatory behaviour and feeding are governed separately, which is why a well-fed cat still stalks things and why "she gets plenty of food" has never stopped anyone's cat catching a bird.

Cecchetti and colleagues tested what actually changes that. They worked with 355 cats from 219 households over three months, with a seven-week baseline in which owners logged every prey item brought home. Then they tried five interventions.

What worked, and by how much.

High-meat, grain-free commercial food: prey brought home fell by around 36%.

Five minutes a day of object play with a fishing-rod-type wand toy and a mouse-type toy: prey fell by around 25%.

A standard collar bell: no significant change in total prey brought home.

A Birdsbesafe collar cover: no change in the total number of prey animals brought home.

And the surprising one: delivering the cat's entire daily allowance of dry food through a food puzzle increased predation by 33%.

That last result is worth sitting with, because puzzle feeders have a good reputation and deservedly so. The likely explanation is that cats given their whole ration through a puzzle were, in practice, eating less — so it became a mild restriction rather than an enrichment. Puzzle feeders are excellent enrichment. They are not a rationing method, and they should not be the only way a cat gets food.

Why five minutes of play does that much.

The predatory sequence has stages: search, stalk, pounce, manipulate, consume. Each part is self-reinforcing, and a cat that never gets to run the sequence has an unmet behavioural need.

A wand toy covers the middle: search, stalk, pounce. A food puzzle covers the end: manipulate and consume. Together, alongside a proper meal, they let an indoor cat run the whole thing.

How to actually play with a cat.

Use a wand toy, not your hands. Hands as toys teaches a cat to bite hands, which is charming in a kitten and a problem in an adult.

Move the toy like prey, not like a toy. Prey moves away from the cat and hides. It does not fly at their face. Drag it along the floor, behind furniture, out of sight and then a twitch. Pauses are what make a cat stalk — a lure in constant motion gives them nothing to plan.

Let them catch it, repeatedly. A hunt that never succeeds is frustrating rather than satisfying. Several catches per session.

Escalate then wind down. Build to a couple of big pounces, then let the movements get slower and smaller, so the session ends with a capture rather than by you putting the toy away mid-chase.

Finish with food. A few treats or a meal immediately after closes the sequence.

Two sessions a day is a reasonable target, and the study's intervention was only five minutes. Ten to fifteen minutes twice a day is commonly recommended and is generous.

Rotate toys. Cats habituate fast. Six toys in a cupboard, two out at a time, swapped weekly, will keep their interest far better than sixteen toys permanently on the floor.

Put wand toys away between sessions. String and thread are a genuine hazard if swallowed — linear foreign bodies do serious damage to intestines — so wand toys are supervised equipment, not furniture.

Around food puzzles.

Start easy. In a survey of 3,192 cat owners, 30% used food puzzles and a further 18% had tried and given up — usually because they started too hard and the cat gave up first. Begin with a puzzle so simple it barely counts, with the cat's favourite food, and make it harder over weeks.

Use part of the ration, not all of it.

Case reports document food puzzles helping with weight loss, anxiety and urination outside the litter box, so it is worth persisting through the awkward first week.

The rest of the enrichment picture.

Vertical space. Cat trees, shelves, cleared windowsills. Height is where cats feel safe and where they watch from.

A window with something happening outside it. A bird feeder placed where the cat can watch but cannot reach is genuinely good television.

Scratching posts that are tall enough to stretch out fully on, and stable enough not to wobble. Both vertical and horizontal options, since cats have preferences.

Boxes, paper bags with the handles cut off, and tunnels. Cheap, and used more than most purchased equipment.

Novelty in small doses. A cardboard box that was not there yesterday is an event.

The thing to take away: five minutes with a wand toy, twice a day, measurably changed cat behaviour in a real study of hundreds of cats. It is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort things you can do for an indoor cat, and it also happens to be good for the local birds.

title: The first sixteen weeks are the ones you cannot redo
summary: The window in which a puppy accepts new things as normal is roughly three to sixteen weeks, and AVSAB is explicit that it should not be spent waiting for the vaccine course to finish.
content:
Most of what a dog will be like as an adult is decided in a period that is over before many owners have finished choosing a vet.

The window.

Between roughly three and fourteen to sixteen weeks, a puppy has an unusual neurological openness. New people, animals, surfaces, sounds and situations encountered in this period tend to be filed as normal, with minimal fear response. AVSAB describes the first three months as the period when sociability outweighs fear.

After it closes, the same experiences are processed differently. They can still be worked with — dogs learn all their lives — but it takes deliberate, patient effort to achieve what would have cost nothing at nine weeks.

The conflict, and how to resolve it.

The window overlaps almost exactly with the vaccination course, which finishes at sixteen weeks or later. This produces the most consequential piece of bad advice in dog ownership: keep the puppy in until the vaccines are done.

AVSAB's position is explicit. Puppies should begin socialisation before the vaccination series is complete — classes as early as seven to eight weeks, after one set of vaccines and with no signs of illness, staying current on boosters.

The reason is a risk comparison. AVSAB states that more deaths in dogs under three are attributable to behavioural problems than to infectious disease, and that incomplete socialisation increases the risk of fear, avoidance and aggression later.

That does not mean ignore infection risk. It means manage both, which is entirely possible:

Carry the puppy in public places. A puppy in your arms in a car park, outside a café, at the school gates, is seeing and hearing everything with no contact with contaminated ground.

Use clean surfaces. Your own garden, friends' houses, a vet's waiting room floor that is disinfected, the boot of your car with the tailgate up in a busy street.

Meet known, vaccinated, healthy adult dogs, in private spaces. One steady adult dog who is good with puppies is worth more than a park full of strangers.

Go to a well-run puppy class that requires proof of first vaccination and disinfects the floor.

Avoid public dog parks, pet shop floors, and areas heavily used by unknown dogs, until the course is finished. Parvovirus persists in the environment for months.

What to actually expose them to.

Not a headcount. The circulating advice to "meet 100 people by 16 weeks" is a rule of thumb rather than a finding, and it drives owners to prioritise volume over the puppy's emotional state — which is the opposite of what the underlying research is about.

The categories that matter:

Surfaces: lino, wood, carpet, concrete, grass, gravel, sand, metal grates, wobbly surfaces, wet surfaces, stairs.

People who look and move differently: men with beards, people in hats and high-vis, people with sticks and wheelchairs and pushchairs, children of various ages and volumes, people running, people on bikes.

Sounds: traffic, sirens, hoovers, doorbells, fireworks at low volume, thunderstorms on a recording, hairdryers, washing machines.

Handling: paws, between the toes, ears, mouth and teeth, tail, collar grabs, being lifted, being held still — each paired with something good.

The vet: several visits that are nothing but standing on the scales, having a treat, and leaving.

The car, in short pleasant trips that do not always end at the vet.

Being alone, for very short periods, from the beginning. This is the one most people skip, and separation-related problems are among the most common in adult dogs.

The rule that makes it work.

Quality over quantity, every time. One rule governs all of it: the puppy should be able to retreat, and should be under threshold — able to take food, able to look away, moving normally.

A puppy frozen in a corner while five children stroke it is not being socialised. It is being frightened, and it is learning that you do not help.

If the puppy is worried, add distance, let them watch, and pay them for looking. Never force an interaction, never let anyone corner them, and end on a good moment.

The other things happening in these weeks.

House-training, which is a management problem more than a training one — take them out on a schedule built around waking, meals, drinks and play, reward outside, and never punish an accident. Full bladder control does not arrive until around five months, so frequency is physiology, not failure.

Bite inhibition. Puppies mouth. This is how they learn how hard is too hard, and it is worth teaching rather than suppressing: play, and when teeth touch skin, the game stops for thirty seconds. They learn quickly.

Sleep. Puppies need an enormous amount of it, and a great deal of what owners describe as an overtired biting monster is a puppy that has not slept in six hours.

Exercise, which should be free, varied and self-paced rather than distance-based. The oft-quoted five-minutes-per-month-of-age rule cannot be traced to a study; the research that does exist found stairs in the first three months associated with increased hip dysplasia risk and free off-lead exercise on varied ground associated with reduced risk.

And the vaccination course itself, on schedule, to at least sixteen weeks, because maternal antibody can block earlier doses.

If you have already missed it.

If you are reading this with a five-month-old who missed out, or an adult rescue with an unknown history: it is not hopeless and it is not too late to improve things. It is slower, and it is worth getting help early rather than after the problem is established.
