title: Size, temperament, activities: what actually makes two dogs a good match
summary: PetPals scores a pair on five things and weights them deliberately: temperament 30, size 25, shared activities 25, breed 12, age 8. Here is the reasoning behind each one.
content:
When PetPals suggests a pal for your dog, it is not guessing. Every pair gets scored out of a hundred across five dimensions, and the weights are not evenly spread. This is what each one is doing and why it is worth what it is worth.

Temperament: 30 points.

The largest single share, because how two dogs handle arousal is the thing that most determines whether a session ends well. Two calm dogs will have a fine time. Two energetic dogs will have a loud, excellent time. A calm dog and a very pushy energetic dog is the pairing most likely to produce a dog who stops enjoying other dogs.

Temperaments do not have to match exactly to work. The app treats some pairs as compatible rather than identical — a friendly dog gets on with almost everything, a highly reactive or anxious dog does much better with calm and friendly partners than with high-drive ones.

Size: 25 points.

Size is second not because small dogs and big dogs cannot be friends — plenty are — but because size difference is the one dimension where a mistake causes an injury rather than an awkward afternoon.

The scoring uses the ratio of the lighter dog to the heavier one, not the difference. That is deliberate. A five-pound and a fifteen-pound dog are three times apart and that is a genuine mismatch. An eighty-pound and a ninety-pound dog differ by more in absolute terms and are effectively the same size. Within about fifteen per cent, the app treats two dogs as the same size. Below a ratio of one to three — say fifteen pounds against forty-five — the score falls to zero, because at that point a completely well-meaning accident can break something.

The other reason to take size seriously is predatory drift: a small, fast-moving, high-pitched animal running and squealing can flip a much larger dog from play into chase, in dogs who have never shown a moment of aggression in their lives. It is rare. It is also the reason well-run daycares separate by size, and the reason a lot of dog parks have a small-dog side.

This is why the app asks for weight and will not let you skip it.

Shared activities: 25 points.

Two dogs who both love fetch have something to do together. Two dogs where one wants to wrestle and the other wants to run in circles will have a session of mutual misunderstanding.

The score uses the overlap between the two lists relative to their combined size, rather than a raw count, so a dog whose owner ticked every box does not automatically out-score a genuinely similar dog. There is a small bonus when the shared activities also suit both dogs' temperaments — a shared love of the dog park counts for more between two extroverts than between two dogs who find crowds hard.

Breed: 12 points.

Breed is in the model, and it is deliberately worth less than half of temperament.

What breed usefully predicts is play style. Herding breeds tend to chase, circle and control movement. Terriers, especially the bull breeds, tend to wrestle and use their bodies. Retrievers and other sporting dogs tend to body-slam and mouth necks. Those tendencies are real and they cause real mismatches: not every dog who enjoys running enjoys being chased, and a dog who plays by grabbing another dog's neck will worry a dog who does not.

What breed does not usefully predict is whether an individual dog is friendly, safe, or fun to be around. It is a hint about style, at twelve points out of a hundred, and that is the right weight for it.

Age: 8 points.

The smallest share. Age gaps matter — a nine-year-old dog often has limited patience for a six-month-old puppy, and a puppy needs partners who will tolerate rudeness while teaching it not to be rude. But plenty of old dogs adore puppies and plenty of same-age dogs have nothing in common. Five years apart scores zero on this dimension, which barely dents a total.

How to read the score you are shown.

The breakdown the app shows you is in weighted points, not percentages. Twenty-seven out of thirty on temperament is a near-perfect fit. Eight out of eight on age is also perfect, and it is worth a quarter as much. Do not compare the raw numbers across dimensions without dividing by what each one is out of.

A pair scoring in the high forties or fifties with excellent temperament and size fit is often a better real-world playdate than one scoring in the seventies on breed and age similarity. Look at where the points came from, not just the total.

What the score cannot know.

Whether either dog slept badly. Whether one of them is sore. Whether your dog has had a bad experience with a dog that looked like that one. Whether today is the day.

The score narrows a field of strangers down to a handful worth trying. The introduction — neutral ground, parallel walking, a short first meeting — is what actually tells you, and no algorithm replaces watching the two of them for ten minutes.

title: Is your pet a healthy weight? The honest version
summary: 59% of dogs and 61% of cats were assessed as overweight in the 2022 APOP survey. Only 39% of dog owners and 45% of cat owners thought their own pet was. That gap is the whole problem.
content:
In the Association for Pet Obesity Prevention's 2022 survey, veterinary professionals classed 59% of dogs and 61% of cats as overweight or having obesity.

In the same survey, 39% of dog owners and 45% of cat owners thought their own pet was overweight.

That gap — roughly twenty points — is not owners lying. It is that we have collectively recalibrated what a normal dog and a normal cat look like, and most people are now comparing their pet to other pets rather than to a healthy animal.

Why it matters more than it sounds.

Excess weight is associated with reduced lifespan, osteoarthritis and reduced mobility, diabetes mellitus in cats, respiratory compromise, heat intolerance — which matters a great deal for summer playdates — anaesthetic risk, and reduced quality of life independent of disease.

It is also the health problem with the largest gap between how modifiable it is and how much attention it gets. Only 46% of owners in that survey said their vet discusses their pet's ideal weight annually; 12% said it never comes up.

Body condition scoring is done with your hands.

The standard tools are nine-point body condition scales, where four to five out of nine is ideal. Weight on its own tells you almost nothing without knowing the animal's frame — which is why "he's 30 pounds and the internet says the breed should be 30 pounds" is not an assessment.

The three checks, done with the animal standing:

Ribs. Run your flat palm along the side of the chest, with light pressure. You should feel the ribs distinctly, with a thin covering over them — roughly how the back of your hand feels over the knuckles. If you have to press to find them, there is too much covering. If they feel like the back of your fingers with nothing over them at all, the animal is too thin.

Waist from above. Looking down at a standing animal, there should be a visible narrowing behind the ribs. A straight line from ribs to hips, or a bulge outwards, means too much. This is the check that catches most cases.

Tuck from the side. The belly line should rise from the bottom of the ribcage up towards the hind legs rather than running level or sagging.

Coat length makes visual assessment unreliable, which is why the rib check is done by feel. In cats, the primordial pouch — the loose flap of skin and fat along the lower belly — is normal anatomy in many cats and is not by itself a sign of excess weight. It swings when they trot. It is not a verdict.

If you are unsure, most veterinary practices will do a free weight and body condition check with a nurse or technician. It takes five minutes.

If your pet needs to lose weight.

Do it with your vet, not from an article. That is not a disclaimer, it is a safety point: weight loss in cats in particular must be gradual, because cats who lose weight too fast can develop hepatic lipidosis, which is life-threatening. Rapid weight loss in a cat is dangerous.

Also, an animal that has gained weight without a change in feeding should be checked for a medical cause before it is put on a diet.

What generally makes the difference:

Measure the food. Not a scoop, not by eye — a kitchen scale, in grams. Portion drift is the single most common cause, and it is invisible without measuring.

Count everything. The dental chew, the training treats, the ends of things from the kitchen, the food the other person in the house gives out. Ten per cent of daily calories is a reasonable ceiling for everything that is not the measured meal, and most households are far over it without knowing.

Feed the food out of something that takes work. For cats, a food puzzle rebuilds part of the hunting sequence and slows eating. One caution from the research: a study of cat predation found that giving a cat its entire dry ration through a puzzle feeder actually increased hunting, plausibly because the cat was not getting enough in practice. Puzzles are enrichment, not a rationing method.

Weigh monthly and write it down. Trend beats impression.

Replace some of the food with attention. A great deal of pet feeding is affection converted into calories. A five-minute play session or a scatter-feed of part of the existing ration delivers the same relationship in a form the animal actually prefers.

The uncomfortable part.

This is a subject people feel judged about, and vets know it, which is part of why it goes undiscussed. It is worth going first: ask your vet directly what your pet's body condition score is and what they would like it to be. It is a far easier conversation to have deliberately than to have implied.

title: Water safety for dogs: algae, too much swimming, and knowing the exit
summary: Blue-green algae can kill a dog within hours and you cannot tell a toxic bloom by looking. Hard-swimming dogs can also take on enough water to drop their blood sodium dangerously. Both are avoidable.
content:
Swimming is one of the best things you can offer a dog: low-impact, cooling, and a genuine workout for dogs whose joints cannot take running any more. There are three specific hazards worth knowing about, and none of them are obvious.

Blue-green algae.

Cyanobacteria — commonly called blue-green algae — grow in lakes, ponds, slow rivers and brackish water, especially in warm weather. Some strains produce toxins that can kill a dog within hours.

You cannot tell a toxic bloom by looking at it. Affected water may be green, blue, yellow, red or brown, often with a scum on the surface that has been described as looking like spilled paint or pea soup. It can also look like nothing much at the edges while a bloom sits further out. Toxicity is not visible.

Two families of toxin matter. Microcystins damage the liver, with death typically between twelve and twenty-four hours after ingestion or within a few days. Anatoxins attack the nervous system and can kill within minutes to hours.

There is no antidote. Treatment is intensive supportive care.

A dog does not have to drink the water. Swimming through a bloom and then licking its coat is enough.

What to do: obey posted warnings, and treat any water with visible scum, discolouration or a strong smell as off-limits. Be more cautious in hot, still weather and late in the season. If your dog has been in suspect water, hose them off with clean water before they can groom, and if they show vomiting, diarrhoea, drooling, weakness, tremors, seizures or collapse, go to a vet immediately and say you suspect algae. Speed matters more than certainty here.

Water intoxication.

This one is less known and it kills healthy dogs. A dog that swims hard, retrieves repeatedly, bites at waves, or plays with a hose or sprinkler can swallow enough water to dilute the sodium in its blood. That causes cells, including brain cells, to swell.

Early signs: pale gums, lethargy, confusion, disorientation, stumbling, glazed eyes, bloating, vomiting. It can progress within minutes to laboured breathing, collapse and seizures.

Highest risk: small dogs, because it takes less water to shift their sodium; high-drive dogs who will not stop; and dogs doing repeated diving retrieves where each grab takes in a mouthful.

Prevention is simple. Take breaks every ten to fifteen minutes and make them compulsory. Use a floating toy that sits on the surface rather than one the dog has to dive and grab with an open mouth. Do not let a dog play in a jet of water from a hose or sprinkler for extended periods. Stop the session while the dog still wants more.

If you see the early signs, stop, get the dog to a vet, and say you suspect water intoxication. It is treatable if caught early.

Drowning and exhaustion.

Not every dog can swim, and this is not a matter of willingness. Deep-chested and heavy-boned dogs, short-legged breeds and flat-faced dogs are all poor swimmers, and some cannot keep their airway above water at all.

More common than a dog who cannot swim is a dog who can swim but cannot get out. Steep banks, pool walls, weed, current and tidal changes all trap dogs who were doing fine right up until the moment they got tired.

Practical rules: know the exit before the dog goes in, and make sure they know it too — walk them out of a pool at the steps several times so the route is learned. Fit a proper buoyancy aid for boats, open water, strong current, or any dog who is a marginal swimmer. Never let a dog swim in water you would not swim in yourself. Watch for tiredness, which shows up as a lower body position and a head that is working harder to stay up. Rinse salt, chlorine and lake water out of the coat afterwards, dry ears well — swimming dogs get more ear infections — and be aware that drinking salt water causes serious problems of its own.

The good news.

None of this is an argument against swimming. It is an argument for swimming somewhere you have looked at, for a length of time you decided, with breaks the dog did not choose, at water the dog is not drinking. On a hot day, water is still the best playdate venue there is.

title: Rabbits and guinea pigs: company and hay, in that order
summary: PDSA found 42% of pet rabbits live alone. Guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C and show signs of deficiency within two to three weeks. Almost everything sold for these species is wrong.
content:
Rabbits and guinea pigs are sold as beginner pets and they are not. They are prey species with specific social needs, complex digestive systems, continuously growing teeth, and a strong instinct to hide illness until it is advanced. The commercial pet trade gets most of it wrong: the hutches are too small, the food is the wrong shape, and the animals are usually sold to live alone.

Here is what the welfare and veterinary guidance actually says.

Rabbits: companionship first.

Rabbits are social animals. The Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund's position is that rabbits should live with a compatible rabbit companion wherever possible.

PDSA's PAW Report found 42% of pet rabbits live alone, with a further 5% living only with another species — an estimated 530,000 rabbits, roughly 48%, whose companionship needs are not being met.

A human is not a substitute. Neither, generally, is a guinea pig: the two species have different dietary requirements and different communication, a rabbit can seriously injure a guinea pig with a kick, and rabbits can carry Bordetella that makes guinea pigs ill. Keeping them together used to be standard advice and is now advised against.

The usual pairing is a neutered male and a neutered female, introduced gradually on neutral ground. Neutering matters for both sexes — for behaviour, for bonding, and because uterine cancer is very common in unspayed female rabbits.

Rabbits: it is nearly all hay.

RWAF guidance is roughly 85% hay, 10% leafy greens and 5% pellets, commonly summarised as around 80% forage. Pellets are a tablespoon-scale supplement, not a meal. Muesli-style mixes are worse than plain pellets because rabbits selectively eat the sugary bits and leave the fibre.

Hay does two jobs at once. Rabbit teeth grow continuously throughout life, and the side-to-side grinding needed to process long fibre is what wears them evenly. A rabbit on a low-fibre diet develops dental spurs and painful malocclusion. And that same fibre is what keeps the gut moving.

Unlimited hay should be available at all times, and it should be good — a rabbit should eat a volume of hay roughly the size of its own body every day.

Gut stasis is an emergency.

If a rabbit's gut stops moving, the system shuts down, and it is frequently fatal.

A rabbit that has not eaten, or has not passed droppings, for around twelve hours needs a vet — not overnight observation and not a wait-and-see. Other signs: hunching, pressing the belly to the floor, teeth grinding, reluctance to move, and much smaller or fewer droppings than usual.

Because rabbits hide illness, a rabbit that visibly looks unwell is usually a rabbit who has been unwell for a while.

Guinea pigs: vitamin C, every single day.

Guinea pigs, like humans and unlike almost every other pet species, cannot synthesise vitamin C. They must get it from their diet daily.

The requirement is at least 10 mg per kg of body weight per day, rising to 30 mg per kg per day for pregnant sows. In practice that is roughly 20–25 mg a day for an adult and 30–40 mg a day for a growing or pregnant animal.

If intake is inadequate, the first signs of scurvy appear within two to three weeks.

What to look for: a poor coat, poor wound healing and reduced resistance to infection, reduced appetite, weight loss, lethargy, dental disease, weak bones, apparent pain and reluctance to move, and bloody diarrhoea.

How to provide it: fresh food daily — bell peppers are particularly high — plus guinea-pig-specific pellets, which are formulated with vitamin C but lose potency over time, so buy small bags and check the date. Vitamin C added to drinking water is not reliable: it degrades quickly and makes the water taste unpleasant, so animals drink less. Talk to a vet about a stabilised supplement if you are unsure.

Guinea pigs: company and space.

Guinea pigs are highly social and should be kept in same-sex pairs or groups. A pair of sows, or two boars introduced young with enough space, are the usual arrangements.

Commonly cited minimum space for one guinea pig is around 7.5 square feet (0.7 square metres), with two to four square feet added per additional animal — and welfare organisations generally recommend considerably more than that minimum. Boars need extra room to avoid territorial conflict.

Most cages sold in pet shops are substantially below this. A grid-and-panel enclosure, or a large plastic storage tub setup, is usually both cheaper and several times larger.

Both species: the vet is a specific vet.

Rabbits and guinea pigs are exotics. Not every small animal practice sees many of them, anaesthesia is different, dental work requires particular equipment and skill, and drug choices differ. Find a practice with genuine rabbit or small-mammal experience before you need one, not during an emergency at eleven on a Sunday night.

Rabbits also need vaccination in many countries — against myxomatosis and rabbit haemorrhagic disease, including RHDV2 — and the schedule is region-specific. Ask your vet.

The short version.

Two of them, not one. Unlimited hay, and very little else. A guinea pig needs vitamin C every day. Much more space than the shop sold you. And an exotics vet you found before the emergency.

title: The kitten window closes before most kittens come home
summary: The feline sensitive period is roughly two to seven weeks. Kittens handled 40 minutes a day between three and seven weeks were still more sociable with people at a year old. Most kittens are rehomed after that.
content:
The single most important fact about socialising a kitten is an uncomfortable one: for a kitten adopted at ten or twelve weeks, most of the window has already closed, and it closed at the breeder's or in the foster home.

The window.

The proposed sensitive period for kitten socialisation is roughly two to seven weeks of age — Karsh and Turner (1988) — extending to around nine weeks in later work by McCune.

Compare that to dogs, where the window runs to around fourteen to sixteen weeks and overlaps neatly with the period after a puppy comes home. The feline window is earlier and shorter, and it is mostly over before the kitten meets its owner.

What was actually measured.

Kittens handled for 40 minutes a day between three and seven weeks of age spent more time in close contact with people at one year old than kittens handled 15 minutes a day. The effect persisted for a year, from a difference measured in weeks.

Handling of five to fifteen minutes a day in early life is associated with a reduced latency to approach unfamiliar people — that is, kittens handled early are quicker to walk towards a stranger as adults.

And it is not only handling by one person. Kittens given extra socialisation in a rescue setting — handling by multiple people, exposure to ordinary household sounds — showed less fearful behaviour towards humans, and their caretakers reported being strongly attached to them at one year.

Handling by several different people matters, because a kitten socialised to one person can generalise poorly to people in general.

What this means when choosing a kitten.

This turns into one genuinely useful question you can ask a breeder, a rescue or a foster carer: what handling has this kitten had, by how many people, and where has it been raised?

A kitten raised underfoot in a busy household, handled daily by several people from three weeks old, exposed to hoovers and doorbells and visitors, is a substantially different prospect from a kitten raised in a quiet outbuilding and handled at feeding time.

This is also the argument against taking kittens home too early. Kittens removed from the mother and litter before around eight weeks miss important social learning from their siblings — bite inhibition, play skills, feline social signals — and there is a body of work associating very early separation with behaviour problems later. Twelve to fourteen weeks is a common recommendation from breeders and behaviourists, and the trade-off with the socialisation window is exactly why what happens in those weeks matters so much.

What to do with a kitten who is already home.

The window may be closing or closed, but the work is still worth doing, done gently.

Let them set the pace. Sit on the floor, do something else, and let the kitten approach you. Chasing, grabbing and hauling a kitten out from under furniture teaches it that you are the thing to get away from.

Pair people with good things. Visitors who ignore the kitten and drop a treat are far more effective than visitors who want to hold it.

Handle in tiny doses, paired with food: paws, ears, mouth, being lifted, being held for three seconds and released. Build this now and every vet visit for fifteen years is easier.

Introduce the carrier properly, as furniture. Leave it out, open, with bedding in it, feed meals in it. A carrier that only appears before something frightening becomes a frightening object itself. Carrier training with positive reinforcement measurably reduces distress around veterinary visits.

Sounds, at low volume, paired with food: hoover, hairdryer, doorbell, traffic, other people's dogs.

Play with wand toys rather than hands. Hands as toys is charming in a kitten and a problem in an adult cat.

Do not force interaction with a hiding kitten. Hiding is coping. Removing the hiding place removes the coping and slows everything down.

And the environment matters as much as the handling: the five pillars from the AAFP and ISFM guidelines — a safe place, multiple separated resources, opportunity for play and predatory behaviour, positive predictable human interaction, and respect for the cat's sense of smell — are what a kitten needs to grow into a confident cat.

For a shy or feral-born kitten.

Progress is measured in weeks and is not linear. Small room, few decisions, food as the currency, no forced handling, and time spent in the room doing nothing in particular — reading out loud is genuinely effective.

If the kitten was born to a feral mother and had no human contact before around seven or eight weeks, be realistic: many such cats become affectionate with one or two people and never with strangers, and that is a good outcome rather than a failure.

The practical things in the first months.

The vaccination course: FVRCP from six to eight weeks with boosters every three to four weeks until at least sixteen weeks; rabies at twelve to sixteen weeks; FeLV in two doses from eight weeks after a negative test.

Two litter trays, in separate locations, large, uncovered, with fine unscented clumping litter.

Scratching posts that are tall, stable and upright, put where the kitten already scratches.

Play that runs the whole predatory sequence, ending with food.

And a vet visit early, while nothing is wrong, so the practice becomes a place where nothing much happens.

title: Play styles, and the mismatches worth knowing about
summary: Chasers, wrestlers, body-slammers and the dogs who just want to sniff. Breed predicts style loosely and temperament not at all — but style is where most playdate misunderstandings come from.
content:
Two friendly dogs can have a bad time together without either of them doing anything wrong. Usually the reason is style.

Dogs play in fairly distinct ways, and the way a dog plays is partly what it was bred to do with its body. This is the most useful thing breed tells you — considerably more useful than anything it tells you about temperament, which is mostly down to the individual, their early socialisation and their life since.

The main styles.

Chasers. Run, be run after, repeat. Herding breeds — Border Collies, Australian Shepherds, German Shepherds, Corgis, Kelpies — often play this way, and frequently add the herding element: circling, cutting off the other dog's line, sometimes nipping at heels or flanks. To another herding dog this is a great game. To a dog who has never been chased, being circled and cut off by a fast dog reads as being hunted.

Wrestlers. Body contact, mouth on neck and shoulders, rolling around, standing on each other. Terriers, especially bull breeds, and a lot of the molosser types. Loud, physical, and completely fine between two dogs who both want it.

Body-slammers. Run at the other dog and hit them. Retrievers, boxers, and a lot of the big sporting dogs. Enormously fun with another dog of similar size and build. Genuinely dangerous to a ten-pound dog and unpleasant to a fifteen-year-old one.

Tuggers and object players. The game is about a thing rather than about the other dog. Two dogs who both like this can play tug together for ages. It also means resources are involved, which raises the stakes if either dog guards.

Sniffers and parallel players. Some dogs, particularly scent hounds and a lot of confident adult dogs, do not really want to wrestle. They want to walk around near another dog, sniff things, and occasionally check in. This is real, valid social behaviour and it is often mistaken for a dog who "does not play". A parallel sniffing walk is a perfectly good playdate for two dogs like this.

The mismatches that cause trouble.

A chaser and a dog who dislikes being chased. This is the most common one. The chaser is having a wonderful time. The other dog is running away, which the chaser reads as the game continuing. The dog being chased escalates from avoiding to snapping, because it tried everything else first.

A body-slammer and a small or elderly dog. Not a temperament problem. A physics problem.

A wrestler and a dog with no contact tolerance. Mouth-on-neck is fine between dogs who both do it and threatening to a dog who does not.

A herding dog and, frankly, most things. Herding behaviour directed at another dog — circling, staring, controlling — is not aggression, but it is pressure, and a lot of dogs find it hard to be on the receiving end of it for very long.

Two dogs who both only want to be chased. Nothing happens. This is a harmless mismatch and quite funny to watch.

How to work out your own dog's style.

Watch three or four separate sessions with different dogs. What does your dog do first? Do they run away invitingly, run at the other dog, drop into a play bow and wait, go for a toy, or go and sniff a bush and glance back?

What do they do when the other dog does not respond? A dog who escalates when ignored — barking, pawing, jumping — is a dog who will overwhelm quieter partners. A dog who gives up and wanders off is easy to match.

Which dogs has your dog liked most? Look for the pattern rather than the breed.

Managing a mismatch.

You do not always need to abandon a pairing. Structure helps a lot.

Give them a job that is not each other. Two dogs who cannot play together directly will often walk beautifully together, hike together, or do scent games in the same field.

Interrupt on a timer. Every couple of minutes, call your dog out for thirty seconds. That resets arousal and gives the other dog a break they may not be able to ask for.

Manage the resource. If one is an object player, either play tug with your own dog separately or remove all toys.

Use space. A big open field lets a dog who wants out get out. A small garden does not, and a lot of conflict is really a dog who could not leave.

Finally: a dog is allowed to not like another dog. Humans do not enjoy every human they meet either, and a dog who has decided a particular playmate is not for them has told you something worth listening to rather than something to be trained out of them.

title: A microchip only works if the registration does
summary: Microchipped dogs went home 52.2% of the time against 21.9% unchipped; for cats it was 38.5% against 1.8%. Where a chipped animal was not returned, the usual reason was out-of-date owner details.
content:
Lord and colleagues looked at 7,704 microchipped animals entering fifty-three US animal shelters between August 2007 and March 2008. The return-to-owner rates:

Dogs without a microchip: 21.9%. Dogs with one: 52.2%.

Cats without a microchip: 1.8%. Cats with one: 38.5%.

Look at the cat numbers again. A lost cat without a chip went home fewer than two times in a hundred. With a chip, nearly four times in ten. There are not many single interventions in pet ownership with that kind of effect size.

And the finding that matters most.

Where a microchipped animal was not returned to its owner, the most common reason was incorrect or missing owner information in the registry database.

The chip worked. The scanner worked. The shelter did its job. And then the phone number belonged to someone else.

A microchip is a number, not a tracker.

This is the most common misunderstanding. The chip is a passive transponder about the size of a grain of rice. It has no battery, no GPS and no location function whatsoever. It does one thing: when a scanner is passed over it, it reports a number.

That number is only useful if it is registered to you, in a database, with contact details that currently work. The chip implanted at the shelter or the breeder is frequently registered to the shelter or the breeder and not to you.

Do this today, it takes ten minutes.

Find your pet's chip number. It will be on the adoption paperwork, the implant certificate, or in your vet's records — just ring and ask.

Look it up in the AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup Tool. It searches participating registries and tells you which one holds the chip. It does not show your details; it shows which registry to contact.

Contact that registry and confirm the record is in your name, with your current mobile number, a second contact who is not you, and your email.

Then set a calendar reminder to check it every year, and add it to your moving checklist, along with changing your phone provider.

Ask your vet to scan the chip at the annual visit. Chips can migrate under the skin and, rarely, fail. Thirty seconds confirms it is still there and still reading.

What else raises the odds.

A visible tag, with a phone number, worn all the time. Most lost pets are found by a neighbour, not by a shelter, and a tag means the animal goes home in ten minutes rather than entering a system. A chip is the backup for when the collar has come off — which is exactly when it usually happens.

For cats, a collar with a proper safety release. There is a real trade-off between strangulation risk and identification, and a breakaway collar is the compromise; many cats tolerate one well if introduced gradually.

Good recent photographs, including one showing any distinctive markings. When you need these, you will be too upset to take them.

Knowing the plan before you need it. Which shelters serve your area, which local lost-pet groups people actually use, and your vet's out-of-hours number.

If your pet does go missing.

Search close first, and quietly. Frightened cats in particular usually hide within a very small radius of where they went missing, often on the property. Look under and behind things at ground level, at night, calling softly and then listening.

Report it to every local shelter and go in person if you can. Descriptions travel badly.

Post in the local groups with a clear photo and a location.

And update the microchip registry with a lost flag if it supports one — many do, and it is what makes the chip do something rather than sit there.

title: Choosing a trainer: what the letters actually mean
summary: Dog training is unregulated — anyone can call themselves a behaviourist. Here is what CPDT-KA, CBCC-KA, CDBC, KPA CTP and DACVB each require, and the one question that tells you most.
content:
In the United States, dog training is an unregulated profession. There is no licence, no required education and no protected title. Anyone can advertise as a dog trainer, and anyone can call themselves a behaviourist.

That means the credentials that exist are voluntary, and the ones worth anything come from bodies that assess people independently rather than certifying graduates of their own paid course.

The credentials worth recognising.

CPDT-KA — Certified Professional Dog Trainer, Knowledge Assessed. Issued by the Certification Council for Professional Dog Trainers. Requires at least 300 hours of dog training experience in the previous three years, a proctored exam, and adherence to a code of ethics and a LIMA policy, meaning least intrusive, minimally aversive.

CPDT-KSA — Knowledge and Skills Assessed. The above plus submitted video of real training sessions, evaluated by the CCPDT. Rarer and harder.

CBCC-KA — Certified Behavior Consultant Canine, Knowledge Assessed. Also CCPDT. For behaviour problems rather than manners training: at least 300 hours of behaviour consulting in three years plus a 200-question exam.

CDBC and CCBC — Certified Dog Behavior Consultant and Certified Cat Behavior Consultant, from the International Association of Animal Behavior Consultants. Advanced behaviour work: aggression, severe anxiety, phobias, complex behaviour modification. Assessed by case study review.

KPA CTP — Karen Pryor Academy Certified Training Partner. A five-month program with online and hands-on instruction and both written and practical assessment.

DACVB — Diplomate of the American College of Veterinary Behaviorists. A licensed veterinarian who has completed a residency in behaviour and passed board examinations. This is the only one on the list who can also diagnose medical contributors and prescribe medication, and it is the right referral for serious aggression, severe separation distress, or any behaviour problem where pain or illness might be involved.

Also worth knowing: ACAAB and CAAB, Certified Applied Animal Behaviorists, which require graduate-level study in animal behaviour.

Note that "behaviourist" on its own means nothing. Many trainers use it. Without one of the credentials above it does not indicate any specific training or assessment.

The one question that tells you most.

Ask: "What happens when my dog gets it wrong?"

The answer you want involves changing something — making the exercise easier, adjusting the environment, improving the reinforcement, going back a step. The dog gets more information and a better setup.

The answer to walk away from involves applying something the dog wants to avoid: a collar correction, a spray, a shock, a leash pop, pinning, "showing them who's boss".

The AVSAB's position, based on current scientific evidence, is that only reward-based methods should be used for all dog training, including the treatment of behaviour problems, and that aversive methods — electronic collars, prong collars, choke chains, leash corrections and other physical or psychological punishment — should not be used. The documented risks include fear, anxiety, stress, aggression, stress-related illness, pessimism, and a worse relationship with the owner.

Other things worth asking.

What equipment will we use? A flat collar or harness, treats, toys, a long line, maybe a clicker. If the answer involves buying an electronic collar or a prong collar, that is your answer.

Can I watch a class before I book? Anyone confident in their teaching says yes.

What is your continuing education? Behaviour science moves. Someone who last learned anything in 2005 is teaching a model that has been substantially revised.

Do you have insurance and can you give references?

For a behaviour case: do you work with veterinarians, and would you refer to a veterinary behaviourist?

Warning signs.

Guaranteed results, particularly with aggression. Nobody can guarantee behaviour.

Board-and-train programs where you cannot observe and cannot visit. You are handing over an animal to unobserved handling by someone you cannot supervise, and it does not teach you anything, which is the part that has to last.

Heavy use of dominance and pack language: alpha, dominance, pack leader, submission. That framework is a misreading of decades-old captive wolf work and has been substantially revised. Its persistence tells you what someone reads.

Refusal to explain the method in advance.

Anyone who tells you to punish a growl. A growl is a warning that stops a bite.

For cats and other species.

A cat behaviour problem is not a job for a dog trainer. Look for a CCBC from IAABC, a veterinary behaviourist, or an International Cat Care accredited cat behaviourist. Litter box problems in particular are a veterinary question first — house-soiling is very frequently medical — and the AAFP and ISFM have published dedicated guidelines on diagnosing and solving them.

For rabbits, parrots and other species, IAABC certifies consultants in several specialisms and an exotics veterinarian is the first call.

The most important thing.

If you leave a session feeling uncomfortable about how your animal was handled, that feeling is data. You do not have to justify it, negotiate, or come back. You are allowed to leave.

title: Birds and reptiles: the two household hazards owners miss
summary: The lowest temperature at which a non-stick coating has been reported to kill birds in peer-reviewed literature is 396F — an ordinary pan. And the CDC does not recommend reptiles in homes with children under five.
content:
Two species groups, two hazards that owners routinely do not know about, and both are entirely preventable.

Birds: the danger is the kitchen.

Overheated non-stick coatings kill pet birds, often before anyone realises anything has happened.

Heating polytetrafluoroethylene — PTFE — releases carbonyl fluoride, hydrogen fluoride and perfluoroisobutylene. These gases are colourless and odourless, so there is no warning at all.

Pyrolysis is usually described as occurring above 260C (536F), but reported cases of toxicosis have occurred lower. The lowest temperature at which non-stick coatings have been reported in a peer-reviewed study to kill birds is 202C (396F). That is a pan preheating on a hob at a normal setting.

Birds are affected so severely because their respiratory system is extraordinarily efficient — a one-way airflow system with air sacs, which extracts far more from each breath than a mammal's does. It is a superb adaptation for flight and a catastrophic one for inhaled toxins.

Acute death from respiratory failure is the most common outcome. Milder exposures show as moist rales, laboured breathing, incoordination, depression or anxious behaviour, and signs can appear suddenly with death following within minutes.

The sources are wider than the frying pan: self-cleaning ovens on the cleaning cycle, PTFE-coated drip pans under hob burners (which exceed 315C/600F within minutes of ordinary use), heat lamp covers, irons and ironing board covers, some space heaters, and some hair appliances.

What to do if you keep birds: remove non-stick cookware from the house — stainless steel, cast iron and ceramic are all fine. Do not use the oven's self-cleaning cycle at all. Check drip pans, irons and heaters for PTFE coatings. Do not house birds in or near the kitchen. And if there is any exposure event, get the bird into fresh air immediately and to an avian vet.

Other airborne hazards worth knowing about, since the mechanism is the same: aerosol sprays, air fresheners and plug-ins, scented candles, strong cleaning products, and cigarette smoke.

Birds: foraging is the enrichment that matters.

Wild parrots are reported to spend roughly four to eight hours a day foraging. A conventional food bowl reduces that to under an hour.

An estimated 10% of captive parrots perform feather-destructive behaviour, and limited foraging opportunity is one hypothesised driver — the redirected foraging hypothesis, which has been tested as a treatment approach in African greys.

Foraging enrichment reliably increases the time birds spend foraging. It should be said honestly that it has not been shown to reach wild time budgets, and it does not eliminate feather-damaging behaviour. It is not a cure.

Practically: stop using a bowl as the only food source. Wrap food in paper, hide it in cardboard tubes, thread it onto skewers, put it in foraging toys, scatter it through shreddable material, place it in several locations so the bird has to travel. Rotate the arrangements, since novelty is much of the point.

And feather plucking is a veterinary problem before it is a behavioural one. The medical causes — skin disease, parasites, infection, nutritional deficiency, organ disease, pain — are at least as common as the behavioural ones. An avian vet first.

Reptiles and amphibians: the danger is Salmonella.

Reptiles and amphibians commonly carry Salmonella as part of their normal gut flora. A perfectly healthy animal sheds it, intermittently, and no amount of cleaning eliminates it.

The CDC's guidance is that reptiles and amphibians are not recommended for households with children under five, people with weakened immune systems, or adults over sixty-five, and that they should not be kept in childcare centres.

For everyone else, the mitigation is straightforward.

Wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water immediately after handling a reptile or amphibian, or anything in the area where they live. Hand sanitiser if soap and water are not available. Adults should supervise young children washing.

Do not clean enclosures, dishes or equipment in the kitchen sink, or anywhere food is prepared. Use a dedicated tub, and disinfect the area afterwards.

Keep the animals out of the kitchen and out of food preparation areas entirely.

Do not kiss the animal, and do not eat or drink while handling it.

Since 1975 the FDA has banned US sale of turtles with shells under four inches, specifically because small turtles end up in small children's mouths.

Reptiles: the other thing that goes wrong.

Most reptile illness seen in practice is husbandry-related, and the two variables that matter most are temperature and UVB light.

Reptiles are ectothermic — they regulate temperature by moving between warmer and cooler places, so an enclosure needs a genuine thermal gradient, not one uniform temperature. Many species also need UVB to synthesise vitamin D3 and absorb calcium; without it they develop metabolic bone disease, which is common, painful and preventable.

UVB bulbs lose output long before they stop emitting visible light, so they need replacing on schedule rather than when they fail.

Every species has different requirements, and species-specific research from a reliable source — a specialist veterinary or herpetological reference, not a pet shop care sheet — is the single most important thing you can do before acquiring one.

And find an exotics vet in advance. There are far fewer of them than there are reptile owners.

title: The teenage dog is real, and it is not defiance
summary: Asher and colleagues found dogs at eight months were slower to obey — but only when the cue came from their own person, not a stranger. It coincides with the peak age at which dogs are given up.
content:
At around eight months your beautifully trained puppy stops listening. The recall evaporates. The sit that was solid for four months now requires three requests. Meanwhile they are fine at class, fine with your friend, fine with the trainer.

The conclusion almost everyone draws is that the dog is being deliberately difficult, or has "forgotten" its training, or is testing boundaries.

What the research found.

Asher, Harvey, Sommerville and England published work in Biology Letters in 2020 examining behaviour across adolescence in dogs. They found a passing phase of carer-specific conflict-like behaviour, with reduced trainability and responsiveness to commands.

The critical detail: dogs took longer to respond to a "sit" cue at eight months — but only when the cue was given by their own caregiver. Not when it was given by a stranger.

The effect was more pronounced in dogs whose behaviour indicated a less secure attachment to their caregiver.

So it is specific to the relationship, it is developmental, and it maps onto something familiar from human adolescence rather than onto disobedience.

Adolescence in dogs runs roughly from five months to two years, varying with size and breed — larger breeds mature later.

Why this matters beyond feeling better about it.

The same paper notes that this phase coincides with the peak age at which dogs are relinquished to shelters for behavioural problems.

That is the whole reason to know about it. Owners hit the hardest six months, conclude the dog is fundamentally difficult or that they have failed, and give up — right before the phase resolves on its own.

What actually happens in this period.

Recall degrades, often dramatically, especially around other dogs and interesting smells.

Previously reliable cues need repeating.

New fears appear, sometimes about things the dog was previously fine with. Adolescent fear periods are commonly described, and a dog can suddenly become suspicious of a bin it has walked past for months.

Reactivity can emerge for the first time — barking and lunging on lead at other dogs — in a dog who was sociable as a puppy.

The dog becomes bigger, stronger and faster while the brakes are still developing.

Play with other dogs may get rougher, and other dogs' tolerance drops. Adult dogs stop giving puppy licence at roughly this age and start telling adolescents off, which is normal, useful, and alarming to watch.

For entire dogs, sex hormones arrive: roaming, marking, interest in other dogs' seasons.

Sleep can decrease, and with it, patience.

What actually helps.

Lower the criteria, do not raise the pressure. This is the central move. Go back to easier versions of everything: shorter distances, fewer distractions, a long line instead of off-lead freedom. You are not undoing progress; you are keeping the behaviour succeeding while the brain reorganises.

Pay more, not less. Higher-value rewards, more often, for things the dog used to do for free. It is temporary.

Use a long line. This is the single most practical piece of adolescent equipment. It lets you keep the dog safe and keeps you from repeatedly shouting a recall that is being ignored — which is the fastest way to permanently break a recall.

Stop repeating cues. If a cue does not work, do not say it four more times; go and make it easy to succeed, then ask again in a simpler setting. Every ignored cue is training the dog that the cue is optional.

Protect them from bad experiences. Adolescent fear periods mean a frightening event now can have longer-lasting effects. Manage distance, avoid overwhelming situations, and do not "flood" a worried adolescent to prove there is nothing to fear.

Keep the exercise varied and the brain busy. Sniffing walks, scent games, shaping sessions, and chewing all help more than more distance.

Do not let them practise reactivity. If lead reactivity is emerging, deal with it now with distance and counterconditioning, and get help early — it is far easier to change at nine months than at three years.

Do not switch to aversive methods. The temptation to escalate is highest exactly here, when the dog seems to be ignoring you deliberately. AVSAB's position, based on current evidence, is that only reward-based methods should be used for all dog training, and the documented risks of aversive methods include fear, anxiety, aggression, and a worse relationship with the owner — which is precisely what an adolescent dog with a less secure attachment does not need.

And the attachment finding cuts the other way too: the more predictable, fair and rewarding you are during this period, the better the ground you are building on.

When it is not adolescence.

Any sudden behaviour change deserves a vet visit. Pain is the great imitator, and a young dog with developing hip or elbow problems, or a gut problem, or an ear infection, can present as an adolescent with an attitude.

And if reactivity or fear is escalating rather than fluctuating, get a qualified behaviour professional involved now rather than waiting it out.

It does end.

Most dogs come out the other side, somewhere between eighteen months and three years depending on size, and are recognisably the dog you were training at six months — with everything you taught them still in there.

The dogs who do not come out the other side are mostly the ones whose owners gave up in the middle, or who spent the period practising problems nobody managed.

title: Tug of war will not make your dog dominant
summary: Fourteen Golden Retrievers, twenty games they were allowed to win and twenty they lost. It made no difference to the dog-human relationship. Here is what actually matters when you play tug.
content:
There is a persistent piece of advice that says you should never let a dog win a game of tug, or better yet never play tug at all, because it teaches the dog that it can beat you and makes it dominant.

Somebody actually tested this.

The study.

Rooney and Bradshaw worked with fourteen Golden Retrievers. Each dog went through two conditions: twenty sessions of tug-of-war against a human experimenter in which the dog was allowed to win, and twenty sessions in which the dog lost.

They then measured the dominance-related dimensions of the dog-human relationship.

There was no effect. Whether the dog won or lost forty games of tug did not change the relationship in the way the folklore predicts.

The authors added one useful caveat: the effects of games may be modified by whether play signals are present. In other words, a game that both parties clearly understand to be a game behaves like a game. A confrontation that neither party framed as play is a different event. That is a real distinction and it is the thing to pay attention to — not who ends up holding the rope.

Why the myth persists.

It descends from a model of dog behaviour built on a misreading of captive wolf studies from the mid-twentieth century, in which dogs were understood to be constantly angling for rank in a household hierarchy. That framework has been thoroughly revised. Dogs are not running a status campaign against you, and the behaviours it was invented to explain — pulling on the lead, going through doors first, guarding the sofa — all have better explanations.

Why tug is worth playing.

It is one of the few games where you and your dog are doing something together rather than you throwing something and the dog fetching it.

It is enormously reinforcing for most dogs, which makes it an excellent reward. A dog who will work for a tug game has a reward you can deliver anywhere without a treat bag.

It builds a reliable "let go", which is one of the more genuinely useful behaviours a dog can have.

It is a decent physical workout in a small space and in bad weather.

For dogs with a strong grab-and-hold instinct, it gives that a legitimate outlet.

How to play it well.

Have rules and keep them consistent. The rules are for clarity, not for dominance.

Start on a cue. "Get it" or "tug". The game begins when you say so, not when the dog shoves a rope into your leg.

Teach a release. Stop moving the toy, hold it still, and wait, or trade for a treat. The instant the dog lets go, mark it and restart the game. The game restarting is the reward for letting go, which is much stronger than the treat.

Let the dog win, often. Winning is what keeps the dog in the game. A dog who never wins stops playing.

Pull side to side, not up and down, and never lift the dog's front feet off the ground. Vertical force and a dog thrashing on the end of a rope is how teeth and necks get hurt. Let the dog do the pulling and you provide resistance.

Stop if teeth touch skin. Not a telling-off — just an immediate, boring end to the game for thirty seconds. Dogs learn that one very fast.

End before the dog is over the top. Two or three short rounds beat one long escalating one.

Skip tug entirely with puppies who are teething and losing teeth, with dogs who have neck, back or dental problems, and with any dog who has resource-guarded a toy from a person. That last one is a behaviour question to take to a qualified behaviour consultant rather than something to practise with a rope.

One more thing.

If a training method is justified to you on the grounds that your dog is trying to dominate you, treat that as a signal about the method. The AVSAB's position, based on current evidence, is that reward-based methods should be used for all dog training including behaviour problems, and that aversive tools and techniques carry documented welfare risks. A game of tug is not a power struggle. It is a game.

title: Kids and dogs: the bites happen at home
summary: 77% of biting dogs belong to the family or a friend, and 89.8% of dogs involved in facial bites to children were known to the child. The dog to supervise is not the stranger's.
content:
The mental image of a dog bite is a loose stray in the street. The data says otherwise, consistently, and the difference matters because it changes where you put your attention.

What the figures say.

77% of biting dogs belong to the victim's family or a friend.

89.8% of the dogs involved in facial bites to children were known to those children.

Children five and under are at high risk of being bitten in the face by a familiar dog, and are more likely than older children to need hospitalisation.

Children under twelve account for close to half of all dog-bite-related emergency department visits. More than half of dog-related injuries overall are to children, and in children under four those bites are frequently to the head and neck — because that is where a small child's face is relative to a dog's.

Children between five and nine are bitten most frequently, usually by familiar dogs in ordinary settings.

Breed is not the useful variable here. The AVMA has published a background paper making the case that breed is a poor predictor of bite risk. Household, familiarity and supervision are much better predictors.

Why familiar dogs.

Because that is where the hours are. A child spends thousands of hours with the family dog and thirty seconds with a stranger's. Familiarity also removes caution on both sides: nobody supervises a dog they trust, and nobody tells a child to be careful around a dog they have known since birth.

Almost every bite has a run-up. Dogs give a long sequence of signals before they bite: looking away, licking lips, yawning when not tired, freezing, moving away, showing the whites of the eyes, a low growl. Most of those are missed, and the ones that are noticed are often punished — a dog told off for growling learns to skip the growl next time.

What to actually do.

Supervise actively. The AVMA's guidance is not to leave children unsupervised with dogs, including the family pet. Active supervision means being in the room and watching, close enough to intervene. Being in the same house is not supervision, and neither is being on the sofa on your phone.

Teach the dog has a place nobody follows. A crate, a bed, a room. The rule is absolute and applies to adults too: when the dog is there, the dog is left alone. A dog with a reliable exit almost never has to escalate, and most household bites happen to dogs who could not leave.

Never let a child hug, lie on, or put their face near a dog's. Hugging is a primate greeting and a restraint to a dog. The photographs people love — small child's face pressed against the dog's — are, in the majority of cases, photographs of a dog showing appeasement signals that nobody in the room read.

Teach children where to touch. The AVMA suggests gentle petting on the back or shoulders, and avoiding the face, tail and ears.

Teach one rule that fits in a child's head. "Ask, then let the dog come to you." If the dog does not come over, the dog said no. That single idea covers most situations better than a list.

Do not disturb a dog who is eating, chewing something, sleeping, or unwell. These are the classic contexts.

Watch the dog, not just the child. Children are unpredictable, so it is the dog's signals that tell you when to end the interaction — and they come first.

Never punish a growl. A growl is a dog choosing to warn instead of bite. It is information and it should be answered by removing the pressure, then working out what caused it. Suppress it and you have a dog who goes from calm to bite with nothing in between.

The two ages that need extra attention.

A new baby or a toddler starting to walk. A crawling and then walking child changes the household completely from a dog's point of view: unpredictable movement at the dog's eye level, in the dog's spaces, grabbing. This is the classic time for management to be set up in advance — baby gates, a dog space that is off-limits, and a plan.

An ageing or unwell dog. Pain lowers tolerance, and hearing and sight loss mean a dog can be startled by a child who did nothing wrong. A previously bombproof old dog snapping at a grandchild is usually a dog in pain, and it is a reason to see the vet rather than to conclude the dog has changed character.

If it has already happened.

Any bite that breaks skin needs medical attention, and dog bites to the face and hands are particularly prone to infection.

And the dog needs a veterinary examination too, because a first-time bite from a dog with no history is quite often a pain response. After that, a qualified behaviour professional — a veterinary behaviourist, or a certified behaviour consultant — not a general obedience class and not advice from the internet.

title: Reading a cat: the signal that comes before the bite
summary: Tail twitch, ear rotation, skin rippling — and the one owners consistently misread, which is a sudden stillness. It looks like contentment. It is the last warning.
content:
Cats are frequently described as unpredictable. They are not. They are quiet, and the signals are small, and most people have never been told what to look at.

Start with the stillness.

If you take one thing from this: a cat that suddenly goes still while being petted is not relaxing. It is the opposite.

Overstimulation during petting builds through a sequence — tail twitching, ear rotating backwards, a ripple of skin along the back, a turn of the head towards your hand — and then a stillness, and then the bite or the grab.

The stillness reads to a human as settling. It is a freeze, and it is the last thing before the cat acts. Stop petting there and almost every "unpredictable" bite disappears.

The tail.

A relaxed cat moving around the house carries its tail down in a loose U, or up.

The upright tail is worth knowing specifically: a tail held straight up, often with a slight hook at the tip, is a friendly approach signal. It is one of the clearest positive signals cats give, and it is an invitation.

A tail held tight against the body signals arousal or defensiveness.

A tail whipping or thumping side to side is irritation. In a dog that would be ambiguous; in a cat it is not. It commonly escalates.

A puffed tail is fear or high arousal.

Slow tip-twitching while watching something is usually focus rather than annoyance — a hunting posture.

The ears.

Upright, pointing forward or slightly to the side, is relaxed and interested.

Rotating backwards from a forward position is a warning. It is a change of state and it is easy to see if you are watching for it.

Flattened fully back against the head — "aeroplane ears" — is extreme fear and readiness to defend. A cat at this point is not being naughty and cannot be reasoned with; it needs space and time.

Ears flicking rapidly between positions signal conflict — the cat is undecided, which usually means it needs you to back off so it can decide.

The eyes.

Dilated pupils mean arousal. That is all. It can be play, fear, or aggression, and it has to be read with the rest of the body. In dim light it means the light is dim.

Constricted pupils in bright-ish conditions can accompany offensive aggression.

A slow blink — eyes narrowing, closing softly, opening again — is a positive social signal. You can return it, and many cats will answer.

A hard, unblinking stare, particularly at another cat, is a threat. Between cats in a household, staring is one of the main forms conflict takes.

Whiskers.

Relaxed and slightly out to the sides is neutral. Pushed forward and fanned is interest or arousal. Flattened back against the face is fear.

The whole animal.

Loose and rounded, lying with the belly exposed and legs loose, is relaxed. A cat showing its belly is usually expressing comfort — it is not always an invitation to touch it, and many cats will grab a hand that accepts the invitation.

Crouched with the feet under the body, tense, is not resting. That is a cat ready to move.

The arched back with the fur up and the sideways posture is a classic defensive threat display: making itself large because it is frightened.

Hiding, wedged into a small space, is a coping mechanism, not sulking. Removing the hiding place does not speed anything up; it takes away the cat's only strategy.

How to greet a cat.

Offer a hand or a finger at the cat's nose height, a little way away, and stop. Let them come and rub on it or not.

If they rub, pet where the scent glands are — cheeks, chin, the base of the ears, along the side of the face. Most cats like this a great deal.

Avoid the belly, the base of the tail and the legs unless you know the individual very well.

Then stop after a few seconds and see whether they ask for more. Consent-based petting — a few strokes, pause, wait — is the single best change most people can make, and cats respond to it noticeably.

Do not pick them up unless you know they like it. Many cats tolerate it rather than enjoy it, and tolerance has a limit.

Two things that are frequently misread.

Purring is not always contentment. Cats purr when relaxed, and also when frightened, in pain, and when dying. Purring plus a tense crouched body and dilated pupils is a cat in trouble, and it is one of the reasons feline pain is missed.

An exposed belly is a display of comfort, not consent.

When the body language changes and stays changed.

A cat that has become less tolerant of handling, or that has started objecting to being touched around the back end, or that has stopped jumping onto things it used to reach, is usually telling you about pain rather than about mood.

Degenerative joint disease in cats is common and remarkably hard to see — in one radiographic study, no obvious pain was detectable on examination in any of the cats with appendicular osteoarthritis. Behaviour change is often the only sign there is.

So a personality change in a cat is a veterinary question first.

title: Grief for an animal is real grief, and it is disenfranchised
summary: Research describes grief after companion animal loss as comparable in intensity to grief after human loss — and as routinely minimised, which is the thing that makes it harder to carry.
content:
Somebody will ask whether you are getting another one. Somebody will say at least it was not a person. You will be expected back at work on Monday.

This article does not have stages, a timeline, or a promise about how long it takes. It has three things that are worth knowing.

One: the intensity is documented, not excessive.

Grief following the loss of a companion animal has been described in the research literature as comparable in intensity to grief following the death of a human loved one.

That is not a sentimental claim. It is an observation about attachment: the relationship involved daily physical contact, a routine built around another creature's needs, and years of continuous presence. Its ending removes all of that at once, and the house is a different shape by dinnertime.

If you feel that this is disproportionate, the reason is probably not that your reaction is disproportionate.

Two: the problem is that it is disenfranchised.

Disenfranchised grief is grief that is not, or cannot be, openly acknowledged, publicly mourned, or socially supported. Pet loss is one of the standard examples.

What that means in practice: there is no funeral leave. There is no ritual most people recognise. Colleagues do not know what to say. And people offer comfort in forms that minimise — get another one, at least it was quick, it was only a cat.

The documented consequence is suppression. Where people sense their grief is not considered worthy of acknowledgement, they inhibit the grieving reaction or hide it. That is the mechanism by which unsupported grief becomes prolonged, and it is why the social response matters as much as the loss.

So if you have found yourself crying in a car park because you could not do it at your desk: that is not weakness. That is disenfranchisement doing exactly what the literature describes.

Three: support exists, and most of it is free.

Several veterinary schools run pet loss support lines staffed by trained volunteers, and the ASPCA operates a pet loss hotline. These exist specifically because this grief has nowhere else to go.

There are counsellors who work specifically in pet bereavement, and the Association for Pet Loss and Bereavement runs support groups.

Your own vet practice will often know local resources, and many will talk to you about it. Veterinary staff are not neutral here either — in one study, 25% of veterinarians reported not feeling supported in their own grief, 30% felt misunderstood, and 30% were unable to express it naturally. The person who was in the room with you may be carrying some of it too.

Some things that people find helpful.

Doing something concrete. A photograph printed and framed rather than left on a phone. Paw prints or fur kept. Planting something. Writing down the things you would otherwise forget — the specific noise they made at the door, the exact place they slept.

Telling somebody who gets it, which is often not the person you would ordinarily tell.

Keeping the routine partly intact for a while. The walk you took every morning is still a good walk, and the hardest hour of the day is usually the one that was theirs.

Allowing the guilt to be examined rather than argued with. Nearly everybody carries some — that they waited too long, or did not wait long enough, or missed a sign, or were not there. It is nearly always a person applying hindsight to a decision made without it. Saying it out loud to somebody, once, does more than deciding privately that it is irrational.

Being careful with the euthanasia memory. If the last day is the image that keeps returning, that is common and it does fade. Deliberately recalling a specific ordinary day instead — a particular walk, a particular afternoon — is a technique many people find works.

If you have children.

Use the actual words: died, dead. Euphemisms like "put to sleep" and "gone away" are frightening to young children in ways adults do not anticipate.

Let them see adults grieve. It is often a child's first bereavement, and what they learn is that grief is survivable and can be spoken about.

Let them take part in whatever you do to mark it.

If there are other animals in the house.

They may be affected — changes in appetite, searching, vocalising, altered sleep. Some of it is response to the absence and some of it is response to you.

Keep routines steady, and see a vet if an animal stops eating or seems unwell rather than unsettled.

Whether to let other animals see the body is a genuine open question with no clear evidence either way. Do what feels right; you will not have got it wrong.

And about getting another one.

There is no correct interval, and the people who suggest one usually mean well. Some people find another animal helps immediately. Some need a year. Some know, correctly, that this was the last one.

The only thing worth avoiding is choosing quickly in order to stop feeling something — mostly because it is unfair to arrive as a replacement for an animal you are still grieving, and it is a lot to ask of a new one.

title: House-training: a management problem wearing a training costume
summary: Full bladder control does not arrive until around five months, so frequency is physiology rather than failure. And punishing an accident produces a dog that hides to eliminate, which owners misread as guilt.
content:
House-training is mostly not training. It is supervision, a schedule, and patience, and the training part is small.

The physiology first.

A puppy cannot reliably hold it. Full bladder control does not develop until around five months of age, so a young puppy needs frequent opportunities regardless of how well the process is going.

A rough guide for how long a puppy can hold: roughly one hour per month of age, plus one, during the day — so a three-month-old is on a four-hour ceiling at best, and much less when awake and active. Overnight is different and longer.

Which means an accident at ten weeks is not a failure of understanding. It is a bladder.

The schedule.

Take the puppy out first thing in the morning, last thing at night, and after every one of these: waking from any sleep, eating, drinking, and playing. Plus every hour or so in between while awake.

Go to the same spot. Scent does a lot of the work.

Stand still and be boring while you wait. If you play, the puppy plays, and remembers to wee ten minutes later on the carpet.

Reward immediately, outside, at the moment they finish — not when you get back in the house, which rewards coming inside. Something genuinely good, every time, for weeks.

Then, if they were going out to play anyway, play. Going in immediately after every wee teaches the puppy that eliminating ends the fun, which is a reason to hold on.

Supervision and management.

Between outings, the puppy is either directly watched, contained, or asleep. An unsupervised puppy in a large house will find a corner, and every accident that happens is a small amount of practice at the wrong thing.

Use baby gates and closed doors to keep the puppy in the room you are in. Some people tether the lead to their belt for a fortnight, which works.

Learn the pre-wee signals: circling, sniffing intently, sudden restlessness, heading for a corner or behind furniture, and drifting away from the group. When you see one, go outside.

Crates, used properly.

A crate exploits a puppy's instinct not to soil where it sleeps, which is why it helps.

Size it so the puppy can just stand up, turn around and lie down. A crate with a spare end becomes a bedroom and a bathroom, which defeats the purpose. Many crates come with a divider for exactly this reason.

Introduce it voluntarily: food in it, a chew in it, door open, never shut in until they go in happily. It must never be used as punishment.

And it has a time limit. A crate is not a solution to being out all day. A puppy left crated beyond its physical ability to hold on is put in an impossible position, and will soil the crate — which then damages the very instinct that made the crate useful.

Accidents.

Do not punish. Not shouting, not the rolled-up newspaper, and absolutely not the nose in it. Dogs do not connect a punishment with something they did earlier, and the lesson learned is not "do not go indoors" but "do not go in front of that person".

That is the origin of the dog who sneaks behind the sofa, and of the dog who will not eliminate on a lead in front of you — a genuinely inconvenient problem to have created.

The "guilty look" is a red herring. It is appeasement behaviour in response to your body language and tone, not an admission. Dogs produce it whether or not they did anything.

Instead: if you catch them mid-act, interrupt gently with a cheerful noise, scoop them up, take them outside, and reward if they finish there. If you find it afterwards, clean it up and say nothing.

Clean with an enzymatic cleaner made for pet urine. Ordinary household cleaners leave scent markers a dog can smell perfectly well, and anything containing ammonia smells like urine and actively invites a repeat.

When it is not working.

Progress is not linear. Regression around adolescence, after a house move, or when a new animal or baby arrives is common.

See a vet if: a previously reliable dog starts having accidents; there is straining, blood, or very frequent small amounts; the dog is drinking noticeably more; or house-training is making no progress at all despite consistency. Urinary tract infections are common in puppies and make house-training impossible until treated, and increased drinking has a list of medical causes worth ruling out.

For an adult rescue dog, assume nothing and start from the beginning, with the same schedule and the same supervision. Many are house-trained and simply do not yet know that this house has rules, or that this surface is the outside. Two weeks of doing it properly usually settles it.

And for a dog that eliminates only when you are out, or only when greeting, those are different problems — separation-related distress and excitement or submissive urination — and they need different approaches rather than more house-training.
