title: When a good match is not a good match
summary: The app scores five things and weights them very differently. A 62 built on temperament and size is a better afternoon than an 82 built on breed and age — here is how to read the breakdown.
content:
PetPals gives you a number out of a hundred and a breakdown behind it. The number is useful. The breakdown is more useful, and most people never look at it.

The first thing to know is that the breakdown is not in percentages.

Each dimension is worth a different maximum: temperament 30, size 25, shared activities 25, breed 12, age 8. What you see in the breakdown is the points earned out of that maximum, not a percentage of anything.

So "temperament 18, age 8" does not mean age scored better. Age scored perfectly out of a possible 8. Temperament scored 60% of a possible 30. The dog with 18 on temperament and 8 on age has a moderate temperament fit and a perfect age fit — and the temperament number is the one that will decide how the afternoon goes.

Divide by the maximum before you compare anything.

Why a 62 can beat an 82.

Consider two candidates for your 55lb four-year-old Labrador.

Candidate A scores 82. Breed 12 out of 12 — another Labrador. Age 8 out of 8 — also four. Size 24 out of 25. Temperament 20 out of 30. Activities 18 out of 25.

Candidate B scores 62. Breed 0 out of 12 — a mixed-breed nobody can classify. Age 3 out of 8 — seven years old. Size 25 out of 25. Temperament 30 out of 30. Activities 25 out of 25.

Candidate A looks better and is worth less. What made A's score was two dimensions that describe paperwork: the same breed and the same birthday. What made B's score was three dimensions that describe an afternoon: the same size, the same temperament, and the same idea of what a good time is.

Breed and age together are only 20 points out of 100, deliberately. They are the weakest predictors of whether two dogs will enjoy each other, and they are the easiest to over-read because they are the most visible.

What each dimension is actually telling you.

Temperament, 30 points. The largest share, because how two dogs handle arousal determines whether things stay fun. Identical temperaments score full marks; certain pairs are treated as compatible rather than identical. A low score here is the one to take seriously.

Size, 25 points. Scored on the ratio of the lighter dog to the heavier, not the difference. Within about 15% counts as the same size. The score falls to zero at a ratio of about one to three — a 15lb dog and a 45lb dog. That is not snobbery about small dogs. It is that size mismatch is the one dimension where a mistake causes an injury rather than a bad mood.

Activities, 25 points. Overlap relative to the combined list, so a dog whose owner ticked every box does not automatically out-score a genuinely similar dog. There is a small uplift when the shared activities also suit both temperaments.

Breed, 12 points. A hint about play style — chasers, wrestlers, body-slammers — and nothing more.

Age, 8 points. Real but small. Five years apart scores zero, which barely dents a total.

How to read your own list in practice.

Sort by temperament and size first. If both are strong, the total almost does not matter.

Treat a zero on size as a hard stop unless you have read up on running a mismatched playdate safely and you are willing to manage it closely.

Treat a low temperament score as a reason to meet on a long parallel walk rather than in a fenced space, at least the first time.

Ignore a zero on breed. It usually means one of the dogs is a mix the table has no entry for, which tells you nothing at all.

Do not chase the highest number in your list. Pick three or four in the fifties and above with good temperament and size fit, and meet them. Meeting is the actual test.

What the score cannot see.

Whether either dog slept badly. Whether one of them is sore — pain changes tolerance more than any dimension in this model. Whether your dog has had a bad experience with a dog that looked like that one. Whether the other owner will actually supervise. Whether today is the day.

The score narrows a field of strangers to a handful worth trying. Ten minutes of watching them on neutral ground tells you the rest, and no algorithm is going to replace that.

title: Measuring a life: the quality-of-life scale, and what it is for
summary: Seven things, scored one to ten: hurt, hunger, hydration, hygiene, happiness, mobility, and more good days than bad. It is not an arithmetic verdict. It is a way to see a trend you are too close to notice.
content:
There is a point in caring for an animal with a life-limiting illness where the question changes from what else can be done to whether continuing is kind. It is the hardest question in pet ownership, and it is made harder by being asked alone, at night, without any way to check your own judgement.

The quality-of-life scale is a tool for that, and it is worth knowing about long before you need it.

The HHHHHMM scale.

Published by the veterinarian Alice Villalobos, who developed it as part of an end-of-life care programme. Seven categories, each scored from 1 to 10 where 10 is best.

Hurt. Is pain adequately controlled? Can the animal breathe comfortably? Pain and breathing are grouped first deliberately — they matter most.

Hunger. Is the animal eating enough, willingly, without assistance?

Hydration. Is the animal drinking enough, or receiving fluids?

Hygiene. Can they be kept clean and dry? Are there pressure sores, soiling, wounds being managed?

Happiness. Do they show interest, respond to the family, engage with things they used to enjoy? Are they anxious, isolated, or withdrawn?

Mobility. Can they get up, move around, get to food, water and the toilet? Do they need help, and how much?

More good days than bad. The overall ratio.

A score above 5 in each category, or a total above 35, is described as an acceptable quality of life for continuing end-of-life care and support.

What it is actually for.

Two things, and the first is the one people miss.

It is a tracking tool. Its stated purpose includes measuring whether a palliative care plan is working and tuning it, not only deciding when to stop. Score weekly, write it down, keep the sheet. A single score tells you almost nothing. Six weekly scores tell you the direction of travel, which is exactly what a person living with the animal every day cannot see.

The reason it works is that decline is gradual and adaptation is invisible. You start lifting the dog onto the sofa; a month later you are carrying them outside; a month after that you are cleaning them twice a day — and each step felt like a small adjustment. A number written down in March, compared with the number in June, does not adapt.

And it is a way to convert a diffuse dread into seven specific, observable things. "Is she suffering" cannot be answered. "Is she eating, is she comfortable, can she get outside, does she still greet you" can be, one at a time.

What it is not.

It is not an arithmetic verdict, and it should never be used as one. A score of 34 does not mean today, and 36 does not mean not yet.

It does not replace a conversation with your vet, who can tell you what is likely to happen next, what pain relief is still available, and what a bad death would look like if you wait for one.

And it does not weigh the categories for your particular animal. For a dog whose whole life was running, mobility may matter more than the scale implies. For a cat who was always fastidious, hygiene may matter more. You are allowed to know that about your own animal.

Other things that help.

Keep a simple daily record — a good day, a bad day, and one line about why. Over a month it becomes evidence rather than impression.

Make a list, in advance and while calm, of five things your animal loves. Greeting you at the door, the walk to the corner, sleeping on the bed, dinner, chasing the wand toy. Revisit it periodically. When most of the list has gone, that is information.

Ask your vet directly: "if this were your animal, what would you be thinking about?" Vets are often careful not to appear to push, and many will answer that question honestly and gratefully.

Ask what a crisis would look like — an obstruction, a bleed, a respiratory decompensation — and whether it is likely. Many people who wait find that the decision is eventually taken out of their hands at three in the morning in an unfamiliar emergency room, and would have chosen differently if they had known that was the alternative.

Ask about home euthanasia if it is available and would matter to you.

The thing that is true and rarely said.

Almost everybody who has made this decision believes afterwards that they waited slightly too long. Almost nobody believes they went too early.

That is not an instruction. It is worth knowing when you are weighing the fear of acting too soon against the fear of letting an animal suffer, because the first fear is much louder and the second is more often realised.

There is no right day. There is a window, and it is usually wider than it feels, and inside that window the decision is yours and your vet's rather than a number's.

title: Old pets hide pain, and cats hide it best
summary: Radiographic studies have found degenerative joint disease in a majority of cats, and in one study no obvious pain was found on examination in any cat with appendicular arthritis. "Slowing down" is a symptom, not an age.
content:
The single most common thing owners say about an old animal is that they are slowing down. It is usually true, and it is usually not just age. It is usually pain.

Cats are the extreme case.

Reported prevalence of degenerative joint disease in cats varies with the study population and how it was measured, and every version of the number is high. One radiographic study found appendicular DJD in 74.26% of the cats examined. Another found radiographic signs in 33.9% of cats with clinical signs recorded in 16.5%, mostly in cats aged ten and over. Review articles commonly cite roughly 60% of all cats and over 90% of cats older than twelve.

The reason the numbers vary so much is the reason this article exists. In one of those studies, no obvious pain was detected on examination in any of the cats with appendicular osteoarthritis.

A cat with painful joints does not limp. Cats are quadrupeds who evolved to conceal weakness, they distribute load across four legs, and they usually have arthritis in more than one joint at once, so there is no good leg to favour. The disease shows up as behaviour change instead.

What feline arthritis actually looks like.

Jumping less, or jumping in stages — using a chair to get to the counter they used to reach in one go.

Hesitating before a jump, or a visibly bad landing.

Sleeping somewhere new, usually lower down. The cat who used to sleep on top of the wardrobe now sleeps on the sofa.

Missing the litter box edge, or eliminating outside it. Climbing into a high-sided box hurts.

Grooming less, so the coat gets matted, especially over the back and hips where they can no longer reach. Or over-grooming one area, which can indicate pain there.

Being less tolerant of handling, particularly around the back end. A cat who has started objecting to being picked up is telling you something.

Playing less. Interacting less. Being described as grumpy in old age.

Notice that a reasonable person could read that entire list as "my cat is getting old". That is exactly the problem.

Dogs are easier to read, and still missed.

Reluctance on stairs, or taking them one at a time. Slower to rise, especially after sleeping or after rest following exercise. Stiffness that eases after a few minutes of movement. Lagging on walks, or wanting shorter ones. Losing muscle over the hind end and the shoulders. Licking a joint repeatedly. Changes in temperament — a patient old dog becoming snappy is very often a dog in pain rather than a dog whose character has changed.

Cognitive change is separate and also treatable.

Canine and feline cognitive dysfunction is a distinct thing from arthritis, and it is worth knowing about because it too is dismissed as age. Disorientation in familiar rooms, standing in corners or on the wrong side of a door, changed sleep-wake cycles with night-time pacing or vocalising, house-soiling in a previously reliable animal, altered interactions, and reduced activity.

There are things that help, including diet, environmental management and medication. It is worth raising rather than accepting.

What to do.

Go to the vet and describe behaviour, not diagnosis. "She has stopped jumping onto the bed and she is sleeping downstairs now" is far more useful than "she seems fine, just old". Take video on your phone of the animal moving around at home, because a stressed cat on an examination table shows nothing.

Ask directly about pain. There are validated owner questionnaires for detecting osteoarthritis-associated pain in cats, and treatment options for both species have expanded substantially in recent years. Effective analgesia exists.

Do not give human painkillers. Ibuprofen and paracetamol are both dangerous to pets, and paracetamol is lethal to cats in very small amounts. Do not give a dog's medication to a cat, or one animal's leftover prescription to another.

Change the environment while you wait for the vet appointment.

For cats: a litter box with a low entry, or a section cut out of one side. Boxes on every floor so nobody has to use the stairs. Steps or a stool to their favourite high place. Food and water at floor level, not raised where it needs a jump. Soft, warm, easily accessible beds. Help with grooming over the back end.

For dogs: rugs or runners over slippery floors, which is one of the highest-value changes you can make. A ramp for the car. A supportive bed off the cold floor. Shorter, more frequent walks rather than one long one. Keeping weight down, which is the single most effective non-drug intervention for arthritis.

The point.

Old age is not a diagnosis and it is not painful in itself. Arthritis is common, it is treatable, and in cats it is nearly invisible unless somebody is looking for it. The animal who has "slowed down" is usually one who could be considerably more comfortable than they are.

title: Scratching: what cats actually prefer, from a survey of 4,331 owners
summary: Rope was used most when offered, though carpet was offered most often. Cats scratched more on simple upright posts at least three feet tall. And the reason to solve it properly is that declawing is amputation.
content:
Scratching is not a behaviour problem. It is a normal, necessary behaviour that happens to be happening on your sofa.

Cats scratch to remove the outer husk of the claw and keep it sharp, to leave a visual and scent territorial mark, to stretch the whole body from the shoulders down, and to defend themselves. A cat that does not scratch anything is a cat with a problem.

So the goal is never to stop it. It is to move it.

What cats actually prefer.

Wilson and colleagues surveyed 4,331 cat owners across 39 countries about scratching behaviour. Some concrete findings:

Of the traditionally recommended substrates — rope, cardboard, carpet, wood — rope was used most frequently when it was offered. Carpet was the substrate offered most commonly, which is a mismatch worth noticing.

Cats scratched the preferred substrate more when the scratcher was a simple upright post, or a cat tree with two or more levels, and at least three feet (about 90cm) tall.

Survey evidence generally favours narrow upright scratchers over flat horizontal ones, although individual preference varies enough that offering both is sensible.

Which produces a fairly specific shopping list: sisal rope, upright, at least three feet, and heavy enough not to move.

Height and stability are the two things people get wrong.

A cat scratching properly extends the whole body. A post shorter than the cat's full stretch cannot be used the way the cat wants to use it, which is why so many cats ignore a small post and use the arm of the sofa — the sofa is tall enough and does not wobble.

Stability is equally important. A post that rocks when the cat pulls on it gets abandoned after one attempt, and no amount of catnip fixes it. If you can tip it with a hand, it is not stable enough.

Placement is not decoration.

Cats scratch where scratching is useful to them, which is not in the spare room.

Put scratchers where the cat already scratches. If the target is the sofa arm, the post goes directly next to the sofa arm, not across the room. You can move it a few inches a week once it is being used.

Put one near where they sleep. Cats stretch and scratch on waking, which is one of the most reliable scratching moments of the day.

Put them at social crossroads — hallways, doorways, near where the household gathers. Scratching is territorial marking, and marking happens where the traffic is.

In a multi-cat home, more than one, in different places, so no cat can control access to the only one.

Making the new thing win.

Reward use. When the cat uses the post, that is the moment for a treat, or praise, or a short play session. Cats are perfectly trainable with food; the myth that they are not has cost a lot of furniture.

Play at the post. End a wand toy session with the toy going up the post so the cat's claws land on it.

Catnip or silvervine on the post, if your cat responds — roughly a third do not respond to catnip, and silvervine works for many of those.

Make the wrong thing less attractive, temporarily. Double-sided tape, a piece of aluminium foil, or a cover on the arm of the sofa, for a few weeks while the new habit forms. Remove it afterwards.

Do not punish. Spraying water, shouting or a sharp noise teaches the cat to scratch when you are not there, which does not save the sofa and does damage the relationship.

Trim the claws. Regular trimming of the sharp tips reduces damage substantially and is a skill worth building slowly — one claw a day, with a treat, is a perfectly good pace.

Soft claw caps are a genuine option for some cats. They are glued over the claw, last a few weeks, and are not painful. They do need a cat who tolerates handling of the feet.

On declawing.

Declawing — onychectomy — is amputation of the third phalanx of each toe. It is not a nail trim; it removes bone.

The American Association of Feline Practitioners strongly opposes it as an elective procedure and states that veterinarians are obliged to offer alternatives. The AVMA strongly discourages elective declawing and supports non-surgical alternatives.

The stated concerns include acute pain, the possibility of chronic pain, maladaptive behaviour, disability and significant mutilation. There is also a practical downside frequently reported: some declawed cats develop litter box aversion, because digging in litter with amputated toes hurts, and some become more likely to bite, having lost their first line of defence.

If somebody is considering it because the furniture is being destroyed, the alternatives above solve that problem in most homes, at a cost of about the price of a good scratching post and a few weeks of consistency.

When scratching is suddenly worse.

A cat scratching much more than usual, or scratching in new places, is often marking in response to stress — a new animal, a new person, building work, a cat outside the window, or tension with another cat in the house.

In that case the scratching is the symptom. The thing to address is what changed.

title: Being left alone: what separation distress actually needs
summary: It is one of the most commonly reported behaviour problems in dogs, and the popular fix — picking your keys up and putting them down again — is not the treatment. The treatment is absences short enough that the dog never panics.
content:
A dog that howls, destroys the door frame, or urinates the moment you leave is not doing it out of spite or boredom. It is having a panic response to being alone, and the shape of the treatment follows from that.

How common, and what it looks like.

Reported prevalence varies with definition and method — commonly cited ranges run from around 14–20% of pet dogs up to 13–38%. It is consistently described as one of the most common canine behaviour problems.

The picture: vocalisation (howling, barking, whining), attempts to escape — often at doors and windows, sometimes causing injury — destruction usually concentrated at exit points, urination or defecation, pacing, drooling, and refusal to eat while alone.

Two things distinguish it from other problems. It happens specifically in the owner's absence, and it usually begins within minutes of departure rather than hours in.

A camera is the diagnostic tool. Most owners have never seen what actually happens, and a phone propped up for twenty minutes tells you more than any amount of guessing: whether the dog settles after five minutes, whether it panics at minute one, and whether it is distressed or simply chewing the sofa because it is fifteen months old and bored.

What it is not.

It is not spite. Dogs do not do revenge.

It is not guilt. The dog that greets you with flattened ears amid the wreckage is responding to your face and your tone, not confessing.

It is not always separation anxiety. Adolescent boredom, insufficient exercise, needing the toilet, noise phobia triggered while alone, and simple lack of house-training all produce similar evidence. The camera separates them.

The core of the treatment.

The principle is straightforward and the execution requires patience: absences short enough that the dog never becomes distressed, extended very gradually.

That means starting where the dog is, which for a severe case might be four seconds behind a closed door, and building from there in small increments — always staying under the threshold at which panic begins. Every absence that provokes panic sets the process back, because you have rehearsed the panic.

It is slow. Weeks to months is normal, and the progress is not linear.

Alongside it: management, so the dog is not left over threshold while training. In practice that means, for a period, not leaving the dog alone beyond its current tolerance — daycare, a sitter, a friend, taking the dog with you, working from home. Owners often find this the hardest part, and it is the part that makes everything else possible. Training progress made in the morning is undone by an unavoidable four-hour absence in the afternoon.

About departure cues.

There is a widespread piece of advice that you should desensitise the departure routine — pick up the keys and put them down, put your coat on and take it off, dozens of times a day.

Specialists in this area question it. The argument is that a dog with genuine separation distress is not frightened of the keys; it is frightened of the absence, and the keys only matter because of what they predict. Work on the absence and the cues stop mattering on their own. Work on the cues alone and you have a dog that no longer reacts to keys and still panics when you leave.

Do not present cue desensitisation as the treatment. The graduated absence is the treatment.

The other things that help.

Exercise and mental work before departure, particularly sniffing, so the dog is genuinely ready to rest rather than artificially exhausted.

Something to do at the moment of departure — a stuffed frozen food toy or a lick mat — which helps mild cases and, importantly, gives you information: a dog that will not touch it is over threshold.

A predictable routine, and a calm, brief departure and return. Not because emotional goodbyes cause the problem, but because a subdued arrival helps the dog come down.

Leaving background sound on, which helps some dogs.

Not getting a second dog to fix it. This is a common and expensive mistake. Dogs with separation distress are usually attached to a person, not to canine company, and you may end up with two dogs with a problem.

Medication.

For moderate to severe cases, behavioural medication is a normal part of treatment rather than a last resort. Typical protocols involve an SSRI or a TCA, prescribed by a vet, with a minimum of six to twelve months and sometimes long-term management.

The reason is practical: a dog in a genuine panic state cannot learn. Medication lowers the baseline enough that the behaviour work can actually take effect. It is not sedation and it is not a substitute for the training.

This is a conversation with your vet or a veterinary behaviourist. It is also the point at which many owners feel they have failed, which is worth naming and dismissing: a panic disorder that responds to medication is a panic disorder that responds to medication.

Where to get help.

A veterinary behaviourist, a Certified Dog Behavior Consultant, or a CBCC-KA. There are also consultants who specialise specifically in separation-related behaviour and work remotely by video, which suits this problem unusually well since the training happens in the dog's own home.

And see your vet first regardless. Pain, gastrointestinal disease and cognitive dysfunction in older dogs can all present as new distress when left alone.

The thing worth knowing.

This is a genuinely treatable problem, and the dogs that do best are the ones whose owners started early and were allowed to go slowly. The ones that do worst are usually those where an escalating series of quick fixes — a crate the dog panics in, a bark collar, a second dog, more exercise — were tried for a year before anyone addressed the panic.

title: The list: when to stop reading and go to a vet
summary: Not a symptom checker. A short list of things that mean now, including the two that kill fastest — a blocked male cat and a bloated deep-chested dog.
content:
This is not a diagnostic guide and it will not tell you what is wrong. It is a list of situations where the right response is to stop looking things up and get to a vet, because the cost of waiting is measured in hours.

Save two numbers in your phone now, before you need them: your own vet, and the nearest 24-hour emergency hospital. Knowing where to drive at two in the morning is worth more than anything below.

Go now.

A cat straining to urinate and producing nothing. Usually a male cat. He may go in and out of the litter box repeatedly, cry, strain, lick at himself, vomit, hide, or become progressively weak. Urethral obstruction can be fatal within 24 to 48 hours. Owners frequently interpret this as constipation, which is the mistake that costs the cat. If a male cat is straining and nothing is coming out, that is tonight, not tomorrow.

A distended abdomen with unproductive retching, in a large deep-chested dog. Trying to vomit and producing nothing or only white foam, a swollen or tight belly, restlessness and pacing, drooling, obvious pain. This is gastric dilatation-volvulus and it needs surgery within hours.

Difficulty breathing. Laboured or noisy breathing, gasping, an extended neck and elbows held away from the body, or gums that are blue, grey, brick red or very pale. Open-mouth breathing in a cat is always significant — cats do not pant casually.

Collapse, fainting, or inability to stand. Also severe disorientation, or an animal that does not respond to its name.

Seizures, particularly a seizure lasting more than a few minutes, or more than one in a day. A first-ever seizure warrants a call even if the animal seems normal afterwards.

Known ingestion of something toxic. Do not wait for signs. Many toxins are far more treatable before the animal is unwell, and several are much harder to treat once signs appear. Call the vet or ASPCA Animal Poison Control on (888) 426-4435 or the Pet Poison Helpline on (855) 764-7661.

Suspected heatstroke. Frantic panting that does not settle, wobbling, confusion, vomiting, very red or very pale gums after exertion or heat. Cool first, transport second: cold water over the whole body and air moving over it, continuing while you travel.

Trauma. Hit by a car, a fall, a dog fight, a crush injury. Go even if the animal seems fine — internal bleeding, a diaphragmatic tear and a pneumothorax can all present as an animal walking around normally for a while.

Bleeding that does not stop with firm pressure after several minutes.

Sudden hind-limb paralysis in a cat, often with crying, and back legs that feel cold. This is a specific and time-critical emergency.

A pregnant animal straining without producing offspring, or a long gap between them.

Eye injuries, a suddenly cloudy or bulging eye, or an eye held closed. Eyes deteriorate fast and are difficult to recover once lost.

Repeated vomiting with a swollen or painful abdomen, or vomiting in an animal known to chew things — foreign bodies are common and obstruction is an emergency.

Call today, even if it is not tonight.

Not eating for more than 24 hours in a dog, or more than 24 hours in a cat — cats in particular develop serious liver problems when they stop eating.

Drinking and urinating markedly more than usual.

Lameness that does not improve, or that moves between legs.

A cough that has lasted more than a few days, or any cough with reduced energy or appetite.

Diarrhoea with blood, or lasting more than a day or two, especially in a puppy or kitten.

A lump that is new, growing, changing, or ulcerated.

Weight loss you did not intend.

Two general rules.

Prey species have a shorter fuse. Rabbits, guinea pigs, birds and reptiles conceal illness until they cannot, so by the time something is visible the animal is usually further into it than a dog or cat would be. A rabbit that has not eaten or passed droppings for around twelve hours is an emergency, not a wait-and-see. For these species, find an exotics vet before you need one — there are far fewer of them.

You are allowed to be wrong. Emergency clinicians would much rather see ten animals that turned out to be fine than miss the one that was not, and no reasonable practice will make you feel foolish for coming in. "I would rather have it checked" is a complete explanation.

What to do while you travel.

Call ahead. It lets them prepare, and they may give you specific instructions.

Take the packaging if a toxin is involved, and the animal's medication list.

Handle a frightened animal in pain carefully — even a gentle animal may bite. A towel for a cat, and a temporary muzzle for a dog if it is not vomiting and not having trouble breathing.

Do not give human painkillers. Ibuprofen and paracetamol are both dangerous to pets, and paracetamol is lethal to cats in very small amounts.

Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinary professional has told you to for that specific substance.

title: Big dog, small dog: how to run a size-mismatched playdate
summary: Predatory drift is rare, sudden, and has nothing to do with whether a dog is friendly. It is why good daycares separate by size rather than by temperament — and why the app's size score falls to zero at a three-to-one weight ratio.
content:
Big dogs and small dogs are friends all the time. Plenty of households contain both and nothing has ever gone wrong. This article is not an argument against it.

It is about one specific, uncommon, extremely serious failure mode, and about the fact that you cannot screen for it by temperament.

Predatory drift.

The term is attributed to the veterinarian and behaviourist Ian Dunbar, adapted from "instinctive drift" in the behavioural literature of the 1960s. It describes a normal social interaction — usually play — tipping over into the predatory sequence.

The scenario most often described: a large dog and a small dog are playing. The small dog runs fast, gets overwhelmed or frightened, and squeals. The squeal and the movement together resemble prey. Something flips, and the larger dog stops treating the small dog as a playmate and starts running a different behavioural program, which ends in a grab and a shake.

For a small dog, a grab and a shake from a large dog is frequently fatal, and it takes seconds.

The parts that matter most.

It is not aggression. The dog was not being aggressive a moment before, is not an aggressive dog, and will not necessarily do it again. Filing it under dog-dog aggression is a category error, which is part of why it surprises people.

It is not predicted by temperament. This is the important one. A lifetime of gentleness does not rule it out, and there is no test for it. Professionals do not manage this risk by assessing which dogs are safe; they manage it structurally.

Which is why well-run daycares separate by size, not by friendliness. That is what the separation is for. It is also what the small-dog side of a dog park is for, and why treating that fence as optional misses the point.

The evidence here is professional consensus and case report rather than controlled study — there is no incidence figure worth quoting, and it is uncommon. It is a low-frequency, high-severity risk, and low-frequency high-severity risks are managed by design rather than by judgement.

Why the app scores size the way it does.

PetPals scores size out of 25, second only to temperament, using the ratio of the lighter dog to the heavier one rather than the difference between them.

A ratio is the right shape. A 5lb dog and a 15lb dog are three times apart and that is a real mismatch. An 80lb dog and a 90lb dog differ by more in absolute terms and are effectively the same size.

Within about 15%, two dogs count as the same size. Below a ratio of about one to three — 15lb against 45lb — the score reaches zero, because that is roughly where a completely well-meaning accident starts being able to break something.

A zero on size is the model telling you this pairing needs management, not that these dogs cannot meet.

Running a mismatched playdate anyway.

Sometimes you want to. The small dog adores the big one, they are neighbours, the households are friends. Here is how to make it as safe as it can be.

Choose the big dog carefully. Low arousal, an interruptible recall, no history of chasing wildlife or small fast animals, and an owner who will supervise rather than socialise.

Keep arousal low and capped. This is the single biggest lever. Predatory drift is described as happening at high arousal, with running and squealing. So: no high-speed chase games, no games that end with one dog fleeing, and mandatory breaks every couple of minutes before either dog is over the top.

Have both people present, watching, and within reach. Not in the same postcode. Within reach.

Interrupt the chase, not just the fight. If the game turns into the small dog running away and the big dog pursuing, that is the pattern to stop, immediately and cheerfully, every single time — even though nothing bad is happening yet. Especially then.

Give the small dog a real exit. Somewhere they can get to that the big dog cannot follow: a raised surface, a gap in a fence, behind a person. A small dog who cannot leave is a small dog whose only remaining option is to panic loudly, which is the trigger.

Keep it short. Ten or fifteen good minutes, ended by you.

Never leave them alone together, even for a minute, even after two years. This is the rule multi-dog households with a big size gap live by, and it is not paranoia — it is the same logic as not leaving a toddler alone with a swimming pool that is usually fine.

Feed separately. Pick up toys and chews. Resource conflict between a 10lb dog and an 80lb dog is not a fair fight.

When to just say no.

If the big dog is a keen wildlife chaser. If either dog cannot be recalled out of a game. If the small dog is frightened rather than delighted — a frightened small dog is running the exact behaviour that starts the problem. If nobody can commit to genuinely watching. And if the small dog is a puppy, elderly, or has a collapsing trachea or any other fragility.

There are other options, and they are good ones: a parallel sniffing walk with both dogs on long lines is a genuinely enjoyable social outing for two dogs who should not wrestle, and the app's matching will happily find you a size-appropriate wrestling partner separately.

title: Ticks: how to check, how to remove, and what to watch for after
summary: Check the whole animal, pull straight out with tweezers or a tick tool, and note the date. CAPC publishes county-level maps of where each tick-borne disease is actually being diagnosed — that beats a national average.
content:
Ticks are worth taking seriously without being frightened of them. The practical work is small: check regularly, remove properly, use a preventive year-round, and know which diseases are actually being diagnosed where you live.

Checking.

After any walk in long grass, woodland edges, scrub or leaf litter, run your hands over the whole animal. Ticks like thin skin and warm folds, so pay particular attention to the head and muzzle, in and around the ears, under the collar, the armpits and groin, between the toes, and under the tail.

A tick that has not yet fed is very small — poppy-seed sized in the nymph stage — and easy to mistake for a scab or a skin tag. If a "lump" has legs, it is a tick.

Removal.

Use fine-tipped tweezers or a purpose-made tick removal tool, and wear gloves. CAPC's guidance is to check the whole animal and remove attached ticks as soon as possible.

Grip as close to the skin as you can, at the mouthparts rather than the body, and pull steadily straight out. Do not twist unless you are using a hook tool designed to twist. Do not squeeze the tick's body — that can push its stomach contents into the animal.

Then clean the area, wash your hands, and dispose of the tick. If you want it identified later, put it in a sealed bag or a small pot of alcohol.

What not to do: do not burn it off, do not smother it in petroleum jelly, nail varnish or oil, and do not use methylated spirits on the attached tick. These are all traditional and all counterproductive — they irritate the tick and prolong attachment.

If the mouthparts break off and stay in the skin, that is not an emergency. It is a splinter. Leave it, keep the area clean, and let your vet look if it becomes inflamed.

Write down the date and where on the body. If your animal is unwell in the following weeks, that note is genuinely useful clinical information.

What to watch for afterwards.

Local irritation at the site for a few days is normal. What is not: lethargy, fever, reduced appetite, lameness that moves from leg to leg, swollen joints, swollen lymph nodes, unexplained bruising or bleeding, or pale gums. Any of those in the weeks after a tick bite is a reason to see a vet and mention the tick.

Do not wait for the classic bullseye rash. That is a human sign; dogs generally do not show it.

Which diseases, and where.

This is regional, and it changes. The Companion Animal Parasite Council publishes prevalence maps down to county level showing how many dogs have actually tested positive in your area, which is far more useful than any national figure.

From CAPC's 2024 forecasts, the broad shape:

Anaplasmosis. Principal risk in the Northeast and upper Midwest, spreading south and west, with forecast increases in eastern Kentucky, eastern Tennessee, and north-western North Carolina. It shares its tick vector with Lyme disease, so co-infection is possible.

Ehrlichiosis. Geographically patchy, with forecast prevalence higher than normal through much of the southern US. There is no vaccine for it, which is part of why routine screening matters.

Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and babesiosis are also in the picture depending on where you are.

Prevention.

CAPC's framing is three-part: limit exposure to tick habitat, use an appropriate product year-round, and check routinely.

Year-round matters more than people expect. Ticks are not reliably killed by winter, and adult deer ticks are active whenever the temperature is above freezing. A seasonal approach leaves a window.

Ask your vet which product suits your animal, because coverage differs — some products cover ticks and some do not, and the right choice depends on your region and your animal's other risks. Never use a dog product on a cat. Permethrin, which appears in some canine tick products, is seriously toxic to cats, and cats in the same household can be affected by close contact with a recently treated dog.

There is a Lyme vaccine for dogs in some regions. Whether it is appropriate depends on local prevalence and your dog's exposure, and that is a conversation with your vet rather than a rule.

Cats and ticks.

Cats get ticks too, particularly indoor-outdoor cats, and the same removal method applies. The product list is different and shorter, and the permethrin warning above is the critical one.

People.

The tick you removed from your dog was in your house, and if the dog was in the long grass so were you. Check yourself and any children after the same walks, use the same removal method, and talk to your own doctor rather than your vet about human symptoms.

title: Dementia in dogs and cats: the diagnosis almost nobody gets
summary: Around 14% to 22.5% of dogs over eight show signs, rising to 68% of owners reporting at least one sign by ages 15 to 16. In one study using a validated questionnaire, only 13% of affected dogs had been diagnosed.
content:
An old dog stands in the corner of the kitchen facing the wall. An old cat yowls at three in the morning in an empty hallway. A house-trained dog of thirteen starts wetting indoors.

These are usually filed under "she's just old". A substantial proportion of the time they are cognitive dysfunction syndrome, which is a recognised condition with real management options — and which is diagnosed far less often than it occurs.

The numbers.

Surveys suggest 14% to 22.5% of dogs older than eight show signs of cognitive impairment.

Prevalence climbs steeply with age: 28% of owners of dogs aged 11 to 12 report at least one sign, rising to 68% of owners of dogs aged 15 to 16.

And the diagnostic gap is stark. In one study that identified a prevalence of 14.2% in dogs over eight using a validated questionnaire, only 13% of those dogs had actually been diagnosed. Other work reports lower rates still. The reason given is consistent: owners attribute the changes to normal ageing and never mention them.

Which means the single most useful thing in this article is: tell your vet.

What to look for: DISHAA.

Veterinarians screen using a six-part framework.

Disorientation. Getting lost in familiar places. Standing in corners or staring at walls. Going to the hinge side of a door. Appearing not to recognise familiar people or rooms.

Interaction changes. Less interest in greeting, in being petted, in the household. Or the opposite — new clinginess. Increased irritability with other animals.

Sleep-wake cycle changes. This is often the one that brings people to the vet, because it is the one that affects the household. Sleeping much more in the day and pacing, vocalising or being restless at night.

House-soiling. Eliminating indoors in a previously reliable animal, sometimes in view of the owner, without appearing to signal beforehand.

Activity changes. Reduced purposeful activity — less exploring, less play — sometimes alongside increased aimless activity such as pacing or repetitive circling.

Anxiety. New fears, separation distress appearing for the first time in old age, increased startle, restlessness.

In cats the picture is similar, with night-time yowling, disorientation, altered social behaviour and litter box lapses being the most commonly reported.

Get the medical causes ruled out first.

This is not a diagnosis to make at home, and it should not be made by exclusion in your kitchen.

Almost every sign above has other explanations in an old animal. Pain, particularly arthritis, causes restlessness, night waking, irritability, reduced activity and house-soiling. Hearing and vision loss cause disorientation and startle. Hyperthyroidism in cats causes night vocalisation and restlessness. Kidney disease and diabetes cause increased urination. Brain tumours, high blood pressure and liver disease all produce behaviour change.

In one trial of 100 senior dogs identified by DISHAA screening, 15 had markedly abnormal laboratory findings. Cognitive signs and medical disease overlap heavily, and often coexist.

So: describe the behaviour to your vet and let them work through it. Take video — an animal pacing at 2am is not going to demonstrate it in a consulting room.

What can be done.

There is no cure, and the honest framing is slowing progression and improving quality of life rather than reversal. That said, there is more available than most owners realise.

Diet and supplements: there are therapeutic diets formulated for cognitive support, and supplements with varying levels of evidence. Ask your vet what they consider worth using rather than buying from a search result.

Medication: selegiline is licensed for canine cognitive dysfunction in many countries. Anxiety and sleep can be addressed pharmacologically where they are the main problem, which is often the difference between coping and not.

Environmental management, which is unglamorous and effective. Keep furniture where it is. Night lights along routes the animal uses. Non-slip runners on hard floors. More litter trays, with lower sides, on every floor. Blocking access to stairs, pools and other hazards. Fencing off gaps behind furniture where an animal can get stuck.

Routine, made rigid. Same times, same walks, same order of events. Predictability substitutes for the memory that is failing.

Continued mental activity, at the right level. Short scent games, food puzzles that are easy enough to succeed at, gentle training. Frustration is not enrichment — the task should be one the animal can complete.

Continued gentle exercise, adapted to their body.

The thing worth saying to owners.

An old animal doing something inexplicable is not being difficult, has not forgotten its training, and is not doing it deliberately. It is confused, and confusion in the middle of the night in a house you no longer quite recognise is frightening.

And "she's just old" is not a diagnosis. It is the sentence that keeps a treatable condition untreated, in an animal that has perhaps two more years and would rather spend them less anxious.

title: The fight you never see: silent conflict between cats
summary: Cats rarely brawl. They stare, they sit in doorways, they block the hallway to the litter tray. In one UK study of cats given up to rescue for behaviour, aggression between cats was the most commonly reported problem.
content:
People generally believe their cats get along because there is no fighting. Open fighting is the rare form of feline conflict. The common form is quiet, slow, and almost invisible unless you know its shape.

Around 44% of cat households have more than one cat. In a UK study of cats relinquished to rescue centres for behavioural problems, aggression between cats was the most commonly reported problem. A great deal of that starts as tension nobody noticed.

What it looks like.

Staring. One cat looking steadily at another who is trying not to look back. This is a threat, and between cats it does most of the work that a growl does between dogs.

Blocking. Sitting in a doorway, at the top of the stairs, in a hallway, or directly in front of a litter tray, food bowl or cat flap. It looks like a cat sitting somewhere. It is a cat controlling access, and the other cat knows it.

Territory shrinkage. One cat spending nearly all its time in one room, on one shelf, or under a bed. A cat that used to use the whole house and now uses a corner of it has lost a negotiation.

Facing away. Two cats in the same room, positioned so neither has to look at the other, keeping the maximum available distance.

Timesharing. The cats are never in the same place, and you had assumed they simply prefer different rooms. Often they have divided the day.

Ambushing at pinch points. Cat flaps, litter trays and narrow corridors.

Overgrooming, particularly the belly and inner thighs. Excessive vigilance. Reduced sleep in the open.

Consequences beyond unhappiness.

Chronic social stress in cats shows up physically. Reported associations include overgrooming, house-soiling, appetite change, reduced immunity, and feline idiopathic cystitis — a painful bladder condition in which stress is a well-documented factor.

That last one is worth taking seriously, because in male cats bladder disease can progress to urethral obstruction, which is fatal within a day or two if untreated.

House-soiling is the most common consequence and the most commonly misread. A cat eliminating outside the tray in a multi-cat home is very often a cat that cannot get to the tray safely, or does not want to be cornered in a covered box in a corner.

The fix is mostly geography.

Feline conflict is almost always about resources and access, so the intervention is to make resources uncontestable.

More of everything, in more places. Litter trays: at least one more than the number of cats, in separate locations on different floors — not a row of trays in one room, which cats perceive as one large tray. Feeding stations in different rooms, not two bowls side by side. Water away from food. Multiple beds, multiple high places, multiple scratching posts.

Vertical space. This is the most under-used tool in a multi-cat house. Shelves, cat trees and cleared wardrobe tops multiply the usable territory without moving a wall, and height itself resolves a lot of disputes — cats that can occupy different levels do not have to compete for the same floor.

Two exits from everything. No cat should ever be in a position where getting past another cat is the only way out of a room. Prop doors, add a second route, and never place a litter tray in a dead end.

Break the sightlines. A cat that can stare has a weapon; a screen, a plant or a piece of furniture that interrupts a long view down a hallway genuinely helps.

Feed on a schedule, separately. Free-feeding from one bowl is a permanent negotiation.

And it works. Buffington and colleagues implemented multimodal environmental modification with cats that had idiopathic cystitis, and over roughly 300 days only 13 of 46 cats (28%) had a recurrence, with median frequency of signs falling from weekly to never. Owners also reported significant reductions in fearfulness and nervousness. That is an environmental intervention producing a measurable medical outcome.

If it has already broken down.

If the cats are actively fighting, separate them completely and re-introduce from the beginning: separate rooms, scent exchange, site swapping, feeding either side of a door, visual access through a barrier, then short supervised meetings. It is the same protocol as introducing strangers, and it works because in an important sense they have become strangers.

Do not punish either cat. Punishment adds stress to a situation caused by stress, and it frequently makes the aggressor associate the other cat with something unpleasant.

See a vet, for both. Pain and illness lower tolerance, and hyperthyroidism, arthritis and cognitive dysfunction all present as changed social behaviour in cats. An older cat that has suddenly become intolerant of a housemate is often an unwell cat.

Then get a cat behaviour consultant if it persists — a Certified Cat Behavior Consultant or a veterinary behaviourist.

And the honest outcome.

Not every pair of cats becomes friends, and the target is not a photograph of two cats in one bed. A house where every cat can eat, drink, toilet, sleep and move without negotiating is a complete success, even if they never touch each other. Polite mutual avoidance in a well-resourced home is a good life.

title: The first five minutes of a playdate
summary: Most playdates that go wrong go wrong at the start — at the gate, on tight leads, with both owners talking. A short procedure for arrival, and the decision to leave early.
content:
You have matched, you have messaged, you have agreed a place and a time. This is about the five minutes that decide how the next hour goes.

Before you arrive.

Exercise your dog lightly first. Not to exhaustion — a tired dog is a shorter-tempered dog — but a fifteen-minute sniffing walk takes the edge off arrival and gets the toilet stop out of the way.

Do not arrive hungry, and do not bring high-value food into a shared space. Food raises the odds of conflict between dogs who otherwise get on, and it is the single easiest thing to remove.

Bring: a well-fitted harness, a normal lead and a long line, water and a bowl, poo bags, and low-value treats in a pocket for recall. Leave: the favourite ball, the chew, the squeaky toy, the retractable lead.

Message the other owner in the morning. "Still good? Everyone well?" This is where a coughing dog gets caught, and it is a normal, friendly thing to ask.

Arrival: do not meet at the cars.

Park separately, get out separately, and do not walk the dogs at each other. The car park is where everybody is excited and the leads are short, and it is a bad first impression to manufacture.

Both dogs get two minutes to sniff their own patch first, apart, before anything social happens. This lowers arousal and lets each dog process where they are.

The first five minutes: parallel, not face-to-face.

Start walking in the same direction, ten to twenty feet apart, humans on the inside, dogs on the outside. You are not trying to get them to meet. You are letting them exist near each other while doing something normal.

Mark and reward calm. Every time your dog looks at the other dog and then looks away, that gets a quiet marker and a treat.

Close the gap three to five feet at a time, and only while both dogs stay loose — soft body, mouth that opens, ears that move, and the ability to take food. A dog who has stopped eating has told you it is too close.

Swap sides so each dog can sniff where the other has been. Scent does a lot of the work.

Let the greeting be brief and then move on. Three to five seconds of sniffing, on loose leads, then call both dogs away cheerfully and keep walking. A short first greeting that ends well is what makes the second one better. Long greetings on lead are where things curdle.

Going off lead.

Only in a securely fenced space, and only when both dogs have been loose and comfortable on the parallel walk. If the space is not properly fenced, keep both on long lines — a long line is not a compromise, it is a perfectly good playdate.

Drop leads rather than unclipping first, if you are unsure. It gives you something to step on.

Both people put phones away. If you cannot watch, the playdate has not started yet.

The first two minutes off lead is where you learn everything. Look for bouncy exaggerated movement, role reversals, self-handicapping by the bigger or faster dog, and natural pauses. Look out for one dog doing all the chasing, a dog trying to leave and being followed, a freeze, or hard staring.

Build in breaks from the beginning. Every two or three minutes, call your dog to you, do something calm for thirty seconds, and release them back. This does two things: it caps arousal before it climbs, and it teaches both dogs that being called out of play is not the end of play. Most conflicts between dogs who like each other are arousal problems, not compatibility problems.

Leaving early is a skill, not a failure.

The best playdate ends while both dogs still want more. Twenty good minutes beats an hour that ends badly, and the dogs do not know how long they were supposed to get.

End it now, without apology, if: one dog is repeatedly trying to disengage and being followed; play has gone silent and stiff; either dog has started guarding a space, a person or the water bowl; a third dog has arrived and changed the maths; either dog is panting frantically and cannot settle in a break; or you are not enjoying watching it.

That last one is a real criterion. If you are tense, you are seeing something, even if you cannot name it yet.

How to say it. "I think we'll leave it there while it's going well" is a complete sentence and no reasonable person minds it. If you want to soften it: "he does better with short ones." You do not owe anyone an explanation for ending your dog's afternoon.

Afterwards.

Water, a calm walk to decompress, and something to chew or lick at home — the wind-down matters as much as the session.

Then message the other owner, honestly. "That went really well, same time next week?" or "I think mine found it a bit much — could we try a parallel walk next time?" The second message is more valuable than the first, and this app only works if people send it.

title: Fleas: the ones on your pet are the small part of the problem
summary: A female lays around 40 eggs a day, and the eggs, larvae and pupae live in your carpet rather than on your animal. Pupae survive insecticide, which is why an infestation takes months rather than days.
content:
The reason flea infestations feel unbeatable is that people treat the animal and expect the problem to end. The animal is where you see the fleas. It is not where most of them are.

The life cycle, and why it matters.

Adult fleas live on the host and feed there. A female lays around 40 eggs per day.

The eggs are not sticky. They roll off the animal and into the environment — carpet, bedding, sofa cushions, floorboard gaps, the car, the soil by the back door. Eggs hatch in about 2 to 10 days.

Larvae hatch out and move away from light, down into carpet fibres and cracks, where they feed on organic debris including adult flea faeces. The larval stage runs about 5 to 20 days depending on temperature and humidity.

Then they pupate. The pupal stage is the problem. Pupae are protected inside a sticky cocoon that picks up debris and camouflages itself, and they are resistant — they cannot be reliably killed by insecticide, by freezing or by drying, and they can remain dormant for months, emerging when triggered by vibration, warmth and carbon dioxide.

That is why you can treat a house, leave it empty for a fortnight, come back, and get swarmed on the doormat. You have just triggered a few hundred dormant pupae by walking in.

The consequence: the eggs, larvae and pupae in the environment vastly outnumber the adults on the animal at any moment.

What actually clears it.

Treat every animal in the household, not just the itchy one. The cat who never goes out is still part of the cycle. A single untreated animal keeps the whole thing running.

Keep treating for at least three months. This is the part people abandon. You are not waiting for the treatment to work — it works on adults quickly. You are waiting out the pupae, which emerge in waves over weeks and have to meet a treated animal when they do.

Treat the environment as well as the animals. Vacuum thoroughly and often, especially where the animals sleep, along skirting boards, and under furniture. Vacuuming physically removes eggs and larvae, and the vibration usefully triggers pupae to emerge into a treated environment. Empty the vacuum outside.

Wash all bedding — animal and human — on the hottest wash the fabric allows.

Do not forget the car, and do not forget any room the animals are not usually allowed in but occasionally get into.

Ask your vet about products rather than guessing. Effectiveness varies, resistance is regionally real, and some supermarket products are poor. Some prescription products include an insect growth regulator that stops eggs and larvae developing, which shortens the whole process considerably.

Never use a dog flea product on a cat. Permethrin appears in some canine products and is seriously toxic to cats. This causes deaths every year and it is entirely preventable.

The health side, beyond itching.

Flea allergy dermatitis is the most common skin allergy in dogs and cats, and an allergic animal reacts violently to very few fleas — you may never see one.

Fleas transmit tapeworm. If your animal has had fleas, ask your vet about worming as well.

Heavy infestations cause anaemia, which is genuinely dangerous in kittens, puppies, and small or elderly animals.

And fleas bite people, usually around the ankles, which is often how households discover the problem.

Prevention is simpler than cure.

Year-round preventive treatment for every animal in the house is the whole strategy, and it is far cheaper and less miserable than dealing with an established infestation.

The seasonal approach — treating in summer only — leaves a gap, and centrally heated homes are hospitable to fleas in every month of the year.

Finally: a flea infestation is not a verdict on your housekeeping. It is a verdict on the flea's reproductive strategy, which is extremely good.

title: Indoor, outdoor, or the third option
summary: The AAFP's 2024 position statement declines to give a simple answer, and it is right not to. Indoor-only removes real risks and adds different ones — and the compromise most people have not considered is an enclosure.
content:
This is the argument that has been running in cat ownership for decades, usually conducted as though one side is obviously correct and the people on the other side are careless.

In March 2024 the American Association of Feline Practitioners published a position statement on indoor and outdoor lifestyles, and the most useful thing about it is that it declines to pick a side.

What the position statement actually says.

An indoor-only lifestyle may decrease the risks of injury, predation, poisoning, and exposure to infectious and parasitic agents.

The same lifestyle may increase the risks of compromised welfare, illness, obesity and behaviour problems, where environmental limitations are not addressed.

Both halves are stated. The obligations run in both directions.

That framing is more useful than a verdict, because it turns the question from "which is right" into "what does this particular cat need from me, given what I have chosen".

A note on a statistic you will see everywhere.

The figure that indoor cats live 12 to 18 years and outdoor cats live 2 to 5 circulates constantly. Treat it with caution: the low end appears to derive from unowned or feral cat populations rather than from owned indoor-outdoor cats, and the two are not comparable.

Outdoor access does carry real, well-documented risks — road traffic in particular, plus fights, infectious disease, poisoning, theft and predators. That case does not need an inflated number, and using one makes the whole argument easier to dismiss.

If your cat goes outside.

Reduce the specific risks rather than worrying generally.

Keep them in at night, and around dawn and dusk. Road traffic risk and fight risk are both concentrated there.

Microchip, and keep the registration current. Lord and colleagues found microchipped cats entering shelters were returned to their owners 38.5% of the time against 1.8% for cats without one — and where a chipped cat was not returned, the usual reason was out-of-date owner details.

A collar with a proper breakaway safety release, with a tag. There is a genuine trade-off with strangulation risk, and breakaway is the compromise.

Stay current on vaccination — outdoor cats have a different risk profile, and FeLV vaccination in particular is relevant for cats who meet other cats — and on year-round parasite prevention.

Neuter. Roaming, fighting, and unwanted litters all reduce sharply.

Consider a bell or a bright collar cover for wildlife, with the caveat that in one controlled study neither a bell nor a Birdsbesafe cover significantly reduced the total prey brought home, while five minutes a day of object play reduced it by about a quarter and a high-meat diet by about a third.

If your cat lives indoors.

Then the environmental obligations in the position statement are yours to meet, and they are not optional extras.

Vertical space, and a lot of it. Shelves, trees, cleared surfaces, a window perch. Height is where cats feel safe and it multiplies usable territory.

Play that runs the predatory sequence: a wand toy moved like prey, several catches, and food at the end. Five minutes twice a day is a real intervention, not a nicety.

Food that takes work — puzzle feeders, scatter feeding — for part of the ration, not all of it.

Scratching posts that are tall, stable and upright.

The litter arrangement the guidelines actually specify: two trays for one cat in separate locations, large, uncovered, with fine unscented clumping litter, scooped daily, away from food.

Something to watch. A window onto a bird feeder is genuinely enriching.

Novelty. A cardboard box that was not there yesterday counts.

The third option.

A catio — an enclosed outdoor structure, from a window box to a full run — is described by the AAFP as the compromise: fresh air, sunshine, weather, birdsong, grass and smells, without the traffic, the fights, the infectious disease or the predation.

They range enormously. A window-mounted box for a small flat, a converted balcony with mesh, a fenced section of garden with a roof, or cat-proof fencing around an existing garden that stops cats climbing out and other cats climbing in.

The other version is a harness and lead, which suits some cats very well and others not at all. It takes weeks of gradual introduction indoors first, and a cat who never relaxes in it is telling you something.

What it comes down to.

Neither lifestyle is neglectful in itself. An indoor cat in a bare flat with a bowl of dry food and no vertical space, and an outdoor cat with no vaccination, no microchip and a road at the end of the garden, are both cats whose owner has taken the risks of one option without accepting the obligations that come with it.

The question worth asking is not which camp you are in. It is: given the choice I have made, what does this cat still need?

title: Small dogs at big-dog parks: the fence is not decoration
summary: The small-dog side exists for a structural reason, not a snobbish one. And a small dog who spends every visit under a bench is not being socialised.
content:
Every dog park with two sides has the same argument going on in it. Somebody's small dog is on the big side, because the small side is empty, or because their dog "thinks he's a big dog", or because the small dogs there were rude to him once.

All of those are understandable. Here is what the fence is actually for.

Why the split exists.

It is not about temperament and it is not about small dogs being fragile.

It is about predatory drift: a normal play interaction between a large dog and a much smaller one tipping into the predatory sequence, usually when the small dog runs fast and squeals. It is uncommon. It is not predicted by whether a dog is friendly, and there is no test for it. The consequences for the small dog are frequently fatal, and it happens in seconds.

Because you cannot screen for it, professionals manage it structurally instead. That is why well-run daycares separate by size rather than by friendliness, and it is the same reasoning behind the second gate at your park.

The second reason is simpler physics. An eighty-pound dog running at full speed into a ten-pound dog does damage without any intent at all. Body-slamming is normal play for a lot of large dogs, and it is normal play that a small dog's body cannot absorb.

"But my dog thinks he's a big dog."

He probably does. That is not the variable. Nothing about your dog's self-image changes what happens if a large dog's predatory sequence engages, and a confident small dog running into a group of large dogs is arguably running the trigger behaviour more, not less.

The dog whose opinion matters here is the other one, and you do not know it.

"But the small side is always empty."

This is the real problem with most parks, and it is worth solving properly rather than working around.

Go at a set time and tell people. Most small-dog sides are empty because nobody has coordinated, not because nobody has a small dog. A recurring slot — Tuesdays and Saturdays at nine — fills up faster than you would expect.

Arrange playdates instead. This is what the app is for: one or two size-appropriate dogs, in a space you chose, at a time that suits both of you, is strictly better than a public park at the wrong hour with unknown dogs.

Use the big side at genuinely empty times, if you must, and leave when large dogs arrive. That is a legitimate compromise as long as you are honest about the leaving part.

The other failure mode: the small dog who hides.

A lot of small dogs at parks are not having a good time. The signs are ordinary and easy to explain away: pressing against your legs, sitting under a bench, tail tucked, ears back, asking to be picked up, or freezing when a group approaches.

This is not socialisation. Repeated exposure to something a dog cannot escape is flooding, and flooding tends to make dogs worse with other dogs rather than better. The dog is not learning that dogs are fine. They are learning that you take them somewhere frightening and do not help.

One thing to avoid: scooping them up in the middle of a group. Lifting a small dog above a crowd of large dogs makes them a moving object above head height, which is more interesting rather than less, and it removes the only options they had. If you need to get them out, walk out.

What to do instead.

If your small dog enjoys other small dogs, find them and organise. If your small dog enjoys one particular large dog they know well, run that as a managed playdate with the rules for a size mismatch. If your small dog does not much enjoy other dogs at all — which is common and completely fine — sniffing walks, scent games, training and time with you are a full life, and a dog park is not a nutritional requirement.

If you use the big side anyway.

Go when it is nearly empty. Keep moving, and keep your dog moving with you, rather than standing in one spot. Stay near the gate you came in by. Leave when a group forms or when a large dog starts fixating. Never let a chase develop with your dog as the one being chased. And do not put a small dog into a group of large dogs to "get used to it".

Being the owner of the large dog.

If you are on the big side with a large dog and a small dog comes in, the useful thing is not to be offended. Call your dog, put them on lead for a minute, and let the small dog settle or leave. Nothing you have to do that afternoon is more important than that going smoothly, and it takes ninety seconds.

title: Leptospirosis became a core dog vaccine, and it is not a countryside disease
summary: The 2023 ACVIM consensus and the 2024 AAHA update recommend it annually for all dogs from 12 weeks, regardless of breed, geography or lifestyle. The reservoir is rats, and worldwide infection prevalence in brown rats is around 30%.
content:
If your dog's vaccination protocol was set before 2024, this is the one worth raising at the next appointment.

What changed.

Leptospirosis used to be classed as a noncore canine vaccine — recommended based on risk, typically framed as a rural, outdoorsy, standing-water risk. Plenty of urban and small-breed dogs were reasonably not given it.

The 2023 ACVIM consensus statement and the 2024 update to AAHA's canine vaccination guidelines changed that. Leptospirosis is now recommended as a core vaccine: annually, for all dogs, from 12 weeks of age, regardless of breed.

The stated reasons are that the disease can be severe or fatal despite treatment, that exposure is not predictable from age, geography or lifestyle, and that it is zoonotic — people catch it too.

What it actually is.

A bacterial infection caused by pathogenic serovars of Leptospira. It is shed in urine, survives in water and damp soil, and enters through mucous membranes or broken skin. It damages the kidneys and liver, and severe cases can involve pulmonary haemorrhage.

The reservoir is rodents, principally the brown rat, Rattus norvegicus, in which a worldwide infection prevalence of around 30% has been identified — exceeding 80% in some regions.

Which is exactly why the "rural disease" framing broke down. There is no shortage of brown rats in cities.

The specific point about city dogs.

The ACVIM consensus statement notes that leptospirosis continues to be diagnosed in small-breed dogs from urban areas, in puppies as young as 11 weeks, in geriatric dogs, in rural dogs, and in dogs that were inadequately vaccinated — including dogs given 2-serovar vaccines in some regions.

So the small city dog who never goes anywhere muddy is not obviously outside the risk group. Urban exposure routes include puddles and standing water, wet gutters and alleyways, parks with rat populations, and communal water bowls.

The vaccine.

Modern products cover four serovars. The consensus notes that where leptospirosis has been documented in vaccinated dogs, those dogs were more likely to have been unvaccinated, years overdue, or vaccinated with an older 2-serovar product.

It is an annual vaccine — protection does not last three years the way some core vaccines do — which is one reason it needs to be a deliberate part of the schedule rather than an afterthought.

The initial course is two doses two to four weeks apart, then annually.

If your dog previously had a reaction to a leptospirosis vaccine, that is a real conversation to have with your vet rather than a reason to quietly skip it. Reaction rates have been a historical concern and modern products differ; your vet can weigh it for your individual dog.

What to watch for.

Early signs are non-specific: lethargy, fever, reduced appetite, vomiting, increased thirst and urination, muscle pain or reluctance to move, and sometimes jaundice — a yellow tinge to the gums, the whites of the eyes or the skin.

Because the early picture looks like a hundred other things, the useful thing you can do is mention exposure. "He was swimming in a pond last week" or "we have rats in the alley" changes what a vet considers.

It is a human disease too.

Leptospirosis is zoonotic. People are infected through contact with the urine of infected animals or with contaminated water and soil.

If your dog is diagnosed, your vet will advise on handling — gloves for cleaning up urine, prompt cleaning of contaminated surfaces, thorough handwashing — and it is worth telling your own doctor if you develop a flu-like illness afterwards.

Vaccinating the dog reduces the household's exposure too, which is part of the argument for making it core.
