title: Bonding rabbits: two weeks to two months, and both must be neutered
summary: Rabbits are social and most pet rabbits live alone. Bonding is slow, it happens on neutral ground, and RWAF does not support the "stress bonding" methods that circulate online.
content:
A rabbit on its own is a rabbit missing the thing it most needs. The Rabbit Welfare Association and Fund's position is that rabbits should live with a compatible rabbit companion wherever possible, and PDSA's PAW Report found 42% of pet rabbits living alone, with a further 5% living only with another species — an estimated 530,000 rabbits whose companionship needs are not being met.

Getting a second rabbit is the right instinct. Putting them in together is not.

Before anything else: neutering.

Both rabbits must be neutered before bonding. This is not negotiable and it is the step people try to skip.

Unneutered rabbits fight over territory and hormones, and rabbit fights cause serious injuries very quickly — castration wounds, torn ears, and worse. Unneutered mixed-sex pairs also produce a great many rabbits.

RWAF recommends castrating males at 10–12 weeks, or as soon as the testicles descend. Females are spayed later, and spaying also removes the risk of uterine cancer, which is very common in unspayed does.

Then wait two to four weeks after surgery before starting introductions, so the rabbit has healed and the hormones have settled. Males can remain fertile for up to six weeks after neutering, so a male and female pair need that gap respected for a second reason.

Which pairing.

A neutered male with a neutered female is the classic and generally the easiest. Same-sex pairs can work, particularly siblings raised together, but are more likely to break down.

Do not pair a rabbit with a guinea pig. This used to be standard advice and is now advised against: the two species have different dietary requirements and different communication, a rabbit can seriously injure a guinea pig with a kick, and rabbits can carry Bordetella that makes guinea pigs ill.

Many rescues offer bonding services, where a rabbit is introduced to potential partners under supervision and you take home an already-bonded pair. If that is available to you, it is by some distance the easiest and safest route.

How long it takes.

Typically two weeks to two months. Some pairs settle in days. Some take longer. The timeline is not something you can compress by trying harder.

The process.

Stage one: side by side, not touching. Set up the two enclosures near each other but with a gap, so they can see and smell each other and cannot reach through to bite. Swap litter trays and toys between them daily so each becomes familiar with the other's scent. Continue until both are relaxed near each other and there is no lunging at the barrier.

Stage two: short sessions on neutral ground. Neutral means genuinely neutral — a room or pen neither rabbit has been in before, so neither is defending territory. A bathroom, a hallway, a pen in a different room. Strip out anything either could guard, and provide two of everything: two hides with two exits each, two water bowls, two piles of hay at opposite ends.

Keep the first sessions short — ten or fifteen minutes — and supervise every second of them with something to separate the rabbits if needed: a dustpan, a piece of cardboard, thick gloves.

Then extend the sessions gradually as they settle, over days and weeks, until they can spend hours together calmly, and finally overnight.

Only when they are consistently calm and grooming each other do they move into a shared space — and that space should be thoroughly cleaned first so it does not smell like one rabbit's territory.

What is normal and what is not.

Normal: chasing, mounting (by either sex, in either direction — it is about status, not sex), light nipping, and a period of ignoring each other. Some circling and grumbling.

Stop the session: if either rabbit is pulling out fur, if a chase does not stop within a few seconds, if either is boxing with the front feet, or if they lock together. Rabbit fights escalate very fast and cause genuine injuries, often to the face and genitals.

Success looks like grooming each other, lying stretched out side by side, and eating from the same pile of hay.

A note on "stress bonding".

There is a method circulating online in which rabbits are put together in a frightening situation — a car journey, a carrier, a washing machine on spin — on the theory that shared fear makes them bond.

RWAF does not support stress bonding methods. It is a welfare problem in its own right, and a bond built on a shared panic is not the same as a bond built on familiarity.

Afterwards.

Bonded rabbits should not be separated, including for vet visits. Take both, and keep them together in the carrier and afterwards — a rabbit that comes home smelling of the clinic can be attacked by its own partner, and separations can break a bond that took months to build.

If a bond does break — often after an illness, a vet visit, or a hormonal event — do not panic. It can usually be rebuilt using the same process, from the beginning.

title: Playdates for a dog who does not like dog parks
summary: A dog can be perfectly social and still hate a room full of strangers. Parallel walks, one-to-one sessions, private rentals and sniffing dates are all real socialising — and for a lot of dogs they are the better version.
content:
There is a widespread assumption that a well-socialised dog enjoys dog parks, and that a dog who does not enjoy them has a problem to be fixed.

Both halves of that are wrong. Plenty of confident, well-adjusted, thoroughly social dogs dislike large groups of unfamiliar dogs in an enclosed space. Humans mostly dislike the equivalent too. A dog who has three good friends and no interest in strangers is not deficient.

The mistake to avoid is concluding that such a dog therefore needs no social life. They usually do. It just is not that one.

How to tell which dog you have.

Watch what happens on arrival and in the first two minutes. A dog who wants to be there goes in, checks a few dogs, and starts moving. A dog who does not stands near you, sniffs the ground very intently, moves along the fence line, hides under a bench, or fixates on the gate.

Watch what happens over repeated visits. Genuine acclimatisation looks like a dog getting looser each time. If visit ten looks like visit one, or worse, exposure is not working, and continuing is flooding rather than socialisation.

And watch for the dog who is having too good a time — the one who cannot be recalled, who body-slams everyone, who cannot stop. That dog is also a poor fit for a park, for everybody else's sake.

The alternatives, roughly in order of how easy they are.

The parallel walk. Two dogs, two people, walking in the same direction ten to twenty feet apart, closing the gap as everyone relaxes. This is the most underrated social activity there is. Nobody has to interact, the dogs get all the information they want by scent, and the shared activity does the work. For dogs who find direct interaction hard, this can be the whole relationship, permanently, and it is a good one.

The sniffing date. Both dogs on long lines in a scruffy field, allowed to choose their own routes at their own pace, occasionally crossing. Low arousal, high satisfaction, almost no conflict potential.

The one-to-one, in a fenced space. One known dog, matched on size and temperament, in a garden or a rented field. This is what most dogs who dislike parks actually want, and it is what the app is built to find.

The private field rental. In many areas you can now rent a securely fenced acre by the hour. For a reactive dog, a recovering dog, a dog in season, or a dog who simply cannot cope with an audience, this is transformative, and it is usually cheaper than an hour of daycare.

The structured group. A well-run training class, a scentwork class, a canicross group. Dogs in proximity, doing a task, with a professional managing the space. Many dogs who cannot handle free-for-all play do beautifully here, because there is a job.

The walk with one steady friend. The single most valuable social resource a dog can have is one compatible dog they see regularly. Familiarity does most of the work that a park cannot.

For the dog who finds other dogs genuinely difficult.

If your dog barks and lunges on lead, that is reactivity, and it usually comes from fear or frustration rather than aggression. Both are workable, and both are worth doing with help rather than alone.

In the meantime: distance is the tool. Every good outcome starts with being far enough away that your dog can still eat, still look at you, and still disengage. That distance is bigger than you think and it shrinks over weeks.

If it is severe, or if there is any bite history, that is a job for a qualified behaviour professional — a Certified Dog Behavior Consultant, a CBCC-KA, or a veterinary behaviourist — not for a park and not for the internet.

What a dog actually needs socially.

Less than people assume, and more specific. Enough exposure to other dogs to stay comfortable in their presence. A small number of individuals they genuinely like. Freedom from being repeatedly forced into interactions they have declined.

Some dogs want a rowdy group. Some want one friend and a long grass verge. Both of those are a social life, and the second one is much easier to arrange well.

The quiet advantage.

A managed playdate beats a public park on almost every axis that matters. You choose the partner, so size and play style actually fit. You choose the ground. You know the other dog's health. There are two dogs rather than eleven, so the dynamic is simple. And you can end it at twenty minutes while everyone is still enjoying themselves, which is the single biggest predictor of whether the next one goes well.

That is not a consolation prize for dogs who cannot cope with parks. For a great many dogs, it is simply the better product.

title: Bad breath is not normal: the most common diagnosis nobody treats
summary: Periodontal disease affects roughly 80% of dogs and 70% of cats by the age of three. It is painful, it is progressive, and animals do not stop eating because of it — which is why owners conclude nothing is wrong.
content:
Periodontal disease is the most commonly diagnosed condition in adult dogs and cats, and probably the most consistently ignored. Prevalence figures are striking: roughly 80% of dogs and 70% of cats have it by the age of three, with reported figures of 80–89% in dogs over three.

The AVMA has campaigned specifically on the point that "doggie breath" is not normal and can be a sign of serious disease. It is worth taking literally. Healthy mouths do not smell.

Why it goes unnoticed.

Two reasons, and both are misleading.

Animals keep eating. There is a widespread assumption that a painful mouth would stop an animal eating. It does not. Dogs and cats with advanced dental disease, loose teeth and exposed roots continue to eat, because the alternative is not eating. Appetite is a terrible screening test for oral pain.

They also do not complain in a way we recognise. What you may see instead: chewing on one side, dropping food, a change in what they will eat (a cat switching to wet food, a dog losing interest in hard chews), pawing at the face, head shyness, reduced grooming in a cat, or a new grumpiness about being touched around the head.

Very often the first thing an owner truly notices is after treatment, when the animal becomes visibly brighter and more playful — and they realise they had been watching a slow decline they had attributed to age.

What is actually happening.

Plaque forms on the tooth surface within hours of cleaning. Left alone it mineralises into calculus, which is the hard brown material you can see. That is not the disease; it is the scaffolding.

The disease is what happens under the gumline: inflammation of the gum, then destruction of the ligament and bone that hold the tooth in place. Once the supporting structures are gone they do not come back.

There is also a systemic dimension. Periodontal disease has been examined in relation to kidney and other organ health, and it represents a chronic source of inflammation and bacteria in the bloodstream.

Which is why what you can see is a poor guide. Most of the disease is below the gumline and only visible on dental radiographs taken under anaesthetic, which is a large part of why a proper dental involves anaesthesia.

About "anaesthesia-free dental cleaning".

It scrapes visible calculus off the crown. It does not clean below the gumline, where the disease is, it cannot take radiographs, and it cannot treat anything. It produces a tooth that looks better to the owner while the disease continues underneath, and it involves restraining a conscious animal for a procedure it has not consented to.

Veterinary dental organisations advise against it. If anaesthesia is the concern — and it is a reasonable concern, particularly in an older animal — the productive conversation is about pre-anaesthetic bloodwork, monitoring, and modern protocols, not about avoiding the diagnosis.

What actually works at home.

Brushing, daily, is the single most effective home measure. Daily, because plaque re-forms within about 24 hours; anything less frequent is a partial measure.

Use a pet toothpaste — human toothpaste contains fluoride and sometimes xylitol, and both are a problem when swallowed. Introduce it slowly over a couple of weeks: let them lick the paste, then touch the brush to the outside of the teeth, then a few seconds a side. You only need the outer surfaces; the tongue does a reasonable job of the inner ones.

For the products that are not brushing — dental diets, chews, water additives, gels — use the Veterinary Oral Health Council seal as your filter. The VOHC accepts products that have met defined standards with supporting research, which is the only practical way to navigate a shelf full of claims.

Avoid genuinely hard chews. Antlers, bones, hooves and hard nylon are a common cause of slab fractures of the large chewing teeth. The usual guidance is that if you cannot make an indent in it with a thumbnail, it is hard enough to break a tooth.

What to ask your vet.

Ask them to look and to tell you a grade. Ask whether dental radiographs are included in their dental procedure — they should be. Ask what they see that you cannot.

And if the answer is that your animal needs a dental, it is worth remembering what the outcome usually is: an animal that is more comfortable than it has been for a long time, in a way the household notices immediately.

title: Find the exotics vet before you need one
summary: Rabbits, guinea pigs, birds and reptiles conceal illness until they cannot. By the time you can see something is wrong, the animal is usually much further into it — and there are far fewer vets who treat them.
content:
This is the least interesting article here and possibly the most useful. If you keep a rabbit, guinea pig, bird, reptile or any other exotic companion animal, find a vet who treats them competently now, while nothing is wrong.

Why the urgency is different.

Rabbits, guinea pigs, birds and reptiles are prey species. Displaying weakness in the wild attracts predators, so they conceal signs of illness until they physically cannot any longer. It is sometimes called the masking phenomenon.

The practical consequence: by the time an owner can see that something is wrong, the animal is usually considerably further into the illness than a dog or a cat would be with equally visible signs.

This inverts the usual advice. With a dog, "let's see how he is tomorrow" is often reasonable. With a rabbit, it frequently is not.

The specific thresholds worth knowing.

A rabbit that has not eaten, or has not passed droppings, for around twelve hours is an emergency. Gut stasis — the digestive system slowing and stopping — is common and frequently fatal, and it does not wait until morning. Other signs: hunching, pressing the belly to the floor, grinding teeth, reluctance to move, and droppings much smaller or fewer than usual.

A guinea pig that has stopped eating needs to be seen the same day, for the same reason.

A bird sitting fluffed on the floor of the cage, with its tail bobbing as it breathes, is a bird in serious trouble. Birds hide illness better than almost anything, and a visibly unwell bird is an emergency.

A reptile that has stopped eating needs its husbandry checked first — temperature gradient, UVB age, humidity — because husbandry is the cause of most reptile illness. If husbandry is right and it is still not eating, it needs a vet.

Why a general practice may not be enough.

This is not a criticism of small animal vets. It is that exotic species are genuinely different in ways that matter clinically.

Anatomy and physiology differ substantially. Nutritional requirements differ. Disease patterns differ. Drug choices differ, and several antibiotics that are routine in dogs are dangerous or fatal in rabbits and guinea pigs. Anaesthesia in a 900g rabbit or a 90g budgerigar is a different proposition from anaesthesia in a Labrador, requiring different equipment and different experience.

Dental disease in rabbits and guinea pigs — extremely common, because the teeth grow continuously throughout life — requires specific equipment and skill to assess and treat properly.

Practices vary enormously in how much of this they do. Some general practices see rabbits every day and are excellent. Some see one a year.

How to find one, and what to ask.

Search for practices advertising exotic, avian or small mammal services. Ask local rescues and breed-specific groups, who generally know exactly who is good.

Then ring and ask directly: how many rabbits (or birds, or reptiles) do you see in a typical week? Do you have someone with particular experience or qualifications in exotics? Do you have the equipment for rabbit dentistry? What are your out-of-hours arrangements, and does the emergency service you refer to see exotics?

That last question is the one people never ask and most regret. Many out-of-hours services are set up for dogs and cats, and finding that out at midnight is a bad time.

Register in advance. Registering, and taking the animal in once for a routine health check, means you are a known client with a file when something goes wrong, and it means the animal has been examined while well — which is what gives a vet a baseline.

Routine care, for animals that "seem fine".

Annual wellness examinations, because "seems healthy" is not evidence in a species built to look healthy. Past about five years old, twice yearly is commonly recommended, as dental disease and age-related conditions progress quickly in small animals.

Weigh them weekly at home, on a kitchen scale, and write it down. Weight loss is often the earliest measurable sign of illness in a small mammal, and it appears well before anything visible. A rabbit losing 10% of its body weight is in trouble; you will not see that by looking.

Vaccination, for rabbits, against myxomatosis and rabbit haemorrhagic disease including RHDV2, where it is available. The schedule is region-specific.

And the cost conversation.

Exotic care is not cheap, and emergency exotic care is less cheap. That is worth knowing before acquiring the animal rather than during a crisis. Budgeting for it, or insuring where cover exists, is part of keeping the animal — and a great deal of exotic suffering comes down to owners who genuinely could not afford a vet and did not know they would need one.

title: The dog who barks on the lead
summary: It looks like aggression and it usually is not. Two different problems — fear and frustration — produce the same noise, and the tell is what happens when the lead comes off.
content:
Your dog sees another dog fifty feet away and detonates. Barking, lunging, up on the back legs, hair up, apparently trying to get at the other dog. Everybody looks at you. Somebody says something about how you should let them meet.

Here is what is actually happening, and what to do about it.

Reactivity is not aggression.

Reactivity is a disproportionate emotional response to a trigger. Aggression involves intent to do harm. They look similar from ten feet away and they are not the same thing, and the difference matters — for how you feel about your dog, and for how other people treat you both.

Most reactive dogs, given the chance to meet the other dog off lead in a neutral space, are entirely normal. Which brings us to the tell.

Two causes, one noise.

Fear. The dog wants the other dog to go away, and has learned that making a lot of noise achieves that — which it does, every single time, because the other dog always eventually passes. Fear-based reactivity is a distance-increasing strategy that works, so it gets stronger.

Frustration. The dog desperately wants to reach the other dog and cannot. This is the sociable dog who has been allowed to greet on lead sometimes and not others, and who has learned that pulling and screaming occasionally produces a greeting.

The diagnostic: what happens off lead? A frustrated dog who gets to the other dog is usually delighted and normal. A frightened dog is still frightened. Both need the same first steps, but they need different things after that, and it is worth knowing which you have.

Why the lead itself is a large part of the problem.

Dogs greeting politely do not walk straight at each other. They arc, curve, approach from the side, look away, and sniff the ground on the way in. A six-foot lead makes every one of those impossible.

Worse, a tight lead changes the dog's posture: head and chest up and forward, which is the shape a confident, pushy dog makes. Two dogs each reading the other as forward and staring, neither able to move away, on a path four feet wide.

Being unable to leave is the core of it. Everything a dog does to defuse a situation — moving away, arcing, breaking off — is removed by the lead. What is left is noise. This is barrier frustration, and it is why the same dog is fine at the park and terrible on the pavement outside it.

What actually helps.

Distance, first and always. There is a distance at which your dog can see the other dog and still eat, still look at you, still move normally. Find it. It is usually much further than you expect — sometimes a hundred feet at the start. Everything useful happens under that threshold. Nothing useful happens over it.

Stop rehearsing. Every explosion makes the next one easier. For a few weeks, prioritise walks where the explosion does not happen, even if that means quiet times, industrial estates, or driving somewhere. This feels like avoidance. It is actually the treatment, because you are giving the behaviour nothing to practise on.

Change the association, do not just suppress the noise. The standard approach is: dog appears at a workable distance, you feed something excellent, other dog goes away, food stops. Repeated, this changes what the sight of another dog predicts. The order matters — the dog appears first, then the food. Food first is a bribe and teaches nothing.

Teach an emergency exit. A cheerful "let's go" that means turn and move away with me, practised when nothing is happening, so it is available when something is.

Use a well-fitted harness with a front and back attachment point, and a lead you can shorten smoothly. No prong collars, no choke chains, no shock collars. Beyond the welfare problem, applying something unpleasant while the dog is looking at another dog teaches the dog that other dogs predict something unpleasant, which is precisely the association you are trying to undo. The AVSAB's position, based on current evidence, is that only reward-based methods should be used for all dog training, including behaviour problems.

Stop letting them greet on lead. Even sometimes. Intermittent success is what builds the most persistent behaviour, and on-lead greetings are a bad format anyway. Make the rule absolute: we do not meet dogs on the lead. Then arrange proper introductions on neutral ground, off lead or on long lines, where a greeting can actually go well.

What to say to other people.

"We're training, please give us space" while walking away, cheerfully, is enough. You do not owe anyone a conversation or an apology, and you are not obliged to let their dog meet yours because they have asserted that theirs is friendly.

An orange lead, harness or bandana marked "give me space" is widely understood in some places and completely unknown in others. Worth trying, not worth relying on.

When to get help.

Reactivity is one of the most common reasons owners seek professional help and one of the most improvable problems there is. Getting help early is faster and cheaper than getting help after two years of practice.

Get help now, rather than later, if: there is any bite history; your dog cannot recover within a few minutes of an incident; you are frightened of your own dog; or you have stopped walking them, which is a common and understandable place to end up and a bad one to stay in.

Look for a CBCC-KA, a CDBC, or a veterinary behaviourist. And see your vet first regardless — pain lowers tolerance, and a proportion of dogs who become reactive in adulthood are dogs who have started to hurt somewhere.

title: When to neuter: the study everyone quotes and nobody reads
summary: Hart and colleagues examined 35 breeds over 15 years. In most of them, age at neutering made no difference to the outcomes measured. Where it did, it tracked body size — and the answer is breed- and sex-specific, not a rule.
content:
Ask when to neuter a dog and you will get a confident answer, and the confidence is the problem. This is one of the most misreported areas in popular dog writing, usually flattened into either "six months, always" or "never neuter early, it causes cancer". Neither is what the research says.

The study.

Hart, Hart, Thigpen and Willits published "Assisting Decision-Making on Age of Neutering for 35 Breeds of Dogs" in Frontiers in Veterinary Science in 2020, drawing on 15 years of records from the UC Davis veterinary teaching hospital.

They looked at three categories of outcome against age at neutering: joint disorders (hip dysplasia, cranial cruciate ligament tears, elbow dysplasia); cancers (lymphoma, haemangiosarcoma, mast cell tumour, osteosarcoma); and urinary incontinence.

What it found.

In most of the breeds examined, the risk of developing these problems was not affected by the age of neutering.

Where an effect did appear, vulnerability to joint disorders tracked body size. Smaller breeds generally did not show the pattern; a majority of the larger breeds did.

And the results differ by sex within the same breed. That is why the authors present a breed-by-breed, sex-by-sex table rather than a single recommendation. The whole point of the paper is that a general rule does not fit.

Why size and timing plausibly interact.

The sex hormones are part of what signals growth plates to close. Neuter before that happens and the plates stay open longer, producing a slightly taller dog with somewhat different joint angles. In a large, heavy, fast-growing breed, that is a plausible mechanism for joint disorder risk. In a 12lb terrier the same shift means much less.

That is the reasoning behind the pattern. It is not a reason to extrapolate to a breed that was not in the study.

What this does not say.

It does not say neutering causes cancer. It says that in some breeds, in some sexes, at some ages, the incidence of certain cancers in this hospital population differed.

It does not say early neutering is harmful in general. In most breeds studied, it made no measured difference.

It does not say leaving a dog entire is the safe default. That is the other half of the decision, and it is frequently dropped.

The other half of the decision.

For females: mammary tumours, where risk rises substantially with each season before spaying; and pyometra, a life-threatening uterine infection which is common in older entire bitches and is an emergency requiring surgery. Both are genuinely serious and both are largely prevented by spaying.

For males: testicular tumours, some prostatic disease, and — depending on circumstances — roaming and the accompanying road-traffic risk.

And, unavoidably, unplanned litters. If you cannot guarantee management of an entire dog through every season for its whole life, that is a real factor rather than a moralising one.

Behaviour is not the reason.

Neutering is often suggested as a treatment for behaviour problems, and the evidence for that is much weaker than the folklore. It reliably reduces behaviour driven by sex hormones — roaming after a bitch in season, some inter-male behaviour, mounting in some dogs. It does not reliably improve fear, anxiety, reactivity or aggression, and there is research suggesting some anxiety-related behaviours can be worse in neutered dogs.

If the problem is behavioural, the answer is a behaviour plan, not surgery.

What to actually do.

Look your breed up. The Hart paper's tables are organised by breed and sex, and UC Davis publishes an accessible summary. Take it to your vet.

If your breed is not in the study — most mixed-breed dogs are not — the practical proxy is adult size. For a large or giant breed, waiting until growth is complete is a defensible position to discuss. For a small breed, the evidence for waiting is much thinner.

Then weigh it against your own circumstances: sex, whether you can manage seasons, whether the dog roams, your household, and your vet's view of this particular animal.

There is no universally correct age. There is a decision with real considerations on both sides, and the honest version of this advice is to make it deliberately with your vet rather than to follow a number you read somewhere.

title: "He bit with no warning": reading a parrot
summary: Almost every parrot warns first. Stiffened posture, eye pinning, fanned tail, ruffled feathers, repeated beak clicking. The bite that came from nowhere was usually the fourth signal.
content:
The sentence that brings most parrots to a behaviour consultation is "he bit me with no warning". It is almost always untrue, and not because the owner is careless. It is because bird signals are fast, subtle, and taught to nobody.

The signals, roughly in escalating order.

A change in posture. A relaxed bird is loose, weight evenly distributed, feathers smooth but not slicked. A bird about to act goes rigid — a stiffened, held posture is often the first thing that changes.

Eye pinning. The pupils rapidly constrict and dilate. Crucially, this is not an emotion in itself; it means intensity. Paired with a relaxed body, it signals interest and excitement — a bird looking at a favourite food or a new toy. Paired with ruffled feathers, a rigid body, or beak clicking, it is a warning.

Feather position. Slicked-down feathers with a tall thin posture is fear or alarm. Fluffed-up body feathers can mean several things depending on context: contentment while resting, a mating display, or aggression. Raised feathers on the nape or crest, held with a rigid body, is arousal.

Tail fanning. Spreading the tail feathers wide makes the bird look larger. In an aggressive context it is a clear display.

Crouching with the head lowered, beak slightly open, weaving from side to side. This is a bird preparing to lunge.

Beak clicking. A single click can be a greeting or an acknowledgement. Repeated clicking is usually a warning, particularly when combined with eye pinning.

Hissing, growling, or lunging without contact — the last signals before a bite.

The context problem.

Almost every one of these signals is context-dependent, which is why owners find them hard. Fluffing can be contentment or aggression. Eye pinning can be delight or a threat. Wing-drooping can be a stretch, a display, or a bird that is too hot.

The reliable approach is not to read one signal but to read the whole bird plus the situation: what changed just before, what is the body doing overall, and is the bird moving towards or away.

The commonest triggers.

Hormonal behaviour, particularly in spring, and particularly around a favoured person. A bird in breeding condition is a different animal, and much of what owners describe as sudden aggression is seasonal.

Territoriality around the cage. Many birds who are perfectly friendly out of the cage will defend the inside of it. Asking a bird to step up from inside the cage, rather than from the top or from a stand, is a common bite scenario.

Displacement. A bird startled or frustrated by something else — a person entering the room, a bird outside the window — may redirect onto whoever is closest.

Being asked to step up when it does not want to leave. This is the ordinary one, and the signals are usually given clearly.

Height. Some birds behave differently when perched above head height.

What to do instead of getting bitten.

Watch before you reach. Two seconds of looking at the whole bird prevents most bites.

Respect a no. If the bird leans away, turns its back, or gives any of the signals above, stop and try later. Pushing through teaches the bird that the earlier, quieter signals do not work — so it stops using them, which is exactly how a bird becomes one that "bites with no warning".

Do not punish a bite. Shouting, tapping the beak, dropping the bird or covering the cage as punishment all damage the relationship, and several of them are reinforcing in their own right — a dramatic reaction is interesting.

Train a step-up properly, with reinforcement, so it is a request the bird chooses to accept rather than a hand appearing under the feet.

Give the bird ways to say no that are not a bite: a stand it can move to, a perch it can retreat along, the choice of coming out or not.

The other half of it: foraging.

A great deal of parrot behaviour trouble is a bird with nothing to do. Wild parrots are reported to spend roughly four to eight hours a day foraging; a conventional food bowl reduces that to under an hour.

An estimated 10% of captive parrots perform feather-destructive behaviour, and limited foraging opportunity is one hypothesised driver. Foraging enrichment reliably increases the time birds spend foraging — though it should be said honestly that it has not been shown to reach wild time budgets or to eliminate feather damaging behaviour.

Practically: stop using a bowl as the only food source. Wrap food in paper, thread it on skewers, hide it in cardboard tubes, put it in foraging toys, scatter it in shreddable material, and place it in several locations so the bird has to travel and search. Change the arrangements regularly, because novelty is a large part of the point.

When it is medical.

Feather plucking is a veterinary problem before it is a behavioural one. Skin disease, parasites, infection, nutritional deficiency, organ disease and pain are all causes, and they are at least as common as the behavioural explanations.

A sudden change in temperament in a previously steady bird is also a reason to see an avian vet. Birds conceal illness thoroughly, and irritability is one of the few things that leaks out.

title: Guarding: toys, water bowls, doorways and you
summary: Most fights between dogs who otherwise get on are about an object. The fix is boring and reliable — remove the object — and the traditional advice to take food away from a puppy is the thing that builds the problem.
content:
Resource guarding is using avoidance, threat or aggression to keep control of something valuable when a person or another animal approaches. Food and food-related items are the most commonly guarded, but the list is longer than people expect: toys, chews, beds, furniture, resting spots, doorways, a stolen sock, and people.

It is common, it is normal behaviour rather than a character flaw, and it is the single most likely cause of a fight between two dogs who like each other perfectly well.

What it looks like before it looks like anything.

The obvious end — growling, snapping, lunging — is late. Earlier signals, in rough order:

Eating faster when someone approaches. Freezing, going still over the item. Lowering the head over it, or curling the body around it. Moving the item away and settling somewhere else. A hard stare, sometimes with the whites of the eyes showing. Lifting a lip. A low growl.

Learn the freeze. It is the one that comes first, it is easy to miss, and it is the point at which stepping back costs nothing.

The advice that builds the problem.

There is a persistent tradition of taking food away from a puppy repeatedly, putting hands in the bowl, and removing chews, on the theory that the dog learns you are in charge and that objects are freely given up.

What the dog actually learns is that a human approaching a valuable thing predicts losing it. That is exactly the contingency guarding is built on. You have run a training program teaching the dog that approach means loss, and then you are surprised by the result.

The same applies to punishing a growl. A growl is a dog choosing to warn instead of bite. Punish it enough and you get a dog who no longer warns — which people describe afterwards as biting "with no warning".

What works instead: trading up.

The principle is to reverse the prediction. A human approaching a valuable thing should predict something better arriving, not the thing leaving.

In practice, with an ordinary dog and no history of aggression: walk past while they have something good and drop a better treat, without stopping and without reaching. Repeat, many times, over weeks. You are not asking for anything. You are simply becoming the thing that adds rather than the thing that takes.

When you genuinely need an item back, trade for it: offer something clearly better, take the item once the dog has left it, and — importantly — give the original back afterwards where it is safe to do so. A dog who learns that giving things up usually means getting them back gives things up easily.

Teach a real "drop" as a game, using two identical toys, long before you need it. And manage the environment so you rarely need it: bins closed, socks off the floor, chews given in a place the dog can eat undisturbed.

If there is any growling at people, snapping, or a bite history, stop and get professional help — a veterinary behaviourist, a CDBC or a CBCC-KA. This is the category where amateur intervention makes things meaningfully worse, and where a plan built for your specific dog is worth the money.

Guarding at a playdate.

Almost all of it is preventable by removing the objects, and this is the part people skip.

Before the other dog arrives, pick up every toy, every chew, every bone, every food bowl, and anything the dog has ever slept with. Not most of them. All of them.

Water is a resource too. Two bowls, in different places, and watch them.

Doorways and narrow spaces are resources. A dog standing in a gateway is controlling access, and the dog who wants past is being blocked. Keep the space open and interrupt the blocking cheerfully.

People are resources. If your dog stiffens when the other dog approaches you, get up and move. Do not sit still and let a dog guard your legs.

Feed separately, always, in different rooms, and never leave food down.

If either dog guards, the sensible venue is a big open outdoor space rather than a garden, because space itself reduces conflict.

And if a fight does start over an object: do not reach in. Make a loud noise, throw water, or use a barrier — a board, a chair, an open umbrella. Then separate the dogs completely before anyone checks anyone over, and take the object out of the equation before there is any discussion about whether to try again.

The uncomfortable one: guarding you.

A dog who growls at another dog approaching you is guarding, and it is very often excused as protectiveness or loyalty. It is not a compliment and it does not need encouraging. Treat it the same way: get up, move, remove the resource — which in this case is your own stationary lap.

Between household dogs, the same principle applies. Feed separately, give chews in separate rooms, provide more beds than dogs, and do not make them compete for the sofa.

title: Most reptile illness is a husbandry problem: heat, light and the bulb you forgot
summary: Metabolic bone disease is among the most common and most preventable conditions in captive reptiles. Early cases can be reversed by fixing the setup; the skeletal deformities cannot.
content:
A reptile brought to a vet is usually a reptile whose enclosure is wrong. That is not an insult to owners — it is that reptiles depend on their environment for functions that mammals perform internally, so an environmental error becomes a medical condition.

Two variables account for most of it: heat and ultraviolet light.

Heat: a gradient, not a temperature.

Reptiles are ectothermic. They do not generate their own body heat; they move between warmer and cooler places to regulate it. So an enclosure needs a genuine thermal gradient — a basking zone at one end and a distinctly cooler zone at the other — not one uniform temperature.

The gradient is what lets the animal choose, and choosing is how it regulates digestion, immune function and activity.

Too cold, and digestion slows or stops. Food sits undigested in the stomach, which leads to impaction, systemic illness and death. A reptile that has stopped eating very often has an enclosure that is too cold rather than an illness.

Too hot with nowhere to escape to is equally dangerous, and it is why the cool end matters as much as the basking end.

Measure it properly. A digital probe thermometer at each end, and an infrared temperature gun for surface temperatures. The stick-on dial gauges sold with many enclosures are inaccurate.

Heat should come from above, as it does in nature, and be controlled by a thermostat. Heat rocks are a common cause of serious burns because reptiles do not reliably move away from contact heat.

Light: UVB, and the bulb that stops working before it stops shining.

Many reptile species need ultraviolet B light to synthesise vitamin D3 in the skin. Without D3 they cannot absorb dietary calcium, regardless of how much calcium is supplied.

The result is metabolic bone disease, which is among the most common and most preventable conditions in captive reptiles. Causes are calcium deficiency, vitamin D3 deficiency, an inappropriate calcium-to-phosphorus ratio, and inadequate UVB, usually in combination.

Signs include lethargy, tremors, a soft or swollen jaw, bowing of the limbs, a kinked spine, reluctance to move or climb, and fractures from ordinary activity.

Early metabolic bone disease can often be reversed by correcting the husbandry — proper UVB, calcium supplementation, appropriate temperatures. Skeletal deformities that have already formed are usually permanent.

Here is the specific trap: UVB bulbs lose usable output long before they stop emitting visible light. A bulb that looks fine can be producing almost no UVB. They are replaced on a schedule — typically every six to twelve months depending on the type, per the manufacturer — not when they fail. Write the installation date on the bulb in marker.

Distance and obstruction matter too. UVB output falls sharply with distance, and ordinary glass and most plastics block it, so a bulb outside a glass lid is doing much less than you think. Fine mesh reduces it as well.

The other four things.

Humidity, which is species-specific and which people either ignore or get wrong in both directions. Too low causes retained shed, particularly around toes and tail tips where a retained ring can cut off circulation and cost the animal a digit. Too high causes respiratory infection and scale rot.

Diet, including calcium and vitamin supplementation on an appropriate schedule, and gut-loading insects so they are worth eating. The calcium-to-phosphorus ratio is a real consideration, not a detail.

Enclosure size and furnishing. Most commercially sold enclosures are smaller than the adult animal needs, and most animals need climbing structure, hides at both the warm and cool ends, and appropriate substrate.

Water, appropriate to the species — some drink from bowls, some only from droplets, some need to soak.

The one piece of general advice.

Every one of the numbers above is species-specific, and the differences are large. A bearded dragon, a crested gecko, a corn snake and a ball python need substantially different setups, and getting one right does not mean you have got another right.

So: research your specific species from a reliable source before acquiring it — a specialist veterinary or herpetological reference, not the care sheet on the shop wall, which is frequently outdated and sometimes wrong.

And find an exotics vet in advance. There are far fewer vets who treat reptiles than there are people who keep them, and the animal conceals illness until it is well advanced.

Finally, the household point: reptiles and amphibians commonly carry Salmonella as normal gut flora, and the CDC does not recommend them for households with children under five, people with weakened immune systems, or adults over 65. Wash hands thoroughly after any contact, supervise children's handwashing, and never clean enclosures or equipment in the kitchen sink.

title: Hosting a playdate at home
summary: Your garden is the most convenient venue and the most territorial one. A checklist for the fence, the objects, the exits, and the fact that your dog lives there and the other one does not.
content:
Hosting is easy, cheap and comfortable, and it introduces one variable that neutral ground does not: your dog already owns the place.

That is manageable. It just has to be managed deliberately rather than assumed away.

Before the day: the fence.

Walk the whole boundary and look at it as an escape problem rather than a decoration. Gaps at ground level. Loose panels. The gap under the gate. Whether the gate latches, and whether it latches when a delivery driver closes it absent-mindedly.

Height matters relative to the visiting dog, not yours. A four-foot fence that has contained your Basset for six years is a suggestion to a Malinois.

Put a sign on the gate for the duration, and if you are the anxious type, a second barrier — a hallway, a closed inner door — so that a dog getting through one thing has not got out.

Check for the things that are only hazards when there are two dogs running: a pond, a pool, a raised deck edge, a slippery patio, glass furniture, a barbecue, a shed with rat bait or slug pellets, and anything sharp at dog height.

Look at your plants. Some are genuinely toxic, and a dog chewing in an unfamiliar garden is more likely than a dog chewing in its own.

Before the day: the objects.

Pick up everything. Toys, chews, bones, food bowls, water bowls you will replace with two fresh ones, the dog bed your dog is precious about, and anything left in the garden from last week.

This is the single highest-value thing on the list. Most conflicts between dogs who like each other are about an object, and the object is optional.

Put out two water bowls in different places, and watch them.

The territorial part, and how to defuse it.

Do not meet at your front door. That is your dog's threshold and the worst place to introduce anybody.

Instead: meet somewhere else first. Walk the two dogs together, parallel, for ten or fifteen minutes in a nearby park or street, and let them arrive at your house having already met. This one step removes most of the territorial problem and it takes almost no extra time.

Then come in together, ideally through a side gate straight into the garden rather than through the house.

If your dog is the possessive sort, let the visitor into the garden first and bring your own dog in second, so nobody is defending a space against an incoming stranger.

During.

Both people outside, watching. This is a genuine social occasion for the humans too, and that is exactly how supervision quietly stops happening.

Breaks every two or three minutes: call your own dog to you, thirty seconds of calm, release. It caps arousal and it makes the recall reliable in exactly the context you need it.

Keep the house out of it, at least the first time. A dog who has learned the layout of your house, found the cat, and discovered the kitchen bin is a different visitor next time.

Give your own dog somewhere to go that the visitor cannot follow — a room with a baby gate, a crate they already like. A dog who can leave rarely needs to escalate. Check on them: a host dog who has taken themselves off and stayed there has told you the playdate is over.

Watch for the shift from playing to patrolling. Your dog following the visitor around, positioning between the visitor and you, or standing in doorways, is the early form of a problem.

Twenty to thirty minutes is plenty for a first visit. End it while both dogs still want more.

If you have a cat, a rabbit or a small pet.

Do not run this playdate at your house. There is no version of a strange dog in a house with a cat that is worth the risk, however good the dog is described as being, and a closed door is not much comfort if the cat is behind it and frightened for an hour.

Either use neutral ground or house the small animals somewhere genuinely secure and separate — a different floor, a closed room the dogs cannot reach, ideally with someone in it.

Afterwards.

Pick up any deposits, refill water, and give both dogs something to lick or chew separately, in separate spaces, to wind down. Licking and chewing are self-soothing, and the come-down matters as much as the session.

Then be honest in the message afterwards. "That was great, ours would love to do it again" or "I think mine found being at home a bit much — could we do a walk next time?" Both are useful. The second one is more useful.

title: Bloat: the one that kills a big dog in an afternoon
summary: The stomach distends and then rotates on itself. Reported lifetime risk in large and giant breeds runs from about 4% to 37%, and after one episode the recurrence rate without surgery has been reported as high as 75%.
content:
Gastric dilatation-volvulus is the reason owners of Great Danes and German Shepherds know a phone number by heart. It is worth knowing what it looks like even if your dog is not in a high-risk breed, because recognition is most of the treatment.

What happens.

The stomach fills with gas and fluid and distends. Then it rotates on its own axis. The rotation seals both ends, so nothing can leave in either direction, and the gas continues to accumulate with nowhere to go.

The expanding stomach compresses the major veins returning blood to the heart, which sends the dog into shock. The twist also cuts off the stomach's own blood supply, so the tissue begins to die. The spleen, attached to the stomach, is often dragged around with it.

This progresses over hours, not days. It requires surgery.

Which dogs.

Large and deep-chested breeds carry most of the risk: Great Dane, German Shepherd, Standard Poodle, Saint Bernard, Doberman Pinscher, Irish Setter, Weimaraner, and similar shapes.

The relevant feature is the height-to-width ratio of the chest — a deep, narrow chest rather than sheer size.

Reported lifetime risk in large and giant breeds spans roughly 3.9% to 36.7%, depending on breed and study. Dogs over 100lb are commonly cited at around 20%. The Great Dane is generally described as the highest-risk breed of all.

Other factors reported in the literature include being fed one large meal a day, eating rapidly, exercise soon after a large meal or a large drink, increasing age, being underweight, and temperament — dogs described as anxious appear at higher risk than dogs described as relaxed.

Small dogs and cats can get GDV. It is uncommon enough that it is not what to worry about.

What it looks like.

Unproductive retching. The dog tries repeatedly to vomit and brings up nothing, or a little white foam. This is the single most characteristic sign.

A swollen, tight or drum-like abdomen, particularly behind the ribs on the left. In a very deep-chested dog it can be surprisingly hard to see.

Restlessness and pacing, an inability to settle, repeatedly getting up and lying down.

Drooling more than usual, often thick and ropey.

Standing with the front end down and the back end up — a stretch that looks like a play bow but does not resolve.

Rapid shallow breathing, pale gums, weakness, and collapse as shock develops.

If you are looking at those signs in a large deep-chested dog, drive. Do not wait to see whether it settles, do not offer food or water, and do not try to make the dog vomit. Call on the way so they can prepare.

Prevention: gastropexy.

Prophylactic gastropexy is a surgical procedure that tacks the stomach to the body wall. It does not prevent the stomach from distending — the dog can still bloat — but it prevents the twist in most cases, and the twist is what kills.

In high-risk breeds it is often performed at the same time as spaying or neutering, which avoids a second anaesthetic. It can also be done laparoscopically.

The case for it is strongest in the giant breeds and in dogs with a first-degree relative who has had GDV. It is a conversation to have with your vet while your dog is young, rather than a decision to make in an emergency.

After an episode, the argument becomes much stronger: without gastropexy, the recurrence rate following an episode of GDV has been reported as high as 75%. Gastropexy is generally performed as part of the emergency surgery for that reason.

The management measures.

These are commonly recommended, and it is honest to say that the evidence behind them is more mixed than the confidence with which they are given.

Feed two or three smaller meals rather than one large one. Slow down a fast eater with a slow-feeder bowl or a puzzle feeder. Avoid vigorous exercise for an hour or so either side of a meal. Avoid a very large drink immediately after exercise.

The raised-bowl question is genuinely unsettled and has been associated with increased risk in some work, so a raised bowl is not a preventive measure.

None of this substitutes for knowing the signs and having a plan. For a high-risk breed, the two things that actually change outcomes are recognition and a gastropexy conversation.

title: You are not buying a fish tank, you are growing a filter
summary: New tank syndrome kills more pet fish than anything else, and it is entirely avoidable. The tank needs four to six weeks to grow bacteria before a fish should be in it.
content:
The most common way a pet fish dies is that it was put into a tank that was not ready, by somebody who was sold both on the same afternoon and told to wait a day.

This is the single most useful thing anybody can be told before setting up a first aquarium.

The problem.

Fish excrete ammonia, continuously, through their gills and their waste. Ammonia is toxic to fish at very low concentrations — it burns gills and causes organ damage.

In an established aquarium, ammonia never accumulates, because bacteria consume it. One group of nitrifying bacteria oxidises ammonia into nitrite. Nitrite is also toxic. A second group converts nitrite into nitrate, which is far less toxic at reasonable concentrations and which you remove with regular partial water changes.

That chain is the nitrogen cycle, and those bacterial colonies live mostly in the filter media, not in the water.

A brand-new tank has none of them. It is a box of water with a pump in it.

New tank syndrome.

Put fish into an uncycled tank and ammonia rises with nothing to consume it. Days later, as the first bacteria establish, ammonia falls and nitrite spikes instead — often to worse levels. Only after that does the second colony catch up.

The fish live through both spikes, if they live.

Signs include loss of colour, clamped fins, hiding in corners, gasping at the surface, red or inflamed gills, and lying on the bottom. Fish that survive are often damaged and prone to disease afterwards.

The water is usually crystal clear throughout, which is why owners do not suspect the water. Ammonia and nitrite are invisible.

Fishless cycling: the right way.

Set the tank up completely — filter running, heater at the right temperature, substrate, plants, decor — with no fish.

Add a source of ammonia to feed the bacteria. Pure ammonium chloride solution sold for the purpose is the cleanest option; some people use a pinch of fish food left to decompose, which works but is harder to control.

Test the water. You need a liquid test kit for ammonia, nitrite and nitrate. The paper dip strips are much less accurate, and this is the one piece of equipment worth not economising on.

Watch the pattern. Ammonia rises, then falls as nitrite rises, then nitrite falls as nitrate appears. That sequence is the cycle establishing.

The tank is cycled when you can add a full dose of ammonia — around 2 to 3 mg/L-N — and by the next day it has all been processed through to nitrate, with no nitrite remaining.

Then do a large water change to bring nitrate down, and add fish — a few at a time, not all at once, because the bacterial colony is sized to the current bioload and needs time to grow with it.

How long.

Commonly four to six weeks, sometimes longer. The active ammonia-and-nitrite phase typically runs two to six weeks.

Seeding the tank shortens it considerably: a bottled live nitrifying bacteria product, or better, filter media, gravel or a sponge from an established healthy tank. With good live bacteria and an ammonia source, a cycle can complete in around a week.

Do not rush it. The bacteria grow at the rate they grow.

The things that break a cycled tank.

Cleaning the filter media in tap water. Chlorine kills the bacteria you spent six weeks growing. Rinse media gently in a bucket of tank water you have just removed, and never replace all the media at once.

Replacing the whole filter cartridge, which is what many cartridge-based filters instruct you to do monthly. That throws away the colony. Where possible, use filters with media you can keep.

Medicating the tank, particularly with antibiotics, which can knock out the bacteria as well.

Adding too many fish at once.

Overfeeding, which adds ammonia faster than the colony can handle. Feed what is eaten in a minute or two, once a day, and remove what is not.

Not using a dechlorinator on tap water at every water change.

Afterwards: the routine.

Test regularly, particularly for the first few months. An established tank should read zero ammonia, zero nitrite, and some nitrate.

Partial water changes — commonly around 25% weekly, depending on stocking — are how nitrate is removed. There is no filter that removes it for you.

Any reading above zero for ammonia or nitrite in an established tank means something has gone wrong: an overstocked tank, a dead fish somewhere, a damaged filter, or a cycle that was never finished.

And stock the tank for the adult size of the fish, not the size in the bag. The common goldfish sold as a starter fish reaches well over a foot and is a pond animal, and a great deal of fish suffering comes down to that one piece of missing information.

title: The cough that travels: respiratory disease where dogs meet
summary: Roughly 80% of dogs exposed to canine influenza develop signs — and about 20% show none at all while still shedding. "He seems fine" is not evidence, which is why the etiquette is to postpone.
content:
Anywhere dogs gather, respiratory disease circulates: parks, daycare, boarding kennels, grooming salons, training classes, and playdates. It is rarely serious in a healthy adult dog and it is thoroughly miserable, highly contagious, and easy to spread without knowing.

"Kennel cough" is a complex, not a disease.

The proper name is canine infectious respiratory disease complex. It is caused by a shifting combination of organisms — most commonly the bacterium Bordetella bronchiseptica and canine parainfluenza virus, along with several others, often more than one at a time.

That is why a vaccinated dog can still get a cough. The vaccine covers some of the common agents, not all of the possible ones.

Canine influenza is a different thing.

Canine influenza virus, principally the H3N2 strain in recent US outbreaks, is a genuine influenza rather than part of the classic kennel cough picture, and it behaves differently.

Virtually all dogs exposed to the virus become infected. Roughly 80% develop clinical signs. About 20% show no signs at all — and still shed the virus.

The characteristic cough persists for 10 to 21 days. H3N2 can be transmitted by direct contact or by airborne particles for up to ten days after infection.

That 20% figure is the one that matters for arranging playdates. A dog can be infectious and completely normal to look at.

What it looks like.

A harsh, honking, dry cough, often described as sounding like something is stuck in the throat, and frequently ending in a retch or gag that owners mistake for vomiting.

Coughing that worsens with excitement, exercise, or pressure from a collar.

Sometimes: nasal discharge, sneezing, reduced appetite, lethargy, and a fever.

Most healthy adult dogs recover with rest. Take it seriously and see a vet promptly if the dog is lethargic, off food, feverish, has laboured breathing or a productive wet cough, or if the dog is a puppy, elderly, flat-faced, or has existing heart or airway disease. Pneumonia is the complication that matters.

Vaccination: what it does and does not do.

An annual intranasal vaccine covering Bordetella, canine adenovirus type 2 and parainfluenza is recommended for dogs whose lifestyles put them in multi-dog settings. Where canine influenza is circulating, an injectable canine influenza vaccine is also recommended.

The honest framing from the AVMA: these vaccines will not necessarily prevent infection, but they can substantially reduce the severity and duration of illness and the amount of virus shed.

That last part is the social argument. A vaccinated dog that still catches something sheds less of it into the park.

If your dog socialises — playdates, parks, classes, daycare, boarding — tell your vet that, because it is exactly the lifestyle information that determines whether these noncore vaccines are appropriate.

The etiquette.

Cancel if your dog is coughing. Not "he's fine in himself" — coughing dogs stay home. This is the single most useful convention in the whole area, and it is routinely broken because the dog seems well.

Cancel if your dog has been anywhere with a known outbreak in the last week or two, even if they are well.

Cancel if anyone in the household's other dogs is coughing.

Say why. "One of ours has a cough, can we push it a week?" is a normal message and every reasonable owner would rather receive it than not.

Isolate a coughing dog properly: no parks, no classes, no daycare, no walks where other dogs are, for as long as your vet advises — commonly a couple of weeks after signs resolve, and longer for influenza.

Wash your hands and change your clothes between an infected dog and other dogs. These organisms travel on people, bowls, leads and toys, not only dog to dog.

Why this belongs in a playdate app.

Because the alternative to the conversation is the outbreak. The whole advantage of a one-to-one playdate over a public park is that two people can simply tell each other the truth about whether their dogs are well, and that only works if both of them actually do it.

title: Heartworm: prevention costs a coffee a month, treatment costs a summer
summary: Prevention runs roughly $5 to $25 a month. Treatment commonly runs $600 to $1,200 — and eight to twelve weeks of strict crate rest, which is the part that is not measured in money.
content:
Heartworm is the clearest cost-benefit case in preventive veterinary medicine, and it is still one of the most commonly skipped preventives. Partly because the disease is invisible until it is advanced, and partly because nobody explains what treatment actually involves.

What it is.

A mosquito bites an infected animal and picks up microfilariae. The larvae develop inside the mosquito, and the next bite deposits them into a new host. Over months they mature into adult worms — up to a foot long — living in the pulmonary arteries and the right side of the heart.

The damage is mechanical and inflammatory: the arteries thicken, the heart works against increasing resistance, and eventually the animal develops heart failure. By the time there are outward signs — coughing, exercise intolerance, weight loss, a swollen abdomen — there has usually been significant damage for a while.

Heartworm has been diagnosed in all fifty US states. Southern states have the highest incidence because of the mosquito population, but the map is not a boundary.

What prevention costs.

Roughly $5 to $25 a month, or about $60 to $300 a year, depending on the product and the dog's size.

Most monthly heartworm preventives also cover several intestinal worms, which is a meaningful bonus given that roughly one in five fresh faecal samples collected at US dog parks in one multi-city survey carried worm eggs.

What treatment costs.

Melarsomine injections are commonly quoted at $400 to $1,000. Total treatment typically runs $600 to $1,200, and severe cases can run several times that. Doxycycline and steroids add to the bill.

Roughly speaking, treatment costs about ten times what a year of prevention would have.

But the money is not the worst part.

The protocol is one melarsomine injection, then a 30-day rest period, then two more injections 24 hours apart.

Around that sits strict exercise restriction: 8 to 12 weeks of crate rest with brief lead walks for toileting only, continuing for at least another month after the final injection, before a gradual return to normal activity.

The reason is that the treatment kills the adult worms and the dead worms fragment. Those fragments travel into the smaller pulmonary vessels, and the more the dog exerts itself, the greater the risk of a fatal pulmonary embolism. The restriction is not caution; it is the thing keeping the dog alive during treatment.

So the true cost of treatment for an active dog is a season of its life in a crate, and the treatment itself is not entirely without risk.

What the guidelines say.

The American Heartworm Society and the FDA recommend that all dogs and cats in the US be on heartworm preventives year-round.

All dogs should be tested annually, even those on year-round prevention. That is not distrust; it is because prevention can fail — a spat-out tablet, a topical applied to a wet coat, a missed month, vomiting after a dose — and finding an infection early matters enormously.

The 2024 AHS guidelines added routine heartworm screening for cats as well as dogs, and recommend microfilaria testing alongside antigen testing in dogs.

Cats are different, and it is worse.

Cats are not natural hosts, so fewer worms mature and the burden is lower. That sounds better and is not.

Feline heartworm disease is difficult to diagnose — screening in cats uses both antigen and antibody tests — and there is no approved adulticide treatment for cats. Even one or two worms can cause severe respiratory disease, and the death of a single worm can kill the cat.

Which means that for cats, prevention is essentially the only intervention available. Indoor cats included: mosquitoes come indoors, and a substantial proportion of cats diagnosed with heartworm are reported to be indoor-only.

The simple version.

A monthly preventive, year-round, for every dog and cat in the household, and an annual test for dogs. That is the whole protocol, and it is one of the few places in pet care where doing the boring thing reliably removes a serious disease from your life entirely.

title: The kit and the plan: being ready before you need to be
summary: A first aid kit is a bridge to veterinary care, never a substitute. Ten minutes of preparation now — a box, four phone numbers and a photograph — is worth more than any amount of reading later.
content:
Almost everything about a pet emergency is easier if a few decisions were made in advance. None of them take long, and all of them are hard to make while frightened.

The four numbers.

Put these in your phone now, under names you will find at 3am.

Your own vet, and their out-of-hours arrangement — many practices refer overnight to a different hospital, and finding that out during an emergency wastes the worst ten minutes.

The nearest 24-hour emergency veterinary hospital, with the address saved in your maps app. Drive past it once so you know where to park.

ASPCA Animal Poison Control: (888) 426-4435. There is a consultation fee. It is worth it.

Pet Poison Helpline: (855) 764-7661, as an alternative.

For a rabbit, guinea pig, bird or reptile, add a fifth: the nearest exotics vet, and their opening hours. There are far fewer of them, and the animal has less time.

The kit.

Keep it in a waterproof container, somewhere you can grab it, and check it twice a year for expiry.

For wounds: gauze pads and rolled gauze, self-adhesive bandage that does not stick to fur, adhesive tape, blunt-ended scissors, and sterile saline for flushing wounds or eyes.

For handling: disposable gloves, a towel or blanket, and a muzzle sized for your dog. That last one is not pessimism about your dog's character. A frightened animal in pain may bite the person it loves most, and it does not mean anything about them. Do not muzzle an animal that is vomiting or having trouble breathing.

For assessment: a digital thermometer, tweezers, a tick removal tool, and a torch.

Paperwork: a card with your vet's details, your animal's medications and doses, known allergies, microchip number, and a recent photograph.

Not in the kit: human painkillers. Ibuprofen and paracetamol are both dangerous to pets, and paracetamol is lethal to cats in very small amounts. Also skip hydrogen peroxide unless a veterinary professional has specifically told you to use it for a specific ingestion — inducing vomiting is actively harmful for caustic substances and petroleum products.

The AVMA's framing is the right one to keep: any first aid you give should be followed by veterinary care. First aid is not a substitute; it is what keeps an animal alive on the way.

The evacuation version.

A separate, larger bag, kept near an exit, for wildfire, flood, hurricane or evacuation.

Several days of food and water in airtight containers, and a bowl. An extra supply of any regular medication, in a waterproof container. Carriers, sized so each animal can stand and turn. A spare leash, collar and harness. Litter, a tray and a scoop — a shirt box with a bag in it works. Vaccination records, or photographs of them on your phone. Temporary ID tags you can write a friend's number on. And current photographs of you together with each animal, which is what actually reunites people with pets in a shelter system.

The planning part matters as much as the bag. Know now which hotels or shelters in your evacuation direction accept animals, and agree with a friend or neighbour who will get your animals out if you are not home.

Two skills worth having.

Know how to check gum colour and capillary refill. Press a finger on the gum until it blanches, release, and count how long the pink takes to come back — normally under two seconds. Pale, white, blue, grey or brick-red gums, or a slow refill, are all urgent. Practise on a healthy animal so you know what normal looks like for yours.

Know how to apply pressure to a bleeding wound: a clean pad, firm direct pressure, and do not keep lifting it to look. If it soaks through, add another layer on top rather than removing the first.

A pet first aid course, in person, is worth a Saturday if you have an adventurous dog or you are far from a clinic. The Red Cross and others run them.

The unglamorous ones.

Microchip registration current, in your name, with a number that works. That is the single highest-value ten minutes in this whole article.

Know your animal's normal: resting breathing rate, what their gums look like, what they weigh. You cannot recognise a change from normal if you have never looked at normal.

And keep a written list, on paper, of medications and doses. Phones run out of battery in exactly the circumstances where this matters.
